In the past few years, researchers have achieved notable advancements in reinforcement learning for locomotion, primarily on bipedal robots. Despite quadrupedal robots being more common and versatile, they had largely been overlooked in RL studies. This paper proposes the Evolutionary Pathway Creator (EPC), a novel multi-objective reinforcement learning method that addresses key challenges in quadrupedal locomotion. Firstly, EPC decouples state and action representations to facilitate the learning of meaningful state features and action policies. Secondly, EPC optimizes diverse gaits in the action-space, allowing for the creation of multiple stable pathways. This is in contrast to existing RL approaches for quadrupedal robots that often overly rely on a single optimal gait. Thirdly, EPC's framework is generally applicable and simple to implement, as demonstrated by its successful application on a quadrupedal robot model and a real Jackal robot, across various environments and scenarios. Experimental results show that EPC surpasses existing RL baselines in learning more versatile gaits. Additionally, the method is demonstrated to great effect in a challenging terrain navigation task. This research showcases that EPC can be an effective tool in a broad range of complex quadrupedal locomotion tasks. Its public code is available for others to build upon at https://github.com/robotx/EPC. Additionally, the related dataset can be accessed at https://robotx.github.io/EPC. This research would be presented at IEEE ICRA 2023. Key parts of the paper have been previously showcased at RobotX 2022 and ARX 2022 conferences. Data shows that the jet has two distinct states: a strong, high-energy state and a softer, more widespread low-energy state. Research reveals that the transition between these states occurs when the distance from the jet's point of origin exceeds 20 kiloparsecs. This phenomenon is similar to the "breeze and storm" model first proposed for radio jets, suggesting that powerful episodes occur less frequently than initially thought, leading to power dissipation within the jet and resulting in a persistent, gentle energy release. Our observations confirm this gentle energy release, and for the first time, we attribute the low-energy state observed in NGC 7213's jet to a warm (at a temperature of around 0.30 keV) component providing most of the observed emission within the innermost region of the jet. This component accounts for 85 percent of observed emission within the innermost region of the jet. Data also shows that the size of the hot emission region decreases as the jet's power increases. This evidence supports the "breeze and storm" model and suggests that a warm emission, gentle energy release, is a necessary component of this theory, and it can be observed in various jet types including radio, X-ray, and gamma-ray jets. Additionally, the low-energy state observed in NGC 7213's jet indicates that the outer regions of the jet contain a large amount of stored energy which could be released in a subsequent powerful episode. This stored energy would result in a much brighter high-energy state if released. This research proposes an approach for switching between different operating points in nonlinear systems using a model-free reinforcement learning technique. Due to limitations in reinforcement learning algorithms for targeting specific points, we divide the task into reaching a intermediate 'hyperbolic' trajectory from the current state, and then moving to the target operating point along this trajectory. Model predictive control models are initially used to define the hyperbolic trajectory and optimal switching paths. A model-free actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithm is then applied to find the optimal paths without requiring a system model, and these paths are connected by MPC models to ensure smooth transitions. Model-free reconfiguration of nonlinear systems via reinforcement learning has previously been challenging Owley et al. (2018), but this approach allows for efficient model-free reconfiguration. When applying this strategy to a pilot-plant example, it took around ten minutes to learn the policy using a standard CPU. The results show that the model-free reconfiguration algorithm is comparable in terms of performance to an optimal linear controller, and even outperforms it in some cases in terms of switching times. Furthermore, the model-free reconfiguration algorithm is robust to hyperbolic trajectory deviations, and can be adapted for systems with input constraints. Future work will involve scaling up this approach to target multiple operating points. Preliminary results indicate that this approach can be scaled up using the concepts of macro-states. In fact, the model-free reconfiguration algorithm has the potential to be a model-free version of the macro-state approach. When we combined our model-free reconfiguration algorithm with the macro-state concept, the results show that the model-free reconfiguration algorithm is robust to changes in scale. In other words, once the model-free reconfiguration algorithm has been developed, it can be applied to systems of any scale without requiring additional adjustments. This is an important property because it means that the model-free reconfiguration algorithm can be generalized to a wide range of systems. When we applied our model-free reconfiguration algorithm to a system with input constraints, the results show that it takes around ten minutes to learn the policy using a standard CPU. The model-free reconfiguration algorithm uses MPC models to ensure that the system remains within operational limits, and connects these models through model-free reinforcement learning. As a result, the model-free reconfiguration algorithm is capable of solving complex control problems, and can be generalized to a wide range of systems. In conclusion, our model-free reconfiguration algorithm allows for efficient model-free reconfiguration, and has a range of desirable properties, including robustness, generalizability, and efficiency

The data, however, comes with built-in challenges: it's inherently noisy, has a high degree of spatial correlation, and often needs to be analyzed in a specific spatial context. Current deep learning methods typically address these issues by employing large models that require extensive training data, making them impractical for monitoring applications. Our research presents a new family of deep learning networks, EarhtNets, designed to monitor the Earth's condition, and we demonstrate their effectiveness over traditional methods on a forest change detection dataset. We also showcase the capabilities of these networks in a practical forester scenario, using a dataset of 30-meter resolution satellite images collected over the state of Pará in Brazil. The results reveal that EarthNets enable us to detect forest changes more accurately while reducing the required training data, and foresters can use them to determine the health of specific areas. Although numerous studies have been conducted on this topic, a comprehensive and systematic investigation of the renormalization group within the context of active nematics is yet to be undertaken. In this research, we undertake a thorough examination of the nonlinear fluid dynamics model governing active nematics using the renormalization group technique in a vibrantly dynamic context. Our study reveals the details of various terms in the model and provides a precise calculation of their contributions, marked by specific symbols, as well as the associated flow equations. Our findings show that the nonlinear terms in the model exhibit a remarkable similarity with the Carr-H Hopf model widely applied in biological and physical phenomena. Upon applying renormalization group techniques to these similar terms, we discover that the nonlinear constants governing active nematics are subject to a specific set of constraints. These constraints hint at a critical relationship between the b and c constants, prompting us to explore this relationship further in the vicinity of the nematic to liquid crystal phase transition. In this transition phase, we observe the emergence of a new parameter, p, associated with a specific scaling exponent, which leads to a deeper understanding of the active nematic model. Through this research, we hope to contribute to a more vibrant and dynamic understanding of active nematics using the renormalization group technique. In the course of this investigation, we encounter a challenge related to the computation of the active nematic model, specifically its fourth-order term. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the active nematic model's fourth-order term in terms of nematic-specific variables, b and c. In this research, we present ReAD, a framework focused on identifying unusual driving behaviors. Compared to existing anomaly detection methods, ReAD accurately identifies all standard and unusual driving behaviors. Artificial intelligence's primary goal is to process code, but current methods are limited to specific paradigms like recursion and tree structures, assuming code's hierarchical nature is sufficient to support its complexity. However, code also contains sequential aspects, such as imports, comments, and nested functions with diverse logic paradigms. To effectively comprehend code, a more universal and embodied representation is essential, one that incorporates various Embodied Reinforcement Learning paradigms to tackle the multiple challenges code poses. By recognizing the failures of current hierarchical approaches and identifying key code features, a novel and embodied architecture is introduced to address code's inherent complexity. The proposed Embodied Reinforcement Learning architecture can be applied to a range of tasks, such as code generation, summarization, and bug detection, to name a few. To validate the new architecture, experiments on code generation as natural language are conducted and yield impressive results, outperforming state-of-the-art models significantly. Additionally, the accompanying library, CodeEmbodiment, is offered to facilitate future research and development. It encompasses the architecture's implementation, along with pre-trained models, experimental data, and an interactive code embedding visualizer. In contrast to traditional hierarchical methods, the proposed Embodied Reinforcement Learning architecture represents code as a sequence of meaningful units, leveraging the recurrent connections between adjacent blocks to capture code's memory and nested dependencies. It embeds each block using a multi-paradigmatic Unifier Embedding that combines recursion, tree structure, and sequence-based Embodiment, preserving key code features. To address multiple bug types, a multi-task approach is employed, where various Embodied Reinforcement Learning tasks are defined to extract critical code features. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this architecture, a comprehensive evaluation is conducted using 190 diverse code benchmarks from six programming paradigms and languages. It compares the proposed Embodied Reinforcement Learning architecture with 23 state-of-the-art hierarchical methods and yields remarkable results, solving over 90% of code generation tasks as natural language, while also surpassing or matching the performance of these hierarchical methods in bug detection, code generation, entity extraction, semantic parsing, semantically similar code generation, and summarization. We conducted a study using data from the ATLAS$^{\rm 3D}$ and SAMI galaxies, which allowed us to examine the relationship between a galaxy's effective radius and its star formation efficiency, and how this changes over time as a galaxy evolves. We found a significant correlation between a galaxy's effective radius and its specific star formation rate, with larger galaxies having higher star formation efficiency. This correlation was present at all stages of galaxy evolution and did not depend on a galaxy's mass in stars. This suggests that a galaxy's rate of star formation is linked to its size, with larger galaxies forming stars at a higher rate. We also found that galaxies with higher star formation efficiency are typically found within less massive haloes, with stronger gravitational potential, and are predominantly early-type galaxies. In contrast, galaxies with low star formation efficiency are found in a variety of halo environments and are predominantly late-type galaxies. We explored various theoretical models that could explain this connection, including one which proposes that a galaxy's size is linked to its angular momentum, with larger galaxies experiencing more collisions that deliver angular momentum, resulting in higher star formation efficiency. We found that this model can reproduce the observed relationship between a galaxy's size and star formation efficiency, although further refinement is needed to fully explain the data. Overall, our research reveals a dynamic pattern in which a galaxy's size influences its star formation efficiency, with larger galaxies forming stars at a higher rate, and ultimately determines the efficiency of star formation. In contrast, a galaxy's mass has little effect on its star formation efficiency, with the exception of very low mass galaxies. This challenges current models of galaxy evolution, with further research needed to fully explain the observed relationship between a galaxy's size and star formation efficiency. This model predicts a star formation efficiency that varies depending on a galaxy's mass, with larger galaxies having higher star formation efficiency, and a star formation efficiency that increases over time as a galaxy evolves. To address this limitation, we introduce a new approach, combining attribute-based design synthesis with neural network optimization, to yield meaningful and relevant designs. By training a neural network to produce valid designs in a design space, our method involves a forward search that utilizes the network's predictions to generate designs based on their fitness relative to a desired specification. A demonstration in the synthesis of acoustic systems reveals that this approach can lead to designs of equal effectiveness to those produced through human expertise, while providing actionable insights into the design process. Additionally, we showcase the method's capacity for incorporating user preferences into the design using multi-objective optimization, enabling designers to select desirable outcomes. To facilitate the development of this method and ensure its transparency, we make available a wide range of design search tools, including a Python library, interactive design visualization, and pre-configured open-source design synthesis problems. Furthermore, we outline the design of an online interface where designers can upload their own synthesis problems and employ our method's tools to discover novel designs. Through this contribution, we aim to establish a framework for neural network-guided design synthesis and encourage the exploration of this method in various engineering domains. Labeling data for machine learning models can be costly, especially when data is dispersed across many users. Federated Extraction addresses this challenge by enabling multiple users to collaborate on data annotation, leveraging their collective talents to create valuable training data while maintaining each user's sensitive information by only sharing annotations, rather than the actual data. Despite this framework's potential, it has several drawbacks: primarily the requirement for users to actively participate in annotation tasks, and the necessity for users to be present when others are annotating, in order to incorporate new labels into the training process. To overcome these limitations, we introduce FE-DYNO, an innovative system within the Federated Extraction framework, which allows users to pre-define detection criteria which automatically trigger the extraction of relevant data when certain conditions are met. By introducing this system, we overcome the issues of user engagement and availability, while also allowing multiple users to collaborate more efficiently. To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted several experiments and observed a notable reduction in communication requirements. Specifically, FE-DYNO achieves a notable compression of the shared data by a factor of 21.13 with respect to other Federated Extraction approaches. Additionally to our system's evaluation, we also analyzed and discussed various important ethical considerations which should be taken into account when designing such kind of collaborative data annotation frameworks. Our results show that by incorporating FE-DYNO, researchers can obtain high-quality training data while minimizing the required communications, thus being suitable for a wide range of machine learning applications. Moreover, by following our proposed guidelines, developers can create valuable and sustainable training data collaboratively. Our code for this system is publicly available.

Initially, we establish a general stability result for linear evolution equations in a star graph. Then, we derive an $L^2$-stability result for the specific case of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation in a star graph. Next, we establish a stronger type of stability, known as exponential stability in a particular $L^2$-norm specific to the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation in a star graph with uniformly distributed weights. Finally, we present a numerical example to verify our theoretical findings. Unlike existing stability studies for the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation, which primarily focus on linearly structured graphs, our work uniquely considers a star graph. As a result, we encounter distinct challenges and complexities, such as dealing with uneven connections between nodes in the star graph. Additionally, we prove a sharp exponent for the $L^2$-stability of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation in a star graph with uniformly distributed weights. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first theoretical study on the stability of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation in a star graph. Notably, PIULA's application extends beyond multi-goal optimization tasks to a range of real-world problems, showcasing its potential for practical use in a diverse set of problems. We provide thorough experimental validation of PIULA's effectiveness, highlighting its potential as a reliable tool in a wide range of optimization tasks. Further details are available in a research article published in Evolutionary Computation, where PIULA's proposed methodology is extensively discussed. The article also addresses related research, including evolutionary optimization, multi-goal optimization, and utility learning, providing a comprehensive literary review. The source code for PIULA is freely available on GitHub, enabling users to replicate the results presented in this study. Reinforcement learning agents can be vulnerable to attacks that exploit their exploration strategies, particularly when they rely on uncertainty estimates. In response to this threat, our research introduces a novel technique called Temporal Insight Estimator (TIE) to facilitate a range of attacks on RL agents without requiring access to their source code or internal workings. Unlike conventional approaches that require direct access to the agent for optimization, TIE-enabled attacks only need historical agent data, making them more practical and scalable. Building on TIE, we have adapted it to support various RL algorithms, including Monte Carlo, tree search methods, and deep reinforcement learning models. Our proposed attack method, called Temporal Exploitation Attack (TEA), can significantly lower an RL agent's performance by around 30-40% when aiming to converge quickly, and up to 50% when prioritizing swift optimization. TEA can also be tailored to compromise an RL agent at specific stages of training, with consequences proportional to the training duration. In order to validate the effectiveness of our approach, we have successfully implemented and tested TEA against multiple reinforcement learning algorithms in both static contexts, such as grid worlds, and dynamic environments, like robotic manipulation simulations. This novel attack presents an opportunity for future improvement in the reinforcement learning field, prompting the development of more resilient methods against attacks like the one described. Our investigation focuses on a 2D non-symmorphic wallpaper lattice with tunable Dirac locations. The desired property of hosting Dirac electrons can be achieved by controlling both the Poyling force and an artificial gauge field within the lattice. Additionally, we explore the dynamic behavior resulting from these two fields and discover that it resembles a 2D topological Hall effect, with its curvature and chiral magnetic effects adjustable via the artificial gauge field. Notably, when the Poyling force prevails, it induces a 2D quantum spin Hall effect characterized by edge states controlled by the frequency. Lastly, we investigate the dynamic response under concurrent exposure to both fields and find that it hosts a 2D Weyl semimetal state, both of whose carrier densities as well as the Weyl points' curvatures can be controlled. Ultimately, our findings suggest the potential for these materials to be used in highly flexible, Dirac-based quantum devices due to the inherent tunability of their properties at various levels.

In the realm of reinforcement learning, our research focuses on an adaptive setting where an agent and a controller interact through a reward system. The controller's motivation is to minimize the long-term cumulative disappointment experienced by the agent. We investigate an adaptive game where the controller's objective is to minimize the agent's long-term cumulative disappointment. The key characteristics of this reward system are non-stationarity and masking of the underlying environment dynamics by the controller's initial negative experience. Building upon this understanding, we break down our approach into three interconnected components. Firstly, we establish a dynamic protocol to manage the controller's resentment towards specific actions in the environment. This protocol ensures that the controller's disappointment adheres to a specific bound in relation to the environment's non-stationary changes and the variance in the environment's dynamics. The second part of our approach involves identifying the underlying environment dynamics based on the controller's resentment management. Finally, we demonstrate that the controller can design a policy that separates the agent's disappointment into distinct components, thereby facilitating the identification of the underlying environment dynamics. We show that our proposed dynamic protocol is universally applicable and provide an in-depth analysis of the identified environment dynamics. Furthermore, we establish that our separation design is compatible with existing risk-averse reinforcement learning methods. Notably, the controller can leverage an adaptive version of the entropy minimization method to identify the underlying environment dynamics and develop a resentment management policy. We illustrate the effectiveness of our approach using a grid-world environment featuring a dynamic non-stationary reward system. Experimental results show that our proposed dynamic protocol and the associated reinforcement learning algorithms are highly robust and adaptable in a variety of changing environments. A compact representation of MacNeille completions for free monoids is established, with an analysis of when the completion results in a Stone space.  Symbolic expressions are used to represent equivalence classes in the monoid's MacNeille completion, with an associated ordering.  By demonstrating that ordered symbolic expressions form a complete lattice under this ordering, the paper shows these expressions are isomorphic to a completed quotient of the first-order logic lattice for the monoid's sentences.  Additionally, the paper identifies when this completion is a Stone space, offering a corresponding characterization for sentences with quantifier elimination.  These results are illustrated with examples. 

For a first-order theory with quantifier elimination, its free reduct and MacNeille completions are equivalent to those of its second-order counterpart.  The paper confirms this equivalence for monoids and trees, providing new decision methods for identifiability in these structures.  Specifically, it decides identifiability for finite trees and monoids within a finite set, with implications extending to other structures. 

The analysis of the MacNeille completion of a monoid's language also yields insight into the compactness theorem, allowing a decision method for infinite sets of sentences with model completion.  The paper further generalizes its findings to semigroups with cancellation. 

The paper's main method involves a new order on symbolic expressions and their associated trees, enabling it to bypass the traditional technical hurdles in completion theory.  By analyzing the orders on trees, the paper derives key properties of these structures, including a characterization of when non-terminating sequences of steps in model expansion lead to terminating sequences.  With a separate combinatorial approach, the paper confirms a long-standing conjecture of Büchi, demonstrating that a finite tree can identify a monoid or $\omega$-automaton. 

The analysis of orders on trees also allows a dynamic characterization of equivalence classes in the MacNeille completion of a monoid.  By examining the behavior of sequences corresponding to model expansion steps, the paper identifies a decision method for identifying whether a given monoid or $\omega$-automaton can be distinguished from all others.  Specifically, the paper determines if a given monoid or $\omega$-automaton is identifiable from all others, and offers a related decision for trees. 

The paper's results have been verified using the Coq proof assistant. 
The associated code is available at https://git.io/IdEnt.

High-quality audio recordings are prone to damage from environmental factors like background noise. Current pre-processing techniques can improve this issue, but they often rely on supplementary data, like clean examples, which can be difficult and expensive to obtain. Alternatively, transmission conditions can vary greatly even in the same recording, making it challenging to apply standard pre-processing methods. This paper explores a new method called immediate transcription, where audio is transcribed simultaneously in the time domain to mitigate noise immediately after recording. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a specific use case – capturing dual-patient respiratory sounds remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our experiments show that, unlike traditional transcription methods, immediate transcription allows us to capture respiratory sounds from a separate room through microphone recordings in a hospital ward, demonstrating its potential to improve remote health Diagnostics. Additionally, the approach enables the creation of dynamic weight adjustments for data augmentation, enhancing the model's robustness to background noises. This solution provides a simple and efficient means to capture audio data under varying environmental conditions, yielding high-quality recordings despite significant background noise. extending the idea of a Riemannian manifold's spectral dimension. 
This parameter has significant implications in predicting a graph's 
topological properties. Researchers have explored the relationship between 
this dimension and the Ahlfors-regular conformal measure on infinite graphs.
This brief survey summarizes existing findings and highlights open issues.

on graphs lacking a clear metric structure. This approach relies on a

We investigate the conditions under which the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing procedure yields a physical solution for a vector of values, and introduce a regularization method to ensure the procedure's feasibility in cases where the expected number of solutions exceeds one. The regularization introduces an undetermined parameter, $\lambda$, which can be determined through additional constraints, including a minimum increase in data points. The impact of $\lambda$ on the results is studied, and a method for selecting an optimal point in parameter space is developed. The analysis is supported by a comprehensive dataset containing 12500 points in the $\eta$-$\eta'$ plane, which is used to demonstrate the procedure's applicability to previously unexplored regions. The associated errors in measurements are investigated, and a method for propagating these errors to the final points is presented. The work presented here represents the first examination of the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing procedure employing a modern, extensive dataset. The study reveals the presence of two solutions corresponding to the $a_1$ particle's coupling with the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ particles, which is in line with expectations generated through different approaches to the procedure. One of the solutions is consistent across various datasets, while the other varies depending on the dataset, and further experimental data is required to clarify the situation. The main advantage of our method in addressing the mixing procedure's physical aspects lies in its simplicity and lack of reliance on theoretical assumptions beyond the context of the procedure itself. The study provides insights into the process's physics, and presents a perspective on the procedure as a purely experimental tool. The work presented here is a precursor to a follow-up study focusing on the procedure's theoretical aspects. This paper addresses four key objectives in the domain of signature-based biometrics, namely ensuring uniqueness, measuring intricacy, assessing consistency, and comparing different biometric models. We developed a comprehensive framework for estimating uniqueness by integrating statistical patterns into an entropy measure. This approach offers a more accurate understanding of uniqueness, as it takes into account not only inter-individual variations but also intra-individual fluctuations. This method can be applied to various feature extraction methods, enabling a thorough comparison of their uniqueness properties. Moreover, we proposed a novel metric for evaluating the intricacy of signatures by analyzing their structural components through the lens of fractal theory. This metric enables precise detection of intricate patterns within signatures. Additionally, we investigated the consistency of online signature verification, examining both intra-individual and inter-individual fluctuations. Our analysis provided a detailed understanding of consistency in different feature extraction methods. Lastly, we conducted an in-depth comparison of different feature extraction methods for unique identification purposes, considering both mathematical and practical perspectives. Our results demonstrate that the optimal feature extraction method depends on the specific application requirements, leading to distinct model selections for uniqueness and intricacy assessment. Graph depiction learning holds significant potential across various domains, 
enabling the conversion of complex graph representations into visually appealing 
images, which in turn facilitate human understanding. In biomedicine, graph 
depiction has applications such as graph visualization and the creation of 
synthetic graph images for medical representation learning purposes. The graph 
depiction problem can be framed as a conditional generative adversarial network 
(GAN) model, where the graph structure serves as input to the generator, 
enabling diverse image outputs based on varying graph configurations. Due to 
the diverse nature of biomedical graphs across different domains, developing 
a universal graph depiction model remains challenging. In this study, we leverage 
the recent advancements in graph representation learning to convert graphs into 
fixed-dimensional vectors, which can then be utilized as input to a graph 
depiction model. Furthermore, we introduce the bio-medical graph depiction 
benchmark (BGRB), comprising over 35,000 graph instances from various biomedical 
domains, along with corresponding annotations and assessments by biomedical 
experts. The proposed approach supports both unsupervised and supervised 
learning configurations, and our experimental results on the BGRB benchmark 
demonstrate the efficacy of our method in producing high-quality graph depictions, 
surpassing competing benchmarks and unsupervised graph depiction models. 
Notably, our best performing model achieves an 82% preference rate among 
biomedical experts. The BGRB benchmark and the corresponding code are 
publicly available at the specified link.

A generalized framework for field theories is established, applicable to both bosonic and fermionic fields, through derivation of Euler-Arnold equations for field-based momentum densities. This approach is versatile and covers various geometric field theories, as well as traditional Yang-Mills and General Relativity with sources. We demonstrate that the complexity of these theories can be quantified by evaluating higher-order corrections in 1/dimension. Specifically, for Yang-Mills geometry, these corrections correspond to helicities in gauge theories and topological invariants in bosonic fields. The proposed method is utilized to analyze geometric field theories in 2 and 3 dimensions. As an example, we show that the Wess-Zumino-Witten term's contribution to helicity can be obtained through our framework. Furthermore, this method's applications are also discussed for theories without local symmetries, such as gravity in 2D and Polyakov's theory, as well as theories involving fermions, such as semion and boson models. By employing our method, we successfully derive the classical effective action for these theories, up to the fourth order in 2D and second order in 3D. Lastly, the geometric field theory framework is used to investigate theories with both bosonic and fermionic components, such as the semion boson model, and this approach is generalized to theories with both non-Abelian and Abelian symmetries. The results of our calculations are compared with existing literature and found to be in line with previously published findings. Lastly, we conclude by outlining future areas of research where our geometric field theory framework can be utilized. Additionally, we provide a supplementary document containing a step-by-step derivation of the classical effective action for Yang-Mills gravity with sources in 3D. This document also explores other potential research directions using our generalized approach. Moreover, we discuss how our method can be applied to various theories with both bosonic and fermionic components in both 2 and 3 dimensions. Finally, we revisit our geometric field theory framework and clarify a particular calculation in the classical effective action for Yang-Mills gravity with sources in 3D. This approach also enables us to derive additional terms in the effective action for this specific case. This correction does not affect the existing literature but does provide further insight into the geometric field theory framework's capabilities. Consequently, this paper is rewritten with the inclusion of these corrections. Additionally, we provide a public code repository containing the used code, including the 2D and 3D point clouds for the classical effective action

which can be optimized using least squares for parameter estimation. 
The conventional reprojection error, however, is an asynchronous loss function 
that does not guarantee convergence. 
This work proposes the use of complete least squares (CLS) for ideal pose estimation, 
which offers a more robust optimization framework than traditional least squares (LS). 
The CLS framework synchronizes the reprojection error for each viewpoint 
by incorporating unknown image positions as optimization variables. 
The key benefit of CLS is its ability to resolve degenerate cases 
where LS fails due to non-positive definiteness. 
The proposed CLS method is evaluated in terms of resolution and reliability 
for single and multi-view pose estimation scenarios, 
which are further integrated into a comprehensive 3D reconstruction framework. 
The code is publicly accessible on the GitHub platform. 
Experiments demonstrate the superiority of CLS over the conventional LS method. 
This research sets a new standard for 3D reconstruction accuracy with respect to resolution. 
Specifically, CLS achieves superior performance in terms of inlier percentage, 
reconstruction distance, and Cameron-Bruce distance. 
The proposed framework is a versatile system that can be applied to 3D reconstruction 
as well as 6 DoF camera pose estimation and other related tasks. 
The research paves the way for further innovation in these areas.

Further analysis revealed that incorporating an inhomogeneous distortion improves the fit, suggesting that the model may need to account for this distortion to accurately represent the universe's structure. Consequently, the results suggest that while some data support the Lambda-CDM model, other data indicate a more complex and distorted structure of the universe. Therefore, the model should be refined to incorporate this distortion. The occurrence of localized moments in disordered one-dimensional Hubbard chains
is investigated and compared to the insulating phase of the Hubbard model when
interactions are strong. We observe that the phase transition from a metallic to an
insulating state can't be reached thermally. Instead, localized moments as seen at
low temperatures result from the repulsive electron interactions and are influenced by
the disorder intensity and chain length. The nature of the resulting many-body state
is examined through the ratio of spin susceptibility to specific heat, which shows a
marked discrepancy from non-interacting scenarios where this ratio increases with
disorder. Consequently, we propose that the insulating state characteristic of
localization should not be referred to as a random singlet. Rather, it represents a
more robust form of localization that resists magnetic ordering due to the presence
of correlated interactions. Local moment characteristics, including magnitude,
distribution, and direction, are examined through the self-consistent Born approach and
shown to be heavily influenced by the strength of electron interactions. Specifically,
we find that increasing interactions weakens the influence of disorder and produce
localized moments with a preferred direction, paving the way for experimental
investigation using techniques like nuclear magnetic resonance or muon spin
resonance spectroscopy. Finally, we observe that the insulating phase's magnetic
entropy can be partially compensated by applying a small external magnetic field. 
The application of magnetic field causes a transition to a partially polarized and
pinned state characterized by slower spin decoherence due to localization and
interaction effects. Overall, we provide a comprehensive description of one-dimensional
localization theory, addressing long-standing misconceptions along the way. 
Lastly, we suggest a possible pathway to achieve and study a local singlet state in
one-dimensional systems that exhibit weak antiferromagnetic bonding between
containing impurities. Although not realized in this work, achieving such a local
singlet state could offer valuable opportunities for exploring three-dimensional
topological phases when the insulating phase's geometry is contiguously connected.

A significant concept in Artin Groups involves the foundation set, a subset of reflections responsible for generating the Coxeter graph's foundation chamber when combined with inverse operations. Theorem 1.1 establishes the existence of a foundation set in Type B Coxeter groups, expanding on earlier work by Mathieu [Math] which only guaranteed its existence when the graph's foundation chamber could be reached by reflecting a maximal Coxeter element. The proof involves a geometric analysis of the order of reflections within the 2-sphere's points, also including a demonstration that this order is always an arithmetic sequence with a common difference of 2. Additionally, the theorem has implications that extend beyond Artin Groups, influencing a broader class of groups known as finite real reflection groups, leading to a correlation between the foundation set and the set of reflections based on odd-order elements. This results in a number of useful consequences, including a characterization of the foundation set in terms of a reflection symmetry group and a method for determining if a given reflection is part of a Coxeter element's foundation chamber. Furthermore, the Combinatorial Length Problem in Coxeter Groups, initially proposed by Jean-Christophemez in 2005, is resolved for the finite real reflection groups, determining the length of elements based on reflections. This Combinatorial Length is shown to be an arithmetic sequence with a common difference of 2. When the foundation set's length is 2, it is proven that its elements are always rank 2 reflections; on the other hand, when the foundation set's length is greater than 2, it is proven that its elements are always rank 1 reflections, specifically wrapping up the classification of finite real reflection groups. Finally, the foundation set in Type B Coxeter groups is shown to be related to a group of rank 1 inversions, a relationship which was initially proposed by Knutson and Miller in 2005. This relationship is confirmed, leading to a correction of their initial hypothesis which suggested that the foundation set would always be related to a group of rank 2 inversions if the foundation set's length is 2. Instead, it is proven that the foundation set's elements will always reflect a symmetry that can be represented geometrically within the 2-sphere's points. This study investigates the potential of a deep reinforcement learning framework with a hierarchical structure, comprising two layers of control systems, to address complex control problems that pose a challenge to traditional deep reinforcement learning approaches. The model architecture is grounded in theoretical findings from the literature on adaptive dynamic programming. By breaking down a difficult control problem into two components, the framework enables more efficient learning processes for each sub-system through the application of targeted policy functions. This research employs a model that incorporates feedback from dark matter cooling to explain the formation of (super)massive dark matter objects, and applies it to a universe filled with dark matter. To gain deeper insight into the behavior of highly correlated electrons in materials, researchers use a complex technique called inelastic neutron scattering (IENS). However, the extensive data generated by IENS is difficult to analyze and often overwhelming, requiring specialists to interpret the results. A promising approach involves using artificial neural networks (ANNs) to make IENS data analysis more accessible to a broader group of people. Yet, the reliability and transparency of ANN predictions in this field are largely untested. In this study, we develop and refine a type of ANN called an adjusted neural network (ANN2), which provides transparent and reliable predictions for IENS data. By adjusting key parameters, we optimize the performance of ANN2 for a specific task and verify its effectiveness through rigorous testing. Furthermore, results show that ANN2 surpasses traditional methods in both qualitative and quantitative assessments. Examples from a model electronic structure and from real-world data on the superconductor La$_2CuO$_4 show that ANN2 makes complex IENS data more understandable to humans. In summary, ANN2 offers a highly effective solution for interpreting IENS data, thus facilitating its use in making data-driven decisions in the investigation of electronic behavior in materials. Utilizing ANN2, researchers can extract crucial insights from IENS experiments even with limited available data, thereby expanding the range of applications for IENS in studying highly correlated electronic systems. With this approach, ANN2 opens up new opportunities for its siblings in the fields of condensed matter research, potentially enabling more widespread adoption of machine learning techniques in these fields. Ann2 is now freely accessible as an open-source software through GitHub at the link provided below. GitHub: https://github.com/SPS-UVA/ANN2\_GitHub/tree/ghpd/Master\_Repository. This platform gives users the opportunity to contribute to, download, and disseminate Ann2 for making IENS data analysis more accessible to a broader group of people. Users can modify and enhance Ann2 by visiting its repository at the link provided above and adding their own code. This will facilitate the evolution of Ann2, making it an even more powerful tool in the investigation of electronic behavior in materials. Ann2's capabilities can be expanded to cover a broad range of machine learning applications in condensed matter research, and we hope that this work will inspire other machine learning methods to be used in making data-driven decisions in this field. High-entropy alloys (HEAs), characterized by equally proportioned principal elements and random atomic arrangements, have unique material properties not found in conventional alloys. Despite recent breakthroughs in materials science, predicting their behavior remains a significant challenge, mainly due to their complex atomic relationships and limited understanding of their collective properties. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) has accelerated HEA research, enabling faster and more accurate predictions of their properties. However, the complexity of HEA phase diagrams, atomic structures, and property patterns demands more sophisticated models that can learn from available data and generate missing information. This article reviews the current state of AI- and ML-based approaches for predicting HEA properties, highlighting their limitations and future research opportunities. Additionally, it discusses the necessary advancements for AI to reach a semi-autonomous or fully autonomous state, enabling the direct design of materials with optimal performance. The potential applications of these breakthroughs are also considered. Achieving this goal will not only solidify ML's role in materials science but also pave the way for a more general and widespread application of this technology. Ultimately, this will enable researchers to design and discover novel materials with the most up-to-date and accurate predictions available. In the near future, AI is expected to shift from predictive to prescriptive, allowing it to identify unknown property patterns and suggest new material combinations with the potential to surpass current technological limits. This paradigm shift will significantly contribute to the development of revolutionary materials capable of transforming modern industry and technology. In the long term, AI will evolve into a collaborative tool, assisting human researchers in identifying promising materials to test and providing essential insights into their properties and performance during the experimentation process. This symbiotic relationship between AI and human materials scientists is essential for developing ground-breaking materials that can change the course of technological history. With ongoing advancements in data collection, AI development, and computational power, the future of ML-driven HEA research appears highly optimistic. This promising future is expected to materialize when more detailed atomic-scale data becomes widely available, enabling the direct design of materials with optimal performance. However, uniform sampling can be inefficient due to the excessive generation of non-useful binary vectors. To optimize pixel mapping, a novel sampling method for binary arrays with a constant margin is proposed. The method is based on a metric that assesses the similarity between binary vectors. Similarity measurement leads to a graph representation where binary array vectors are connected to form clusters. By targeting the densest of these clusters, the sampling process can be accelerated. An efficient algorithm for selecting the most representative binary array vectors has been developed, along with a method for determining the optimal sampling rate. The proposed technique demonstrates improved efficiency over traditional uniform sampling methods. For instance, the densest clustering approach can reduce the number of binary array vectors by up to 90% compared to uniform sampling, while achieving comparable generalization performance. A comprehensive implementation of this method is available on GitHub. It has been validated that the technique performs equally well to traditional uniform sampling methods in various numerical test cases. Specifically, it achieved a 90% reduction in binary array vectors when sampling at a rate of 10% using the metric-based clustering approach. The associated reduction in memory usage was also demonstrated. Additionally, the technique's dependency on the binary array's topology and structure was characterized, with the finding that similar methods can be employed for other constant margin binary array designs. The parametric sowing technique is a potent tool for constructing multiple mode-
spectrum within a microresonator via a single pump photon energy. This method
enables the creation of an optical frequency comb with high mode purity by
generating a fundamental mode family and then injecting a parametric driver to
activate higher order modes at evenly spaced intervals. By applying sowing to
temperature-control microresonators, we achieve high purity (greater than 85%)
combs with up to 16 mode families spanning an 80THz range. To characterize the
microresonator's properties, we analyze the comb's structure and identify the
Schwinger phase associated with the intracavity field. Utilizing sowing to excite
multiple mode families simultaneously, we demonstrate the capability to measure
microresonator effective length, twist angle, and refractive index. This method
also allows for the exploration of non-Kerr photonic materials through optical
frequency combs with up to 16 copies of the optical spectrum. The parametric sowing
approach provides a new, efficient strategy for constructing microresonator-based
optical frequency combs and enables unique applications for microresonator
characterization and exploring new photonic materials. \textbf{Editor's note: This

We've explored the generalization of Fefferman-Graham expansion for extreme surfaces in AdS$_{d+1}$ spacetime. Our analysis shows that the near-extreme surface behaves like a conformal manifold in d-dimensional spacetime, with the near-extreme surface expansion taking a form similar to the FG expansion. This conformal series allows for a structured breakdown of the holographic entropy bound based on the number of relevant coordinates. This structured bound is similar to the one observed in quantum critical points in conformal field theories. Additionally, our near-extreme surface expansion helps clarify the relationship between the bulk geometry and surface energy-momentum tensor. This connection may provide valuable insights for measuring bulk fields in holographic duals. Finally, our near-extreme surface expansion facilitates a precise computation of entanglement entropy across extreme surfaces, with this approach giving rise to distinct entanglement entropy terms. A comprehensive study is conducted to examine how intersection multipliers emerge in the context of solvable lattice models, particularly those with a combinatorial foundation. Using the examples of the dimer, monomer, and polymer models, this research demonstrates the relationship between intersection multipliers and factors derived from bond correlation functions that are measurable on the grid. Furthermore, the investigation derives exact expressions for the intersection multipliers of both the dimer and monomer models. In contrast, the polymer model yields an expression with a complex mathematical representation. This study also applies the principles of intersection multipliers to analyze the properties of loop-weight distributions in lattice models. By applying these principles, this research is able to derive a precise formula for the loop-weight distribution in the dimer model. Similarly, the investigation provides an accurate expression for the weighted polymers' distribution. Notably, the derived expressions exhibit a transition from a discrete to a continuous form as the parameter in question approaches either zero or infinity. Ultimately, this study verifies that the intersection multipliers of the monomer model can be expressed as a specific combination of the bond correlation functions, thereby validating the model's consistency. A comparative analysis is also conducted with the intersection multipliers of the free fermion model, which is known to be equivalent to the monomer model. As a result of this comparison, this research is able to reveal a striking similarity between the two systems' underlying structures. A conceptual diagram is included to illustrate this connection, which sheds new light on the previously mysterious intersection multipliers of the free fermion model. Additionally, this study proposes an innovative, non-traditional method for measuring the bond correlation functions of the free fermion model using the principles of the intersection multipliers. As a further contribution, this research is able to offer an original, comprehensive explanation for the system's known non-local properties. By extending its scope, this study is also able to examine the properties of the intersection multipliers in the context of the Bose-Einstein condensate. As a result of this examination, this research is able to derive an accurate expression for the condensate density. Moreover, the investigation is able to confirm that the system exhibits a transition from a discrete to a continuous form as the parameter in question approaches either zero or infinity. Ultimately, this result is found to be consistent with the predictions made by both the mean-field approximation and the renormalization group. Several sparse signal recovery algorithms have been proposed under the assumption that iterates converge to a fixed point. However, in practice, convergence is often not guaranteed due to issues like ill-conditioning, random data, or implementation limitations. This paper addresses these challenges by introducing various techniques - extrapolation, regularization, and residual updating - to stabilize iterative methods. These techniques are shown to work effectively with algorithms like Iterative Shrinkage, Thresholding Algorithm, Coordinated Descent, and Nesterov's method, across various settings, and can be applied to recover sparse signals from underdetermined measurements, as well as to achieve joint sparse solutions to multiple underdetermined systems. Experimental results validate the efficacy of these stabilization strategies. An open-source implementation of the code used in this paper is publicly available. Formulas for calculating the point spread function (PSF) of combined images taken at different wavelengths under a Krabbe model are developed, including situations with and without optical dispersion. The derivation involves expressing the PSF as a product of an angular PSF and an amplitude transmission, and then applying a weighted integration based on the wavelength-dependent response of the telescope-atmosphere system. For images affected by dispersion, the weighted integration is replaced with a spatial integration along the direction of the dispersion, using the linearly connected pixels of the image plane. The implementation of these algorithms in a Python package, pyPSF, is also described. This package includes functions for computing the PSF of combined images, as well as for analyzing the properties of atmospheric PSFs and accounting for geometric distortions and image rotation. The pyPSF package was specifically designed to support the operations of large ground-based observatories, including the Yepun instrument on Mauna Kea's VLT, where the staff needed a reliable software tool to handle the tasks associated with analyzing images of the atmospheric point spread function. The code has been successfully tested in the analysis of images from the Yepun instrument, demonstrating its practical value. Despite being general enough to be applied to other applications, the algorithm was initially developed to address specific requirements of the Yepun project. Those requirements involved dealing with images taken at wavelengths of 1.575 micrometers to 1.625 micrometers, but with the possibility of extending the application to images taken at wavelengths up to 5 micrometers. The images in question typically have a small diameter of less than 10 arcseconds and are characterized by a very low signal-to-noise ratio in the range of 10 to 50. The corresponding values of optical dispersion are also quite limited, ranging from 0 to 50 pixels per arcsecond. The images in question are also subject to various geometric distortions with an amplitude of up to 0.5 arcseconds. This investigation concerns solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations for a viscous incompressible fluid in a periodic environment. We examine the most extreme norm as a measure of solution behavior in time. Our key findings are twofold. Firstly, when the initial data are finite under a specific mathematical criterion (the Leray criterion), we establish that the most extreme norm of the velocity field grows over time at a constant rate, albeit slower than a straightforward exponential function. This outcome is significant as it represents a first analysis of solution behavior outside of a limited time frame (known as the blow-up time frame) for the Navier-Stokes equations. Secondly, by incorporating a particular mathematical structure into the analysis, we derive an approximation for the most extreme norm of the velocity field, demonstrating decay over time with a shift in frequency. In this context, frequent oscillations lead to increased decay rates. It is worth noting that similar trends have been observed in an unrelated study on Schrödinger equations. Furthermore, our most extreme norm estimates can be seen as a variant of a broader theoretical framework in analysis, specifically regression analysis in frequency space. Recent success in generative neural networks has led to increased interest in implicitly representing shapes using neural networks, especially suitable for modeling complex biological cell types. This research explores the effectiveness of implicit neural representations in modeling 3D biological cell shapes through generative neural networks. By leveraging the symmetry present in many cell types, this method achieves a significant reduction in data requirements, allowing for better generalization. The results demonstrate that the learned implicit shapes can be reliably produced even when the input coordinates are slightly modified. Additionally, the generated cells exhibit notable similarity to real cells in terms of overall shape and volume distribution. This approach is primarily designed for single-cell types but may be extended to model diverse cell populations by incorporating auxiliary conditions to capture the relevant variability. With further advancements, this method has the potential to be even more versatile and widely applicable to a broad range of biological cell types. Experimental evidence demonstrates that training these networks on small datasets can produce high-quality cell shapes that are largely unaffected by changes in the network architecture and sampling method. This robust performance even holds when the datasets are significantly undersampled. By metaphoring the network to a cellular process, the research further investigates the role of active cell shape formation through generative networks. By incorporating an objective function that rewards networks for consistently producing cells with similar shapes, the research shows that these implicit neural networks can be optimized to produce unique and uniform shapes across numerous generated cells. This'shape formation' technique holds promise for a variety of biological cell types due to its ability to produce numerous variations of a single shape, much like stem cells giving rise to diverse cell types. In total, the research contributes several novel methods for implicitly modeling 3D biological cell shapes through generative neural networks, and the accompanying code is publicly available at https://github.com/alexalex1989/implicit-neural-representations-for-cell-shapes. The visualized results can be found at https://alex1989.github.io/implicit-neural-representations-for-cell-shapes/. To maintain stable internal environments despite changing external conditions, living organisms engage in feedback regulation, where physiological responses are adjusted in accordance with the results of previous actions. This process can be modeled as a Markov process governed by a quantum master equation, allowing us to derive the mathematical structure of this equation and determining its requirements for ensuring the process's conditional independence, an essential property for regulating mechanisms. Furthermore, we derive a quantum Fokker-Planck equation for the probability distribution of this process and discuss its specific case when the process is self-regulating, offering a new theoretical framework for analyzing complex regulatory systems. We demonstrate the application of this framework using the example of glucose regulation in humans. We also establish that, under certain conditions, the quantum state of this process converges to a stationary state known as quantum equilibrium, a concept first introduced by Neumann in the 1930s. Wildfire aerosols are causing significant decreases in solar radiation and optical depth, which in turn are being reflected in satellite solar radiation data and optical depth measurements. Utilizing satellite imagery feeds can provide analysts with real-time wildfire aerosol optical density measurements. However, these readings are often marred by noise, which must be removed to extract accurate atmospheric conditions. By combining machine learning with physical laws governing atmospheric conditions, it is possible to create a noise-reducing model that aligns with real-world physics. This paper introduces such a method, which utilizes machine learning to filter out noise from satellite aerosol data while ensuring the generated data complies with real-world physics. By doing so, it is possible to obtain accurate aerosol optical depth measurements, which can inform wildfire risk assessment models. Our experiments using California wildfire data reveal that physics-informed machine learning outperforms traditional methods in retrieving accurate aerosol optical depth measurements. Additionally, we observed that noisy inputs can negatively impact model performance, which is reflected in decreasing predictive accuracy with increasing noise levels. Notably, while deep learning methods exhibited high variability in predictive accuracy due to noisy inputs, physics-informed machine learning demonstrated more stability. The advancement of location tracking technology has sparked significant discussion regarding privacy issues. By employing conditional expectation methodology, this study devises and evaluates privacy preservation strategies for individuals seeking to hide their actual trajectory. It determines the degree to which releasing an initial segment of a trajectory reveals the person's ultimate destination. These privacy metrics are calculated for several privacy-enforcing mechanism schemas, including the well-known $\epsilon$-diffusion mechanism and variants involving geometric differential privacy. Furthermore, this study investigates the dynamic release of location data and assesses the impact of varying mechanism parameters on privacy outcomes. These analytical results are supported by computational experiments demonstrating the trade-off between privacy strength and data utility. Ultimately, this study contributes to the body of location tracking privacy research by offering a location privacy framework centered on conditional expectations. It provides a comprehensive mathematical analysis of privacy outcomes, facilitated by the use of orthogonal systems in Fourier transformation techniques. This research aims to investigate how pressure affects the superconducting properties of the H$_{3}$S hydride material. To investigate the causal importance of this mean impact, we created a simulation where traits were generated based on a mix of heritable and random factors, similar to real-world data. We found that the mean impact can be significant in explaining the shared genetic variation inherited by offspring in large populations, also known as narrow-sense heritability. However, this causation is not inevitable, as the mean impact depends on factors like the number of contributing traits and their correlations. We observed that evolutionary convergent traits tend to have a lower mean impact than those that are highly divergent. Ultimately, the mean impact is not a fixed property, as its value can be optimized by the order in which traits are developed during evolution. From a methodological standpoint, we discovered that estimating heritability through trait correlations is sensitive to the order in which traits are analyzed and can produce varying results, especially for complex models with many interacting factors. Additionally, we found that trait correlations can be sufficient for estimating heritability, eliminating the need for individual parameters, simplifying statistical analyses and calculations. Finally, we observed that evolutionary response to artificial selection is often modeled as a linear change in the selected trait over time. While this model is generally accurate and can be linear, it may not always be the best representation, as the distribution of individual traits within the population can change non-linearly, affecting the mean impact and evolutionary response. Nonetheless, the traditional linear model is a reliable approximation, as the extent of non-linear changes is relatively small and can be accounted for. In general, we observed that population-level quantities, like heritability, are only marginally affected by trait distributions beyond ensuring that selected individuals inherit more of the contributing traits. Notably, evolutionary responses are highly resistant to non-linear changes, as the rate of convergence is largely determined by population-level heritability and the strength of selection, making the mean impact a reliable predictor, especially in large populations where the rate of convergence is largely the same as the population mean. Visual relocalization, a challenging task in robotics and computer vision, becomes more feasible with additional information about geometry. Existing methods rely heavily on SURF features which are insufficient for relocalization in complex environments due to their limited descriptor capacity. Recent advancements in deep learning feature extraction have shown superior performance in this area but often neglect to incorporate geometric information. We propose a method that integrates both geometric and deep learning-based features to achieve more accurate relocalization results. Our approach uses a surfel map database, derived from LiDAR sensors, to provide geometric information and combines it with learned features through a machine learning-based voting system. To validate our method, extensive experiments were conducted in various real-world scenarios, revealing improved performance when geometric information is integrated with deep learning features. Code and datasets are available for reproduction of these experiments. Our method has been found to be particularly effective in difficult situations such as one-shot localization, indoor-outdoor scenarios, and localization after LiDAR data loss. For instance, accuracy improved from 0.41 to 0.83 for one-shot localization, and from 0.62 to 0.88 for localization after LiDAR data loss. These breakthroughs were achieved with our method through integrated geometric and feature information. To confirm the dependency of these results solely on our method, comparisons were conducted against 12 baseline approaches, revealing a significant superiority of our approach. These findings have led to new research directions and insights, prompting the following question: can geometric information be replaced with deep learning features entirely? To investigate this, a new baseline model was devised, and results showed a 0.16 difference in accuracy scores, underscoring the replacement feasibility. These research findings and new models will facilitate advancements in visual relocalization, enabling robots to localize more accurately even in complex environments. To showcase the efficacy of these models, demonstrations have been prepared and will be made available for download. To evaluate the validity of our approach, assessments were conducted at two existing testing sites, selected for diverse conditions. Numerical simulations of second-long black hole-neutron star collisions have been conducted, incorporating various initial magnetic field configurations in order to understand their role in mass ejection and gravitational wave characteristics. Key findings reveal significant differences in outcomes depending on the magnetic field setup, properties of the neutron star, and collision angle. Notably, our simulations demonstrate that late-stage mass ejection occurs within a time frame of 10-20 seconds following the collision, and that late launches are typically softer and more compact than earlier ones. It has also been found that late-stage launches may survive for minutes and even up to a hour, and that their characteristics are largely independent of the neutron star's equation of state. Our results show that late-stage launches are more likely to occur with stronger magnetic fields and in collisions at certain angles, and that they often result in larger final launches than initially observed mass ejection. Furthermore, our findings indicate that late-stage mass ejection can significantly affect the neutron star's mass retention, and that its extent is largely dependent on the final mass ejection's properties. Our study also shows that late-stage launches may result in long-lived nebulas, and that their properties vary based on the initial magnetic field and neutron star equations of state. Our findings contradict previous theories that late-stage launches are typically confined to specific parameters, and instead suggest that they are more versatile and less equation-of-state dependent than previously believed. Key uncertainties were also identified, and it was recognized that more simulations are needed in order to understand potential variations in late-stage launches across different systems. Our work represents the first simulation to model second-long black hole-neutron star collisions while accounting for magnetic fields and neutron star equations of state, and offers insights into late-stage mass ejection and its associated processes. Our study also demonstrates the importance of late-stage launches in understanding various phenomena following the collision, and highlights the need for future numerical studies and theoretical work in this area. This research investigates sequences of linear optimization procedures driven by probabilistic models, where the probability distribution is updated after each iteration based on observed data. We show that, under specific conditions, these sequences of optimization procedures converge to a solution that is consistent with the ultimate probability distribution, thereby resolving an open question posed by Crambon and Graham in 2007. Moreover, our findings broaden the scope of several existing theorems, including those by Graham in 1981, Crambon and Graham in 2007, and Feijer and Pauzat in 2010, while also addressing a practical issue highlighted by Graham in 1981. We illustrate the applicability of our theoretical results through numerical experiments focusing on two specific problems: a support-bounded optimization problem and a complementarity problem. Additionally, our theoretical work subsumes that of Feijer and Pauzat, building upon their earlier research and making a significant extension to their findings. We have also developed code to demonstrate our theoretical conclusions, which can be accessed via a public GitHub repository. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the interplay between linear optimization procedures and probabilistic models, thereby shedding new light on the underlying theoretical framework. 

\textit{Keywords:} linear optimization procedures, probabilistic models, ultimate probability distribution, convergence results, various applications.

Research has examined the interactions between the Chiral Magnetic Effect (CME) and charges in Pb-Pb collisions at various energies. Contrary to expectations, lead-ion collisions showed a dependence on charged particles' collective movements, which is restricted by local charge conservation rules. In this study, collisions are analyzed at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV energies, focusing on observed phenomena. The investigation's results are presented in relation to simulated models, including one that considers local charge conservation constraints. The analysis includes consideration of collisions' spatial variations. The study found that CME influence is largely overcome by other factors in lead-ion collisions, regardless of observed spatial patterns. The investigation also discusses implications of local charge conservation rules on understanding the Chiral Magnetic Effect in heavy-ion physics. The discovery may restrict CME detection in experimental settings. The virtual fundraiser's initial impression is crucial for a successful outcome, making it essential to study the characteristics of online crowds that influence donor donation amounts.  Past research has focused on the impact of social media crowd behavior on donation amounts but has not compared the effects of crowd behavior metrics across different platforms.  To address this gap, we conducted an in-depth analysis of donation data from Twitter and CrowdTangle to determine the crowd behavior characteristics that affect donation amounts in both environments.  Our results show that the magnitude of donation amounts is linked to the engagement rates of relevant tweets in both platforms, with higher rates associated with larger donation amounts.  While there are similarities in the predictors of donation amounts between Twitter and CrowdTangle, there are also distinct predictors specific to each platform. These findings highlight the value of combining data from different platforms to gain a comprehensive understanding of the factors driving online crowd behavior.  Moreover, they suggest that platforms can optimize their design to enhance user experience and increase donation amounts by promoting features that yield higher engagement rates. The problem of optimal movement planning for robotic systems with multiple arms has been addressed by various methods which either ignore the arms' interactions or treat them as a single entity. However, these approaches fall short in capturing the inherent complexities arising from arm interaction. In this paper, we present an efficient and interactive algorithm inspired by greedy decision-making, capable of ordering tasks for multi-point robotic systems. By simulating the movement of each arm through a simplified process, our method identifies optimal task sequences taking into account the limitations and capabilities of each arm. As a result, this approach outperforms existing methods in generated collision-free paths, particularly in scenarios involving complex geometries and numerous obstacles. Furthermore, our method exhibits a linear time complexity, making it suitable for everyday use in manipulator task planning. The efficacy of our algorithm is validated through comprehensive simulations involving various configurations of tasks and arms. Additionally, our studies reveal that this method produces nearly optimal results, as confirmed by experimental comparisons with exact algorithms. Consequently, this method provides a practical solution for efficiently planning interactive movement in multi-point robotic systems. The code for this algorithm is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ferdyur/Interactive-MP-Robot Planning. The authors have also established a website for demo purposes at https://interactive-mp-robot-planning.github.io/. Future work on this research will focus on extending this method to tackle the more challenging problem of concurrent movement planning. The novel approach presented in this study can be considered an extension of the state-of-the-art in this field. In particular, our method shares connections with the concepts of clustering, interactive decision-making, and artificial potential fields. Although this algorithm is presented in the context of multi-point robotic systems, its underlying ideas can be applied to other areas such as mobile manipulation and interactive path planning for single-arm systems.
