We introduce modulated cyclic activations, a type of local feature representation widely employed in CNNs. The specific architecture of the modulated cyclic activation layer lies at the core of our proposed neural network design, as well as various modification ideas that we will be introducing. Our research indicates that combining the modulated cyclic activation with ReLU and Leaky ReLU results in a significant improvement in the local feature representation capability of the network. Furthermore, integrating a modulated cyclic activation-based hidden layer into a shallow network enables it to exhibit depth-wise convolutional characteristics on par with state-of-the-art models. Notably, our modulated cyclic activation-based model exhibits exceptional generalizability, as evidenced by our findings that it outperforms renowned CNN architectures on multiple datasets. Specifically, our model achieved impressive results on the MNIST dataset, boasting a test accuracy of 99.73%, and displayed a notable 5-6% improvement in test accuracy compared to leading CNN designs. Moreover, our modulated cyclic activation-based model displayed a test accuracy of 44.46% on the Protein Substitution dataset, surpassing the ProLasso sparse linear model's test accuracy of 43.17%. Additionally, our model's performance in the 3D MNIST and Protein Substitution datasets exceeded that of the benchmark CNN models by a margin of 4-5%. A copy of the source code is available at https://github.com/hjdw2/Modulated-Cyclic-Activation. Additionally, the weights used in our experiments can be downloaded at https://drive.google.com/drive/folderview?id=9BU9M0nskYkxkx4p0bT5vPvV1pU0.

We introduce Semi-Generative Model, a novel method to tackle covariate shift in deep networks through the use of supplementary information. This involves assigning cause and influence tasks to existing data and using the obtained features to adapt to distribution changes. Unlike previous approaches, our method requires minimal additional resources as it leverages the features extracted by the network itself. Since these features may not always convey the necessary information for the covariate shift, we propose an efficient means of incorporating the influence characteristics directly into the prediction task. Through theoretical analysis and experiments involving synthetic and real-world data, we validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. Notably, SG has a reduced memory requirement of $O(N)$ compared to zero-shot and few-shot approaches with a depth of $O(L)$. Importantly, SG's evaluation task can be performed offline, thus enabling it to be distinguishable from online adaptive methods that require continuous data streams. Code for SG is available on GitHub at https://github.com/AKSHAYU/Semigen Model. Further details on the dataset can be found at https://github.com/AKSHAYU/Semigen Data. SG has demonstrated superior performance across various domains, such as image classification, language modeling, and link prediction. Nonetheless, we have identified a few limitations of our approach, which we aim to address in the upcoming variants of SG. Specifically, we are exploring the incorporation of a causal generator network to address feedback loops in dynamical systems. Another potential area of improvement is the integration of a memory mechanism to store the influence characteristics, particularly for scenarios where the number of influence dimensions is vast. Lastly, we are developing a semi-supervised variant of SG, which utilizes unlabeled influence data to extract relevant features for the prediction task. Overall, SG has shown remarkable potential in tackling the covariate shift, and we are confident that addressing these limitations will further enhance its effectiveness. Notably, our current results already reveal a 5% average performance improvement over the established baselines, and we are open to collaborating with other researchers to push the boundaries of SG further. Ultimately, we are excited about the vast applications of SG, and we believe it has the potential to become a fundamental approach in building robust and adaptable deep networks across various domains. Specifically, we are exploring its potential in developing deep networks that can thrive in dynamic and uncharted environments. To demonstrate the versatility of SG, we have successfully applied it to domains as diverse as computer vision and NLP, and we are confident that its feature extraction mechanism will pave the way for novel deep network

Deep learning techniques recently achieved a high level of success in various applications. Despite their effectiveness, the underlying principles of these methods are still poorly understood. This study aims to shed light on the fundamentals of deep learning by translating it into a geometric framework. We chose to apply the theory of free differential groups and its 3-dimensional extension, known as the Sharpley Spencer complex, to deep learning models. We developed a novel geometric representation of deep learning architectures, allowing us to derive algebraic expressions for the complexes of convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and their combinations. We also introduced a concept for the covering complexity of RNNs, paving the way for further research and analysis of deep learning methods from a geometric perspective. We applied the developed geometric approach to investigate the properties of recurrent neural networks, such as their ability to memorize information, and to generalize from small datasets. We also found that certain RNN architectures with a covering complexity of 2 can solve linear prediction tasks, and that their performance improves as the size of the dataset grows. We discovered through numerical experiments that the Sharpley Spencer complex of RNNs depends on the order of the recurrence and the matrix inversion methods used to update hidden states. We also found that certain RNN architectures with a covering complexity of 2 can learn task-dependent features, generalizing this finding to deep learning models based on quadratic Sharpley Spencer complexes. The geometric framework we applied might not be the only suitable representation for deep learning models. We suggest exploring other geometric approaches, such as turning the parameter space of deep learning models into a Riemannian manifold or applying the theory of free differential groups to the space of functions represented by neural networks. We believe the geometric framework we presented can serve as a useful tool for analyzing the fundamentals of deep learning methods. Let R be a ring, and consider the set of non-negative integers, including 0. For each element in R, we can define its 'chief length' as the smallest number within this set that is greater than or equal to its lattice depth. It has been proven that the chief length function is additive along finitely many chains in R. Additionally, it has been shown that if R satisfies a specific condition, then the chief length function is actually an ultrafilter on Boolean rings consisting of ideals within R. This enables us to establish a connection between this length and a different measure of elements known as the lattice depth. Specifically, it has been found that for any element in R, its lattice depth is less than or equal to its chief length, with the difference between these values being proportional to the number of significant components within the element's prime factorization. It has also been shown that for any element in R that is not a zero divisor, its lattice depth and chief length will eventually become equal as the element generates a maximal ideal in R. These findings indicate that the chief length function provides a more precise representation of elements' properties than the lattice depth. Based on these results, several questions and potential areas of research have been suggested for further exploration. Firstly, it would be interesting to establish whether the chief length function is additive along infinitely many chains in R. It would also be beneficial to determine whether the difference between the lattice depth and chief length is indeed proportional to the number of significant components, or if a different relationship exists between these values. Finally, it is proposed that the concept of chief lengths should be extended beyond rings to other types of rings, such as valuated rings and nearrings. Additionally, it is suggested that the term 'chief length' be borrowed from the field of lattice theory and incorporated into the existing vocabulary of ring theory. It is further proposed that the study of chief lengths within rings could serve as a means of developing a more localized and detailed understanding of rings' properties, specifically those related to localization and quasilocalization. Finally, it is concluded that the notion of chief lengths is inherently tied to the idea of localizing rings and can be represented as a collection of functions that assign positive integer values to elements in localizations of R. It is suggested that this idea be explored further in future research. It is also proposed that the concept of chief lengths be viewed as a collection of integer-valued localizations of R, which could provide a more refined and detailed understanding of rings' properties. We apply this approach to solve the 1D Hubbard model, a challenging problem, using a type of network that can handle complex values, and find that as the number of layers increases, the error associated with approximating the true solution diminishes. Additionally, we observe that even with a relatively low number of layers, the approximate solution already demonstrates a high level of accuracy, and the signature of low-lying excitations in the dynamical structure factor is accurately reproduced. Notably, the approximate solutions obtained through this method not only retain the correct phase structure but also exhibit smooth and analytic behavior, in contrast to solutions derived using other approaches such as the Lanczos trapezoid algorithm. We further observe that the approximate solutions obtained through this method exhibit an exponential decay of high-frequency sign fluctuations, and the low-lying spectral weight is accurately reproduced. These findings demonstrate that deep complex-valued neural networks can provide a precise and detailed understanding of the quantum dynamics of the 1D Hubbard model. We suggest that this approach, due to its exponential convergence, can be an effective tool for studying quantum matter, and potentially other complex many-body systems, where traditional algorithms may face a significant computational barrier due to the sign problem. Therefore, this approach could be a valuable complement to these algorithms, and potentially used to determine critical temperatures and other critical parameters. In this review, we explore various composite models where Flavon-Higgs bosons are made up of new gauge forces and are comprised of two components: Flavons and Higgses. We offer a general description of these models and then examine specific cases where the fundamental bosons are linked to a specific flavor symmetry, resulting in the natural emergence of the CKM matrix. We also discuss potential connections between these models and recent observations, including the baryon asymmetry, dark matter, and the anomalies seen in semileptonic $B$-meson decay data. We conclude by analyzing various constraints these models must adhere to. We also delve into an alternative version of these models where the Higgs boson is a Flavon-Higgs combination. We look at both the type-I and type-II versions of this framework. In the type-II case, we examine the impact of the Flavon-Higgs on the $\rho$-parameter and $T$-matrix calculations. We derive new constraints from electroweak precision tests. We further explore an extension of this framework where additional Flavon-Higgs combinations are introduced to strengthen the model's ability to explain recent anomalies in semileptonic $B$-meson decay data. We demonstrate that this model is capable of generating a sufficient dark matter density to account for the Earth's rotation deceleration. We ultimately discuss how this model can be probed through direct searches for new bosons and precision tests at the LHC. We show the experimentally testable range for different parameters in this framework. We also illustrate the potential of this model to resolve issues within the Standard Model that have long been unsolved or problematic. We provide relationships between these model parameters that can help researchers in the SM identify potential issues. Our understanding of high-level machine learning-led synthetic image synthesis can be deepened by studying how human perception handles artificially created visuals. Real-world lab settings are used to test whether people can distinguish between real and artificially rendered scenes. To enhance realism, researchers employ VR technology, but there's an ongoing debate about its effectiveness. This paper focuses on a specific aspect of perception, specifically the shadow feature in VR, and presents two experiments investigating its influence on image synthesis. The findings reveal that more realistic shadows in VR do not significantly affect participants' ability to distinguish real from fake, although this effect persists across various domains, including a dataset featuring kitchen items. Additionally, the experiments' results are consistent across different levels of artificial realism, and further analysis explores how participants' judgments are influenced by the presence of shadows. The study's findings are two-fold - it offers practical guidance for real-world applications and contributes to theoretical knowledge on human perception, facilitating the development of more realistic synthetic images that better align with human perception. In a recent study, it was demonstrated that when a star-forming core collapses under its own gravity, a mass ratio of typically around 0.5 is achieved, regardless of initial core spin and mass. This research is expanded upon by investigating more extensive scenarios, specifically those involving more massive cores that can give birth to twin stars, by analyzing how they split during the collapse. Utilizing a detailed hydrodynamic simulation, a series of initial conditions involving core masses from one to ten times that of our sun, along with varying levels of angular momentum, were examined. It was discovered that as a core collapses, its surrounding disc extends inward, ultimately leading to the simultaneous formation of new, smaller core objects, and a reduced disc that can give birth to additional stars. The resulting mass ratios of these new core objects to their parent core increase in line with the initial core mass, resulting in a new set of typical mass ratios, with values ranging from 0.5 to 0.9, and these ratios rise rapidly above a threshold of around one sun's mass. The implications of these findings for the formation of binary and multiple star systems are discussed. Additionally, it was found that during the collapse, the angular momentum of the system is redistributed in a way that minimizes the spin of the new core objects, and this is a key factor contributing to the widespread occurrence of low-rotational velocity stars, including those with virtually no rotation at all. Lastly, it was determined that the formation of star systems via this mass generation process may prefer certain mass ratios over others, and this could potentially explain observed patterns in the distribution of mass ratios among close binary stars. Further research will be necessary to fully explore the potential connections between this process and the properties of these systems. The primary objective of the M-ar-K-Fast method is to identify the fundamental characteristics of a dataset, making minimal assumptions about its structure in the process. This is achieved through an iterative algorithm that identifies autonomous components, characterized by a lack of external influence, and extracts features from data along these components, effectively simplifying the dataset. As the number of samples increases, the M-ar-K-Fast method converges to a component analysis method rooted in information theory, minimizing potential biases in the process. Empirical evaluations have shown the M-ar-K-Fast method to be more robust and efficient than existing methods. The method has been further validated by its ability to detect artificial anomalies in synthetic data and distinguish between known and unknown states in real-world sleep data. The M-ar-K-Fast algorithm is now open-source and available on GitHub for public access. It is also planned to be integrated into the scikit-learn library as a contributing module. Furthermore, a standalone Python package named M-ar-K-Fast will be provided, offering a range of features and functionalities to support users. The package will encompass a range of features and functionalities, including enhanced visualization tools and comprehensive documentation, to facilitate easy understanding and use of the M-ar-K-Fast method. Additionally, the package will include a sleep analysis module, demonstrating the application of the M-ar-K-Fast method to real-world data in the field of sleep studies. The sleep analysis module will serve as a prototype, showcasing the ability of the M-ar-K-Fast method to distinguish between known and unknown states in sleep data, and a similar approach can be applied to other multi-label datasets in various domains. The choice of loss function in deep learning is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, but a comprehensive understanding of its impact remains elusive. Current knowledge mainly stems from rule-of-thumb experiences or empirical observations. In this study, we systematically investigated how modifying loss functions affects the performance of well-established deep learning classifiers in a robust, repeatable manner. Our experiments, conducted across 13,589 Amazon Mechanical Turk worker evaluations and involving 11 commonly used loss functions, revealed the optimal loss function for a specific task to be the average of 4 distinct methods. Interestingly, our findings also showed that even near-optimal loss function variations can degrade model accuracy. By examining the training dynamics of different loss functions, we gained valuable insights on how to design and evaluate them more effectively. Our research provides a foundational framework that can be further expanded to explore the properties of more complex and less well-established models. Ultimately, this knowledge can promote more informed decision-making in deep learning, fostering a deeper understanding of the loss function's role in modeling development.

The proposed method can accurately determine the exciton's size, energy, and formation energy. We have successfully applied this to a 2D material, specifically a monolayer of TiSe2, where we discovered that strong electron-phonon coupling triggers exciton condensation and gives rise to a superconducting property. The results show that the magnetic field's orientation has a substantial effect on the spatial distribution of the Cooper pairs' $d$-wave order parameter. In contrast to singlet Cooper pairs, which exhibit opposing and in-phase spin components, the response to magnetic alignment varies significantly between the two triplet Cooper pair configurations ($ab$- and $z-componental'). In the field of online nonconvex zero-sum games, where multiple agents compete in a sequence of actions, a leading approach involves using an iterative algorithm called online optimality matching. Notably, the first such algorithm was proposed by Blum et al. in 2008. This method has several beneficial characteristics, including being universally compatible and regret minimizer. However, its major shortcoming is the potential for exponentially growing regret in the number of players. In an attempt to address this limitation, we have developed a new algorithm capable of achieving linear regret in the number of players. In particular, we have improved the regret bound for online optimality matching by reducing the exponent, thus narrowing the gap between the known lower and upper bounds for the regret in this setting. Additionally, we have applied our new algorithm to education as a game, where the teacher seeks to match the student's knowledge, and the student strives to surpass the teacher. By engaging in a minimax educational contest, the minimax student learns at a rate proportional to 1/t, while the minimax teacher learns at a rate proportional to 1/t^2. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that both the minimax student and teacher can be identified through a finite number of rounds of interaction. In a related educational setting, we have also optimized the online optimality matching algorithm to achieve the lowest possible regret, and derived a constant regret bound independent of the number of players. In particular, we have achieved a regret rate of 1/3 for both the teacher and student in online optimality matching. In a final educational scenario, we have demonstrated that the presence of multiple teachers can hinder the student's learning, resulting in a reduced learning rate compared to a single teacher. In an attempt to mitigate this adverse effect, we have modulated the student's query strategy, and through nonconvex online zero-sum gaming, we have achieved a superior regret bound compared to traditional methods in this setting. To study the time-dependent characteristics of music, we employed a sophisticated network approach based on eight detailed audio features extracted from popular songs over the past 50 years. Our analysis reveals significant shifts in music generated by temporary changes in song selection criteria applied by a leading music streaming service. For instance, we found that music labeled as "mellow" is distinguished from "hot" music by a higher concentration of songs with slower beat speeds. Additionally, we identified substantial changes in the characteristics of modern music when comparing it to music from the 1970s, particularly in regards to its spectral density. Our findings provide insight into how music evolution is influenced by explicit selection criteria and may serve as a framework for an automated music discovery system. However, we also report some complications encountered during our analysis, such as the rapid distribution of some features across different genres and the challenge this presents to our method of categorizing music by its attributes. Nonetheless, our study demonstrates that an in-depth analysis of music can yield meaningful, statistically-supported results. It is hoped that our work will stimulate further research into music complexity and the development of more effective methods for music recommendation. Our data includes information on over 1 billion songs from various styles and enables researchers to access additional audio features through online databases, such as Magnatune, MusicBrainz, and SoundCloud. Suppose we have a difficult assignment problem where we need to rank a large number of items under specific categories for better organization. Typically, labeling all items individually would be the most efficient method, but it can be very time-consuming and impractical if there are many items. Alternatively, each item is only partially labeled with relevant information, and we need to rank them quickly. To tackle this issue, we propose an efficient ranking method that uses partial labels from a small subset of critical items to evaluate the category competitiveness of the remaining items. Building on this idea, we developed the Visually Supported Cluster Ranking algorithm (VSCR), which can handle assignments with any level of complexity. VSCR works by dividing items into distinct categories based on support from key labeled items and uses sub-clusters to organize assignments efficiently. Notably, VSCR surpassed or matched the performance of the competing algorithms in nearly all experiments, and it demonstrated superior scalability and adaptability to real-world data. Moreover, VSCR demonstrated impressive time savings of up to 86% compared to the baseline algorithms while achieving similar or better overall accuracy. These remarkable results validate the potential of VSCR as a time-efficient method for processing assignments in visual data ranking tasks. A widespread issue in ensemble prediction systems is the generation of unreliable forecasts for limited areas directly from global or regional models. This study proposes an analytical solution based on Bayesian concepts to address this problem, focusing specifically on spatial upscaling. Initially, the theoretical framework is established, after which a practical implementation using neural networks is demonstrated through a straightforward example. Ultimately, the proposed method's theoretical underpinnings are reinforced by experimental results in the field of hydrology. The findings show that neural networks can be relied upon to provide accurate probability distributions over a wider area, even when individual predictions are unreliable due to high uncertainty levels. This implementation using neural networks enhances existing inverse likelihood weighting techniques, making them more feasible for practical use. The proposed algorithm is computationally efficient and thus well-suited for post-processing a variety of meteorological models, including global numerical weather prediction systems and shallow Lagrangian models. Finally, the challenges and potential avenues for exploring other ensemble techniques in the ensemble filtering framework are discussed. In order to achieve precise results from theoretical particle physics predictions, especially when dealing with tau leptons, we must carefully examine our numerical methods. This study evaluates the performance of various integration techniques used in predicting tau decay rates, revealing both highly accurate and highly unreliable methods. We identify specific challenges associated with different phases of these decays and demonstrate the necessity of employing tau-specific mesh refinement to generate accurate physical outcomes. Ultimately, our research underscores the need for more sophisticated mesh design in the domain of tau physics, either through ground-breaking theory developments or more practical mesh-adaptation techniques. We also propose a potential solution, leveraging the principles of arithmetical first-fermion calculations to generate highly accurate results without relying on grid-based methods. This approach could notably simplify predictions for tau decays into electrons or muons. We provide both traditional and tau-specific numerical validation for our findings. Additionally, we include a comprehensive bibliography on the numerical methods used in this research, covering publications from the last twenty-five years. We also outline specific future challenges related to numerical mesh difficulties that might arise in future particle physics research, potentially involving the simulation of heavy charged particles. We expect our research to contribute to the development of more reliable and accurate numerical tools not only in the field of particle physics but also in related areas such as quantum field theory and condensed matter research. These tools can also be applied to other complex problems, like simulations involving heavy charged particles. A standard method for modeling extreme values involves considering the occurrence of exceedances as a Poisson process over a threshold. While this approach has a straightforward link to statistical inference, it lacks a clear connection to common extreme value distributions. We develop a unified framework that bridges this parameterisation by exploring its relationship with extreme value distributions. This study calculates asymptotic Bayesian credible intervals using two different estimators, one based on the generalized extreme value family and the other on a more general approach, both of which are aligned with the Poisson process reparameterisation. A simulation study evaluates these intervals along with empirical estimates, comparing their performance under varying levels of data availability. Ultimately, this method is demonstrated in an empirical analysis of maximum wind speeds measured at Cork Airport in Ireland over a 40-year period. We also provide a package called Extremes in R that implements this approach, enabling users to conduct this analysis. This package includes functions for estimating extreme value distributions within the context of this Poisson process model, calculating asymptotic Bayesian credible intervals, and a simulation study that evaluates its performance. A version of this package that includes the code for this study can be found at https://github.com/paulpap/Extremes/tree/main R_extremes. In the field of offline reinforcement learning, particularly in RL for mobile robot navigation, real-world state observations are often marred by noise and corrupted data. This leads to misinterpretation of the robot's environment, resulting in inaccurate representation and reduced performance. Current approaches in RL are typically vulnerable to corrupted data inputs, which are readily available in real-world settings. This research presents an initial framework for robust offline RL in noisy and corrupted data scenarios, which affects both state and action representations. Our framework, called \textit{Corruption-Resilient Offline RL}, aims to develop an almost optimal policy under the assumption of a limited number of corrupted data instances. By applying this concept, we achieve a viable solution for robust offline RL in scenarios involving corrupted data, which is supported by experimental results in simulated environments. Future research will focus on evaluating this concept in real-world settings. Additionally, we note that although this work addresses state corruption, the problem of action corruption remains unresolved and warrants further investigation. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at the provided link.

Developing self-propelled devices at the molecular and nanoscale offers significant potential for innovative technology, including molecular motors and transport systems. One promising engine type leverages variations in fluid drag as a power source, with a particular example being Brownian motors based on an unusual phenomenon where charges moving near a metallic nanobridge generate distinct tunneling currents when charges are either added to or removed from the bridge's tunneling barrier. This engineering challenge can be addressed through a more fundamental understanding of the dynamical behavior underlying this nanoscale tunneling current device. By developing an analytical model that incorporates both the device's transverse and longitudinal dynamics, researchers find that its dynamic behavior is influenced by the device's size, charges moving on the bridge, and the flow dynamics surrounding it. This analytical model is validated through comparison with finite element method simulations, and it is discovered that the dynamic system has a special property where the device's movement in one direction is inversely related to its movement in the opposite direction. Furthermore, it is found that the static average position of the device, as measured after many cycles of movement, is not zero, indicating that the device can efficiently convert tunneling current into mechanical energy. This research demonstrates that by harnessing the power of tunneling currents, it is possible to develop innovative nanoscale engines with significant practical potential. Given the complexity of these systems, involving both electronic and fluid dynamics, a comprehensive analytical model is essential for advancing research in this field. This model can be applied to various engine configurations, such as those with moving charges within a circular orbit or an oscillating charge near a metallic nanobridge. As such, the developed framework has broad applications in designing self-propelled molecular and nanoscale devices. Additionally, the models and methods employed in this research can be used to investigate other complex systems involving coupled electronic and fluid dynamics. In an attempt to simplify this complexity, researchers often rely on uniform mixing models, where contacts occur randomly throughout the population.  While such models have been effective in certain settings, there are instances where this approach may not be the most accurate.  For example, in a study examining the spread of infectious disease on an urban bus, it was discovered that a uniform mixing model failed to accurately reflect actual interactions among passengers.  In contrast, an agent-based model revealed a high frequency of repeated close contacts among fellow passengers on the urban bus.  As a result, predictive models based solely on average contact rates may underestimating the true rate of disease transmission, particularly if such models do not account for the unique patterns of interaction observed in this setting.  In light of these findings, it is recommended that agents-based models be used to inform public health policy regarding urban bus systems before relying on more simplified models for forecasting disease transmission. Additionally, it may be beneficial to implement targeted strategies to mitigate the spread of disease within urban bus systems, such as increased cleaning regimens, to reduce the risk of outbreaks within this setting.  Ultimately, these findings emphasize the need for tailored public health interventions that take into consideration the distinct social dynamics present in settings such as urban bus systems.  Given the commonality of urban buses as a mode of transportation in many countries, it is hypothesized that the patterns of interaction observed in this study may also be applicable to other settings, such as trains, airports, and other enclosed environments where individuals congregate. The dynamic mode decomposition algorithm has undergone numerous enhancements since its introduction in 2010. A novel approach, termed linear and nonlinear clarification optimization (LANDO), is presented here with two distinct iterations. LANDO's first iteration optimizes the kernel in a linear fashion, taking into consideration possible nonlinearity in the data, while its second iteration optimizes the kernel in a nonlinear Neumann series with respect to the data's nonlinearity. When nonlinearity is not a factor, LANDO reduces to the standard dynamic mode decomposition (SDD) and, if the kernel is optimized in a linear fashion, it is similar to the sparse dynamic mode decomposition (SDD) algorithm. A kernel-dependent regularization parameter is a key component of the LANDO algorithm, particularly when dealing with noisy data, as it ensures the stability and robustness of the algorithm. A number of numerical experiments are presented here, demonstrating the performance of the algorithm under a variety of conditions, particularly in relation to noisy data. Furthermore, a theoretical low-bounding on the regularization parameter is provided, ensuring that it remains large enough to guarantee the algorithm's stability and robustness. The latter part of this paper examines the resilience of the algorithm in the presence of sensor failures, particularly regarding the loss of sequential sensors, while also investigating what happens when multiple sensors are lost over an extended period of time. A graphical user interface (GUI) is presented here, providing users with a visual understanding of the algorithm's performance in the presence of sensor failures. This paper culminates with a number of numerical experiments, examining the algorithm's resilience in a variety of contexts. Additionally, a comprehensive set of MATLAB codes are made publicly available, in accordance with the algorithm's name, kernel education for resilient dynamic mode decomposition. These codes may be accessed via the following link: https://github.com/Aziz Ghaddar/lando.git. In graph layout designs, upward graph layout is a crucial concept that ensures edges are drawn above vertices, facilitating clear and understandable visual representations. While downward graph layout is relatively well-studied in the context of circular arrangements, upward graph layout remains less explored, especially in the framework of parameterized complexity. Our research focuses on evaluating the feasibility of applying parameterized methods to upward graph layout problems. Specifically, we examine whether upward graph layout issues can be addressed through tractable parameterized approaches by analyzing the relationship between these problems and their corresponding tractable counterparts in circular downward graph layout. Our findings reveal that most upward graph layout problems have tractable parameterized versions when applying the matrix-pair representation, except for one problem, for which we demonstrate a parameterized complexity dichotomy. Another significant outcome of our research is the development of new fixed-parameter tractability results for several upward graph layout problems as well as novel parameterized algorithms for these issues. To contribute to this area, we create necessary toolkit concepts, including matrix-pair compression and efficient exact algorithms for matching and orientation problems within this context. Additionally, we introduce new NP-hardness results for certain parameterized versions of upward graph layout problems, thus establishing a parameterized complexity dichotomy for one such problem. Overall, our research showcases the feasibility and utility of applying parameterized methods to upward graph layout problems, thereby expanding the graph layout design toolkit with more efficient algorithmic tools. With this, we pave the way for future research to further investigate the applicability of parameterized complexity to graph layout design problems. As a result of our research, we can now efficiently solve numerous upward graph layout problems for graphs with specific characteristics, such as planar graphs, where the parameter value corresponds to the treewidth. Moreover, our findings enable more detailed analyses of the complexity of applying parameterized methods in graph layout design. Ultimately, our research advances the area of graph layout design by incorporating the powerful toolkit of parameterized complexity to better understand and efficiently solve graph layout problems. With this, we expand the graph layout design toolkit, thereby facilitating more clear and understandable visual representations of graphs. In particular, our results are expected to contribute significantly to the design of upward external graph layouts, for which various algorithmic tools are currently unavailable. By generalizing our findings, we can also extend our research to other graph layout design problems, such as convex external graph layouts. This paper introduces two types of dynamic hypergraphs, one where edges can change size and another where edges can shift, and develops the necessary framework to study these structures. It formally defines the concepts of weak and strong connectivity for these dynamic hypergraphs. Additionally, the paper shows that on discrete time-continuous spaces, a dynamic hypergraph with movable edges has weak connectivity if and only if it has a certain input-based threshold value, and that on metric spaces, a dynamic hypergraph with edges that can change size has strong connectivity if and only if it exceeds a specific threshold value. These findings expand on previous research that studied static hypergraphs. Furthermore, the paper provides examples and theory on how to calculate the threshold values for these dynamic hypergraphs. Finally, the paper proposes a method to approximate threshold values for a given dynamic hypergraph. These ideas and theories are then applied to an example that illustrates a dynamic hypergraph representing connections between individuals in a village. Research questions are also posed for future study. Finally, the paper ends by summarizing its main conclusions. A future work is proposed. Please find the introduction in the attached document. We investigate operator expansion for two-point functions within context of asymptotically free quantum field theories, specifically quantum electrodynamics and scalar field theories with non-zero and zero mass. The evolution of an operator's size as it moves in space-time is described by a regularization-independent parameter called the size parameter. Since the size parameter depends on the ultraviolet fixed point of the coupling, it is not suitable for studying interactions at nearby coupling values. For a general class of local operators, we present a new criterion for evaluating their expanded representation along a specific trajectory and derive key properties such as the ordering of expansion for scalar and vector operators. Moreover, we introduce a novel expansion for the two-point function which is regulated by the size parameter and is characterized by a complex power-law dependence on the parameter. This new expansion exhibits a striking similarity with the Roy Ginzburg formula for the Regge expansion, revealing a profound connection between these seemingly distinct expansions. We also devise a resummation technique at finite parameters, analogous to the Borel resummation at zero size parameter. Furthermore, we investigate the structure of expanded representations for scalar field theories with non-zero and zero mass. In this process, we establish a relationship between the regime of expansion and the Page-Fredenhagen framework for decomposing the renormalized two-point function into a product of two distributions. Specifically, by summing certain subleading logarithmic terms at both large and small size parameters, we show that the expansion is equivalent to a resummation of the renormalized two-point function near its ultraviolet and infrared fixed points. Ultimately, we propose a method called resummation by regions, where we use the expansion at one parameter value to resum the theory at a different parameter value. We hope that this newly discovered relationship will guide similar investigations in the context of asymptotically free quantum field theories. Additionally, we discuss potential future extensions of our research, such as exploring higher-point functions and examining regeneration in the context of these theories. In a related study, we explore the structure of expanded representations for the scalar field theories at large and small size parameters and examine connections with Regge expansion, conformal Collins and soft factor decomposition. We discovered a novel relationship between the expansion and Regge trajectories, linking the size parameter with the momentum parameter in these theories. In this process, we derived important properties such as the ordering of expansion for Regge trajectories and regrouped the primary components of Regge expansion. We investigate finite state compression under two conditions: feedback from the decoder to the encoder and knowledge of the communication channel's state at the encoder. Feedback allows the encoder to gain insight into the complexity of the data being sent, while having access to the channel state enables the encoder to select optimal representations based on the channel's condition. Unlike classical information theory, our framework does not restrict the encoder and decoder to memoryless behavior. Rather, we allow them to possess any amount of memory. Despite these relaxations, our results reveal that the amount of information transmitted is bounded by the same minimum rate as in the traditional model, thereby validating the sufficiency of the classical shannon theorem under these specific conditions. Our findings can be applied to compression problems involving channels that transition between distinct states over time, such as channels affected by weather or channels that vary by location. These findings also generalize to the case where multiple encoders share knowledge of the communication channel's state. In such scenarios, our results demonstrate the existence of optimal codes that utilize feedback and state information, and we show that these codes are achievable through methods involving the creation of code sequences from state-dependent channel capacity sets. Additionally, our results generalize the concepts of finite state compression, expanding it to applications involving multiple input sequences and confirming that the transmitted information remains within a finite boundary. Finally, our results demonstrate the existence of codes with finite length that approach optimal performance, and we show that these codes are attainable through methods involving the hybrid and soft Viterbi algorithms. Our findings also reveal that these codes can be generated from repeated sequences of the communication channel, known as the repeated channel, and provide a formula to calculate the information transmitted per repetition of the repeated channel. This formula utilizes the maximum mutual information between the repeated channel's input and output sequences. Our results further show that the information transmitted per repetition of the repeated channel provides a lower bound on the information transmitted per trial of the original channel, and we show that this information transmission rate achieves the classical shannon theorem's optimal rate under these specific conditions. Furthermore, our results generalize the concepts of finite state compression, expanding it to applications involving multiple input sequences and confirming that the transmitted information remains within a finite boundary. This boundary is calculated as the maximum information transmitted per trial of the original channel multiplied by the trial number. A theoretical model demonstrating the concept of spin-singlet topological superfluidity is established in a two-dimensional gas with Rashba spin orbit coupling and attractive interactions, supported by experimental evidence in certain materials. Under specific conditions, as in the case of half-filling in the presence of electron pairing, the Rashba term's tunability via applied magnetic fields incurs a Chern number change, thereby creating a second-order topological superfluid phase via a quantum phase transition. This spin-singlet topological superfluid phase is characterized by both zero and two Chern numbers, separating the phase at half-filling and filling levels, respectively. This novel superfluid phase exhibits distinct properties, such as fractionalization, nonAbelian character, and supporting zero-energy nodal rings, distinct to both gapped and zero-energy states. These properties can be observed through both numerical and analytical analyses using exact diagonalization and variational approaches on a torus. These findings indicate the capability of the Rashba-harmonized system to showcase a diverse array of quantum phases. Additionally, this study provides an approach to categorize and differentiate topological phases, such as superfluid phases, based on spin-symmetry despite the presence of dynamic spin degeneracy. This study also proposes an experimental design to identify the spin-singlet topological superfluidity by means of interferometry using a spin-polarized atom optical microscope. Ultimately, this theoretical model presents an attractive framework for realizing spin-singlet topological superfluidity through the combination of Rashba spin orbit coupling and attractive interactions in two-dimensional gases. This theoretical model may be applied to the development of novel quantum technologies based on topological superfluidity. This study involves two key areas: verifying factual information and uncovering supporting evidence within scientific documents. To address these challenges, a new dataset called SEM-TAB-FACTS was created for the 2021 SemEval competition. This data set consists of two-section papers that include a marked-up tabular section and an unstructured text segment. Contestants were asked to verify individual table cells containing quantitative data and locate corresponding references in the document's text section that match the values found in the tables. This proof-discovery component requires more complex reasoning skills compared to traditional fact verification tasks. To measure success, two metrics were employed: mean average precision at k=5 and mean average precision at k=10. A total of 15 teams entered the competition, with 5 teams specifically focused on addressing the proof-discovery challenge. The winning teams used various transformer-based models, incorporating data augmentation techniques and table-based evidence for informing text-based proof retrieval tasks. In a secondary evaluation, we analyzed the impact of using table evidence for guiding proof discovery and discovered a notable 9.0% relative improvement in the mean average precision at k=5 when incorporating this approach. When comparing the mean ranks of the top teams in our competition, we found that the new method of using table evidence had a statistically significant 94.7% relative improvement over the original mean rank. Finally, we determined that a particular team, named 'tData', achieved the best overall mean average precision at k=5 with a 0.07 ranking improvement greater than the runner-up, named 'tData2'. This abstract will focus on presenting the underlying principles of IUI, with a particular emphasis on the relevance of intrinsically linked quantities in quantum physics, before delving into a comparative analysis with other interpretations of quantum physics in a subsequent publication. The graph property of being a complete graph is closely linked to its vertex set ordering, which means that the shortest path distance between any two vertices in a complete graph corresponds to their relative position in the ordered set. Building upon this connection, we introduce the concept of shortened metric dimension by adapting the metric dimension formula for complete graphs. The metric dimension of a graph is defined as the minimum number of vertices needed to form a linear ordering of the graph, where the position of each vertex in the ordering is determined by its distance to the reference vertices. In contrast, the shortened metric dimension is the minimum number of vertices needed to form a linear ordering of the graph, where each vertex's position is determined by its distance to the reference vertices, but with distances truncated to the top k closest paths. We investigate the relationship between the metric dimension, shortened metric dimension, and other graph parameters such as the graph's diameter and the number of vertices. Specifically, for finite graphs, we prove a number of upper bounds on the shortened metric dimension that take into account the graph's diameter and the number of vertices, and we demonstrate that these upper bounds are tight. Moreover, we enforce the assumption that k is less than or equal to a certain fraction of the graph's diameter for our results to hold. The goal behind this assumption is to create a useful metric dimension property that can be utilized in specific graph types. We test our theoretical findings on various graph applications, including circulant graphs, grid graphs, and torus graphs. Additionally, we introduce a metric dimension sampling algorithm that utilizes the graph's diameter and the number of vertices to determine a sampled set that can form a linear ordering of the graph. The effectiveness of this algorithm is then evaluated on the graph diameter problem, where it achieves comparable results to existing algorithms. Specifically, the sampled set obtained through our algorithm is shown to have a diameter no greater than three times the graph's actual diameter, and the number of vertices in the sampled set is proportional to the graph's logarithm. Therefore, the algorithm can be employed effectively when the graph's parameters satisfy a particular condition. We provide extensive numerical evidence and experimentation on various graph applications to validate our theoretical findings. Ultimately, the goal behind our research is to develop a useful graph property, where the position of each vertex in the ordered graph is determined by its distance to the reference vertices with some distances truncated to the top k closest paths, and we introduce the concept of shortened metric dimension to achieve this goal. Current state-of-the-art systems for applied logic can provide certain conclusions 
based on certain assumptions, but often struggle with cases that are inherently 
ambiguous.  As a result, these systems tend to treat all information as certain 
and treat irrelevant facts as true, which can lead to inaccurate conclusions. 
This study proposes a new representation framework, called Acyclic Decision Forests 
(ADF), that can represent and draw conclusions from knowledge bases affected by 
quantified uncertainty, utilizing specialized rules.  Using this framework, we 
can redefine frequently used concepts, like decision trees and forests, with 
clear definitions and demonstrate that key properties, such as uniqueness and 
unfalsifiability, can be maintained even in ambiguous cases.  Furthermore, we 
can show that systems based on ADF can still be computationally efficient, 
specifically, complete for fixed-point complexity classes, while remaining sound 
for certain types of conclusions.  Using a simple example, we illustrate how 
ADF Forests can model and draw conclusions from a situation involving a person's 
height, demonstrating the utility of this framework.  Finally, we outline possible 
extensions and applications of ADF, including its potential to describe human 
decision-making and algorithms for generating decision trees.  This research was 
supported by a document that outlines the steps to solve a particular problem in 
deductive systems.  This document can be found at the provided link.

In recent years, deep neural networks have gained significant attention for their outstanding performance in a variety of complex tasks. However, the process they use to make decisions is often difficult for people to understand. As a result, there's a growing need for more transparent models that can provide clear explanations for their predictions. Although some studies have explored using explanation-based learning to improve the interpretability of DNNs, these methods typically rely on simple rule-based models, limiting their ability to tackle complex tasks. A more recent approach involves using concept analysis, a methodological framework within a broader paradigm called concept-based AI, to represent decision-making processes in a more understandable way. By integrating concept analysis with ILP (Inductive Logic Programming), we've developed a novel method that goes beyond traditional DNNs by incorporating the ability to learn interpretable decision boundaries and integrate them into the model. This method has shown promising results in a data set commonly used for evaluating image recognition algorithms. You can find more information about our approach in the attached paper. It includes a detailed description of the method, an evaluation of its effectiveness and some preliminary experiments that indicate it can also be applied to data sets representing natural language and scientific text. These findings suggest that concept analysis can provide a valuable alternative to traditional DNNs by enabling the learning of more transparent models. We're currently exploring ways to extend our approach and make it available to a broader range of tasks. This includes integrating it with DNNs that use other types of data representation, such as vectors and graphs. Additionally, we're working on incorporating a user interface that can assist humans in identifying the key concepts used by the model to make decisions. This interface will enable humans to interact with the model, asking questions and receiving answers in the form of clarifications regarding the model's predictions. These clarifications will provide a simpler explanation for the model's decisions, thereby meeting the growing demand for more transparent deep learning models. The code for our approach is currently being hosted on a public repository. We're willing to collaborate with others by sharing our documents, data and software tools, and are happy to receive feedback and suggestions on how to further develop our method further. With a total integrated luminosity of approximately 137 fb$^{-1}$, the study focused on events where the Z boson rapidly disappears, and only missing energy is recorded. We propose a new set of rules to govern dependencies in transverse momentum, $k_\perp$, for parton distribution functions, which are crucial for understanding the nature of hadrons and underlying quantum chromodynamics. These distribution functions, used to describe the interactions between hadrons and charged particles, must conform to certain requirements. Unfortunately, the rules governing $k_\perp$ dependence are still not well established, which hampers our understanding of certain phenomena, such as the evolution of parton distribution functions and transverse momentum effects in inclusive processes. To address this shortage, we present a comprehensive framework that includes precise formulas for the $k_\perp$ dependence of various distribution functions, such as those for single partons and gluons, and for distribution functions that depend on the relative momentum of two partons. This framework also enables us to derive the rules governing the evolution of parton distribution functions in the presence of interactions between partons. Furthermore, we present a new method for calculating the parton distribution functions of certain hadronic states, such as the pion, without relying on assumptions about their quark-antiquark composition and the relationships between quarks. This novel approach represents a significant advancement in the field and provides a framework for further research. We also report our findings for the gluon parton distribution function of the proton at a low momentum scale of $\sim 1$ GeV, and our results demonstrate that the gluon $k_\perp$ distribution is directed in a direction perpendicular to the proton's momentum, which is an expected characteristic of parton distribution functions within protons. This work also represents the first instance where parton distribution functions of gluons have been calculated using a specific mathematical framework, and our results are consistent with observations from other studies, which show that partons exhibit $k_\perp$ distribution patterns in accordance with the rules of symmetries, for different types of partons. Finally, we present our findings and plan to further explore and analyze our results in future studies. We also make available a computational software tool that can be used to calculate parton distribution functions, which is based on the rules and characteristics that govern them. This software tool can be accessed through the following link: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.hepph.2022.103001. We also outline our plans to extend and enhance this software tool with even more features and capabilities in the future. Their widespread epitaxial application is hindered, however, by the difficulty in controlling their growth mechanisms. Bidders in private auctions often encounter a critical decision point when deciding how much to bid - too little and you'll lose the auction, too much and you'll leave money on the table. Our research explores how bidders calculate this optimal bid amount. We've developed a new metric called the trustworthiness difference (TD) which measures the difference between a bidder's expected revenue when participating in an auction and when withdrawing. Our TD metric varies depending on the auction's rules and offers insight into bidder behavior. In our experimental study, we investigated the effects of TD on bidding patterns in second-price auctions with a variety of private values. Our results show that bidders tend to bid slightly higher than their minimum bid amounts, indicating a degree of risk aversion. We've extended the traditional concept of risk aversion to incorporate trustworthiness, categorizing it into three distinct categories: risk, caution, and cowardice. We've observed a notable shift in bidding patterns among more trustworthy bidders, while less trustworthy bidders' bids remained relatively unaffected. Notably, we've observed a notable presence of cowardly bidders in auctions with larger TDs. In our analysis, we've controlled for a range of factors that might influence bidding, including revenue maximization, risk aversion, and the bid-rigging equilibrium. Our empirical results align with our theoretical predictions, offering a fresh perspective on bidding behavior in second-price auctions. Our research demonstrates the significance of understanding bidder behavior through the lens of auction trustworthiness, offering a fresh perspective on bidding behavior. We've observed that bidder behavior is sensitive to changes in auction trustworthiness, even when bidders privately know their values. By excluding the possibility of bid-rigging, our results reveal a nuanced understanding of bidders' decision-making processes. Our findings are relevant not only to auction settings but also to broader decision-making contexts, where bidders may encounter varying levels of 'trustworthiness'. In retrospect, we've identified key areas of our research that merit further exploration, paving the way for a potential sequel. In our proposed follow-up study, we'll delve into how bidders behave when auction trustworthiness falls outside a certain threshold, as well as how bidders perceive and manage risks associated with uncertain auction outcomes. By addressing these questions, we'll offer a more comprehensive understanding of bidding behavior in second-price auctions. Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a widely prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder typically diagnosed between the ages of 6 to 12. Although the behavior pattern suggests its link to the central nervous system, diagnosing ADHD mainly relies on behavioral observations rather than direct CNS evidence. Recent advancements in diffusion-weighted imaging and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) allow researchers to study ADHD's brain basis more accurately. Past studies used rs-fMRI in various ways, such as identifying common regions between ADHD and control groups or training a model to classify subjects based on individual data. This study aimed to explore the potential of deep learning technology to diagnose ADHD by reducing data complexity while maintaining diagnostic power. Several studies have used rs-fMRI data from ADHD and control subjects, and we conducted ours using a dataset from the ABIDE database, which contains pre-processed data including PCC region. Our results show that incorporating rs-fMRI data into ADHD diagnosis enhances accuracy compared to behavioral observations alone. Additionally, we found that excluding non-essential brain regions reduces data complexity without compromising diagnostic power. These findings indicate the value of rs-fMRI data in enhancing ADHD diagnosis while also highlighting the importance of data reduction strategies to prevent information loss due to data simplification. Ultimately, this study's outcomes may facilitate the development of a diagnostic system combining behavioral and rs-fMRI data to aid in ADHD diagnosis. Quantum Hall systems offer a unique opportunity to study the interaction between electronic transport and heat transfer within highly controlled environments. We investigate a quantum Hall junction setup that enables the realization of distinct thermoelectric states through the manipulation of an interference effect. This finding leads to the possibility of regulating charge transport direction by engaging heat transfer, effectively triggering thermoelectric toggling. Additionally, by adjusting a single magnetic flux quanta, the heat transfer device can be switched between two distinct states with opposing heat flow preferences. The theoretical model supporting these claims is based on coherent tunneling and is accurately described using linearized Boltzmann transport equations, parameterized using a single transport coefficient. Our proposed setup also offers a means to experimentally measure the tunneling matrix element, an important quantity in studying quantum coherent tunneling phenomena. This research contributes to the advancement of quantum thermal technology and may lead to novel applications in quantum thermal charging and dissipation processes. Furthermore, the conceptual framework underlying our findings has broader applicability, potentially influencing the development of quantum thermal machines. The proposed device operations are eligible for observation in existing quantum Hall setups, employing standard measurement techniques and materials. The detailed numerical data supporting our research findings are publicly accessible online. We introduce two variational methods that yield sublinear algorithms for estimating the von Neumann entropy of a mixed quantum state. Both methods leverage a set of unitary operators and their associated states to approximate the entropy. We analyze the algorithms' convergence and provide upper bounds on their convergence rate. Specifically, we show that one method converges at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{K}\log^2(1/\epsilon) \right)$ and the other at a rate of $\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{K}\log^3(1/\epsilon) \right}$, where $K$ represents the number of state preparations. These results hold even in the scenario where the entropy estimate is limited by the information gained from preparing only a single state. We show that existing entropy estimation algorithms are essentially one-shot methods, whereas our approach can leverage prepared states more efficiently. We also present experimental results illustrating the algorithms' performance in approximating entropy on random quantum states and the exponential growth of their convergence rate with state dimension. Additionally, we propose a modification to the algorithms that enables them to remain stable under noisy state preparation conditions. We demonstrate the potential for these algorithms to contribute to studies of quantum Markov chain mixing times, illustrating an exemplary case where their entropy estimates differ from those obtained via sample average approximation methods. Ultimately, we believe these algorithms offer an exciting possibility for reducing the sample complexity involved in such mixing time studies. The code for reproducing the numerical results in this paper can be found at https://github.com/edwardpeters/sublinear-entropy-estimation. To determine the optimal point for a quantum maximum-causality (QMC) query rule in a quantum environment, we compared its performance with traditional Q-learning on a superconducting quantum system. Our research highlighted the challenges posed by the limited coherence time in non-quantum versus quantum supervised learning setups. To overcome these limitations, we developed a novel quantum monitoring technique, quantum variance ratio (QVR), as a substitute for the traditional quantum monitor, variance monitoring (VM). The QVR method demonstrated better performance under non-ideal conditions, leading to a lower probability of state collapse to a non-physical state. Furthermore, we discovered that the QMC rule with both unmonitored and monitored learning may yield suboptimal results, especially in situations with a low coherence time. However, with the assistance of QVR, the QMC rule showed notable performance improvements, up to a 30% gain, in comparison to the traditional Q-learning approach. This study paves the way for the adoption of quantum machines in machine learning applications. The 2018 analysis from the KMTNet observed a significant anomaly, similar to previous anomalies in 2015-2017, with microlensing parallax planes overlapping and then diverging as the anomaly develops. Research on this anomaly is ongoing, with a focus on identifying new anomalies in 2018. To accomplish this, we used the KMTNet data from the prime-field of the Galactic bulge to implement an automated anomaly-detection algorithm. This algorithm successfully detected four anomalies, two of which correspond to microlensing binaries with previously reported anomalous parallax shifts. In addition, we were able to derive the 2018 anomaly's characteristic features, including the anomaly's total shift of $0.24 \pm 0.06$ in the parallax vector's magnitude. To further investigate the cause of these anomalies, we used the sampling rate to analyze various celestial object characteristics related to the anomalies, with a sample of 2018 prime-field anomalies complete at a rate of 5 new anomalies per month per camera system. Further studies are necessary to determine the cause of these anomalies. It is possible that the anomalies are a result of incomplete unblurred sampling, as well as other factors. Shadows play a crucial role in understanding object shapes, but their computation in real-world scenes is complex due to factors like occlusion, depth uncertainty, and surface roughness. In contrast, many existing shadow algorithms are non-differentiable, hindering their application in shape recovery tasks. To address these limitations, we've developed an innovative, efficient, and flexible method for shadow computation, especially useful in real-world settings. Our technique leverages neural networks to estimate shadow maps, taking into account common factors like light source direction, object orientation, and surface normal. Unlike previous methods, our approach is differentiable, enabling seamless integration with variational networks for shape recovery. Furthermore, it incorporates a unique, accurate shadow loss function, enhancing network training and performance. We've thoroughly tested our method on various datasets, achieving superior results compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, we've introduced a novel application of our shadow estimation technique for surface roughness estimation, demonstrating excellent results. The source code for our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/PC-3-TU-Berlin/DeepShadow.Kit.

When the oscillators are only slightly connected, diverse oscillators maintain their individual patterns and move in synchronized groups. As connectivity increases, the array's movement becomes more uniform and synchronized patterns emerge more easily in the array. Furthermore, in a scenario where the majority of oscillators have a simple restoration force, we found that increasing connectivity can lead to the emergence of complex and less common patterns of restoration. A temporary equivalence was discovered between the Aldous-Broder algorithm and Wilson's depth-first spanning forest construction, showing that both methods produce uniform spanning trees with a two-phase approach. The first phase creates a general forest through recursive divisions, and the second phase merges child sub-trees to form a single tree. Furthermore, a direct one-to-one correspondence was established between the generated trees at each stage, which led to a method for efficiently determining the generation time of a uniformly distributed spanning tree. It was also observed that, in the case of Wilson's algorithm, the first tree generated is always a perfect binary tree, and the second phase merely discards child nodes to obtain a spanning tree. Based on these insights, a modified Wilson's algorithm was proposed with reduced memory usage and temporal equvalence to the Aldous-Broder algorithm, which still yields uniform spanning trees. The algorithm reduces memory usage by deleting child nodes before each division, which means only one level of children is kept, effectively reducing the number of levels when expressing the forest as a binary tree. As a result, the forest is still a general binary forest and can be used to obtain a spanning tree. Additionally, a detailed analysis was given of why the first tree generated in Wilson's algorithm is always a perfect binary tree. It was observed that, in the worst case, the first tree would have few child nodes and these nodes would be evenly distributed among its children, which means they would be spread out over multiple levels when expressing the forest as a binary tree. The algorithm was also given theoretical time and space complexities for analyzing its performance, which includes a temporal equivalence analysis and efficient determinism for determining the generation time of a randomly distributed spanning tree. The proposed algorithm was verified using extensive numerical examples to confirm its effectiveness. The development of a single unified model for music representation remains a major challenge, with current methods limited to specific data types such as audio, text, or sheet music. Recent breakthroughs in music representation learning have primarily focused on individual data types, overlooking their combined potential. To bridge this gap, we created a comprehensive music dataset consisting of sheet music, lyrics, and audio, enabling a unified model for music representation learning. Our dataset, MusicTM, features a comprehensive collection of 1,000 songs from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including standard sheet music, translated lyrics, and accompanying audio generated from the original scores. MusicTM is designed to facilitate a range of tasks, such as domain adaptation, data fusion, and multi-task learning. As a test of MusicTM's capabilities, we developed a model that can perform domain adaptation between data types while achieving comparable performance to models optimized for each data type alone. Our model and dataset enhancements are now available to the public.

This research project centers around enhancing the user experience of Ontodia, a diagramming tool, by optimizing its semantic capabilities with natural language processing. We combined Ontdia with various visualizations and searched the Wikidata database using spoken or written queries to create an interactive interface for data exploration. Initially, users can view general information about entities, but collecting and displaying additional characteristics requires subsequent clicks. A comprehensive overview of entity properties can also be obtained from the Wikidata page for a particular entity, enabling users to export selected data or share relevant links. Moreover, we developed enhancements for Ontodia's hub-and-spoke diagramming system, enabling the representation of complex relationships among entities via subsequent clicks. For instance, clicking on an entity in a hub can add a new spoke with related entities, facilitating the exploration of entity connections. Numerical simulations have shown that under specific conditions, this combination of factors can result in the formation of an attractive potential well, where bright solitons emerge. Through both local and global mode analysis, we have determined the conditions under which dark solitons exhibit oscillatory and collapsing behavior. Furthermore, we have derived an analytical equation for the effective Middelham constant and found that negative values of this constant lead to oscillatory behavior, while positive values lead to collapse. We have also found that dark solitons with sufficient energy can collapse, but only in the area surrounding the soliton. We have also determined the conditions under which small changes in the soliton's core can result in the soliton's collapse. We have found that the radius of the potential well, as well as the effective Middelham constant, are directly affected by the soliton's energy. We have also determined the conditions under which the soliton's core's shape does not affect its properties. The effective heat transfer between a fluid flowing through a porous bed and the solid particles that make up the bed is largely determined by the fluid's velocity and the resistance to flow within the bed. Prandtl numbers of the fluids in question enable further insight into the temperature gradients that develop within the bed. Studies have demonstrated that, under specific conditions, heat transfer is not simply proportional to fluid velocity, but rather is influenced by a complex interplay between convection and conduction within the bed. Through the use of rapid Magnetic Resonance Imaging, we have conducted an in-depth examination of the heat transfer process in a stationary gas-solid bed at different flow regimes. Our measurements, taken at different Peclet numbers ranging from 0.06 to 26.4, have allowed us to visualize the temperature distribution within the bed with precision. The resulting data confirm that common correlations used in industry practice, which assume uniform temperature within the bed, are insufficient for accurately predicting heat transfer under all circumstances. In addition, we have recorded temperatures that differ from the average bed temperature by as much as delta T = 0.5 K. The observations made in this study are highly relevant to research into hot air treatment of materials. Furthermore, we have observed that, in cases where the Peclet number is high, the temperature distribution within the bed is not constant, but rather is characterized by a gradient that increases linearly with the distance from the bed's top surface. This phenomenon is thought to be the result of the presence of hot spots within the bed. In cases where the Peclet number is low, the temperature distribution within the bed is not linear, but rather is characterized by a more complex distribution. All of the data collected in this study are available online for public access. Additionally, we have made available a series of films showcasing the temperature distributions within the bed, captured using MRI. Normally, the balance between formation and breakdown of aggregates maintains a thermodynamic equilibrium that supports life. However, this equilibrium can be disrupted by external factors, such as toxins, leading to imbalanced aggregation dynamics. Drawing from examples in biochemistry, we introduce a general theoretical framework for the self-organization of biomolecular aggregates, incorporating multiple species sharing common components through linear thermodynamic relations. In November 2013, a powerful eruption in NOAA AR 11429 triggered an extraordinary wave of disturbances that shook the Sun's rotational system, resulting in the disappearance of several central sunspots over a two-day period. Contrary to initial expectations, our study reveals that the rapid disappearance of sunspots was not solely the result of one dominant large sunspot, but rather the cumulative effect of several smaller sunspots rotating into a leading position, filling the gap left by the missing major spot.
