This series of events points to a complex and interconnected role of low-frequency magnetic signals in the Sun's rotational dynamics. This note addresses one of the key aspects of the b-principle, referred to as the fragile version of the confluence principle. We establish a criterion for confluence applied to a certain geometric structure, denoted as b-geodesic, which is based on a specific combinatorial property called b-distance. This finding complements earlier work presented in arXiv:2201.05046. As an application of this new structure, we prove a novel version of the Mumford conjecture, initially proposed in [Mumford, 91]. Additionally, we derive an alternative formulation of the confluence principle, referred to as the b-transversality theorem. This theorem possesses a versatile nature and can be applied to various other scenarios beyond the b-geodesic structure. It has potential implications and applications in fields such as geometry, PDEs, and condensed matter physics. Wherever the b-principle is applied, the b-transversality theorem emerges as a corresponding effect. We illustrate the power of the b-transversality theorem through several concrete examples. One of these examples resolves the Mumford conjecture. We further demonstrate the versatility of the b-transversality theorem in a wide range of other scenarios, encompassing not only b-geodesic but also other types of situations, such as those involving b-collapse or b-fold structures. In a separate section, we even explore the far-reaching implications of the b-principle on general geometric structures, extending beyond the scope of the precise mathematical definitions and the specific examples examined in this study. This includes a discussion on category-theoretic aspects, along with their potential connections to homotopical algebra and coherent sheaves. We expect the material presented here to contribute to the development of a comprehensive theory of the b-principle in geometry. We hope it serves as a useful resource for those working on related topics and can be used as a versatile toolbox for novel applications. We envision a bright future for research in this field, which we believe will lead to significant breakthroughs in various areas of physics and mathematics. In particular, we anticipate a significant advance in our understanding of the bulk-boundary correspondence, along with the extraction of physical metrics based on the b-geometry structure. We expect this to be accompanied by novel insights into the nature of quantum gravity and black hole physics. We believe the material presented here will lead to novel perspectives and insights in both physical and geometric contexts. The study of cardiac mechanics involves intricate tissue movement, which is governed by mechanical systems within the heart. To simplify this process, a two-dimensional model that assumes fluid is being transported within a heart tissue structure is examined under the principles of the Stokes-Continuity system. To enhance the stability of numerical solutions without regard for problem complexity, an iterative algorithm combining Stokes-Continuity solvers with multilevel corrections is utilized. In a series of numerical experiments, the algorithm's performance is assessed, focusing on 16 different implementations that combine various stochastic multilevel methods with iterative algorithms for the Stokes-Continuity system. To evaluate these implementations, a set of five benchmark tests is developed, which examine both the stability of numerical solutions for different mesh configurations and the accuracy of numerical solutions as grid density decreases. Our findings indicate that some of these implementations exhibit stability on extremely fine meshes, while others do not perform as well, even on coarser meshes. Nonetheless, by analyzing the underlying characteristics of stable implementations, a set of criteria is established that can forecast which algorithms will produce stable results. Consequently, this research enables the efficient development of complex cardiac mechanics simulations using the Stokes-Continuity system, which may be applicable to other complex physical systems. At the same time, our research also reveals a significant challenge in solving the Stokes equation under highly distorted grid configurations and sets the stage for future research aimed at developing stable algorithms for this task. This study conducts an extensive analysis of user-generated tags across seven large-scale image databases, uncovering new insights into the collective behavior of tag creators.  By distinguishing between unique contributors and repeated engagements from the same users, we identify patterns in contribution frequency.  Our observation reveals a power-law distribution for both aspects, indicating exponential decline in likelihood as frequency increases.  By applying time-series analysis, we break down the dynamics of tag creation into components and investigate user activity linked to specific tags.  Through network analysis, we examine collaboration among tag creators and the role of time in shaping these interactions.  Notably, we observe a core group of active contributors driving tag creation and collaboration within these systems.  By comparing system evolution, we reveal time periods influencing tag creation and understand how interest shifts across different datasets.  Our comprehensive analysis sheds new light on the underlying behavior of tag creators, paving the way for a deeper understanding of social tagging systems.  Ultimately, this knowledge may guide developers in designing more effective social annotation tools, informed by collective behavioral patterns and principles of social complexity.  Code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/dsbox-tuberlin/Understanding-Tag-Creation.  Datasets have been made available here: https://github.com/dsbox-tuberlin/Understanding-Tag-Creation/tree/master/data.  Datasets were selected based on availability, closure and modularity, reverse engineering, and quality (as measured by tag density).  Specifically, these datasets include SteadyState, ImageNet, Flickr, Delicious, Technorati, CiteULike, and CiteULike2 with respective sizes of 105K, 21M, 1.2B, 181M, 1.2B, 35.6K, and 35.6K.  Tags were analyzed using the Semeval2010 toolkit. Implementing interactive augmented reality (AR) on mobile devices through Internet of Things (IoT) devices via wireless connections like Bluetooth LE is gaining traction in the industry and among researchers. Bluetooth LE's low power consumption and data transmission capabilities make it an ideal choice for supporting mobile AR applications that rely on IoT devices. This paper serves as an updated introduction to the mobile Internet of Augmented Binary (IAB) technology, providing an updated overview of related concepts, techniques, and methodologies, as well as discussing potential challenges and obstacles. Furthermore, the paper outlines a plan to address these issues through IAB-related research and presents possible areas for future investigation. Key areas of investigation include IoT device discovery, data transmission, and processing to support AR functionality, as well as enabling secure mobile-device-to-IoT connections. Potential research avenues are also identified to support the development of mobile AR applications using IoT devices, such as enabling multi-device connections, supporting 3D rendering, and promoting the adoption of mobile AR across various industries. These research directions are anticipated to contribute significantly to the development of mobile AR on IoT devices, shaping the future of mobile IAB technology and its applications. This work is expected to spark further research and serve as a foundation for ongoing investigations within the mobile IAB community. Specifically, the following topics will be explored: implementing secure IoT connections, optimizing data transmission, and enhancing the overall user experience through mobile AR applications. Advances in these areas will drive the advancement of mobile IAB technology and its widespread adoption across diverse applications. Key words: mobile IAB, IoT, Augmented Reality, AR, Bluetooth LE, Internet of Things, discovery, security, 3D rendering, multi-device connections. In this study, we assessed the performance of six global sensitivity analysis methods on the hyperparameters of seven evolutionary algorithms, including their ranking and efficiency. To this end, we conducted extensive experiments involving 21 sampling scenarios, 13 benchmark functions, and 13 investment problems, obtaining a vast number of samples for analysis. Our results indicated that the performance of these methods varied significantly depending on the type of hypersparameter, optimization problem, and benchmark function. Nevertheless, the Pearson's correlation and effect size metrics proved effective in comparing the performance of these methods. Interestingly, the global sensitivity analysis failed to capture the optimal hyperparameters for these algorithms, suggesting the presence of interaction effects between hyperparameters. To address this issue, we proposed a method for assessing the local performance of evolutionary algorithms, showing that their efficiency and ranking improve as the number of function evaluations increases. Furthermore, we observed consistent trends in the performance of these algorithms across different benchmark functions and investment problems. To validate the findings of this study, we compared the performance of genetic algorithms with and without global sensitivity analysis, revealing a substantial time-saving advantage for the latter. Given the diversity of scenarios in which these methods performed well, we identified and presented the most suitable global sensitivity analysis methods for future research. Based on our observations, we also recommend adjusting the hyperparameters of these algorithms based on their rank rather than their absolute value, as this may accelerate their convergence. To facilitate the replication of this study, we made available the source code, benchmark functions, and results on diverse platforms. Additionally, we provided a comprehensive roadmap for researchers to follow in the future. In a words, global sensitivity analysis offers numerous perspectives for the optimization of evolutionary algorithms, suggesting a range of potential applications beyond hyperparameter tuning. To summarize, this study provides a comprehensive overview of global sensitivity analysis, showcasing its potential as a guiding principle for the optimization of evolutionary algorithms. These inequalities are rooted in a fundamental property of the Laplacian in quantum mechanics, namely the min-max principle, which is a key aspect of our discussion. The conclusions reached are particularly relevant to our work on a recent open problem in PDEs and quantum mechanics, where similar methods were initially not sufficiently conclusive. This can hinder the transfer of RL algorithms to real-world applications, as they may not be adequately trained on diverse environments representative of such challenges. To address this issue, we present L2Explorer, a comprehensive framework that enables the training and testing of RL algorithms on a vast array of learning-to-learn challenges. This adaptive infrastructure automatically generates various environment configurations based on predefined rules, effectively expanding the scope of evaluation for RL algorithms. Through L2Explorer's support, researchers can engage in comprehensive evaluations of their algorithms, thereby increasing their confidence in their work and facilitating fair comparisons with existing methods. To showcase the utility of this resource, we have conducted an in-depth evaluation of multiple state-of-the-art RL algorithms on a range of learning-to-learn problems. Our results reveal that L2Explorer offers precise control over the evaluation process, allowing for the discovery of situations in which existing algorithms may struggle. This illustrates the potential for L2Explorer to streamline RL algorithm development and promote more effective benchmark design. In particular, we show that these waves' trajectories decay at a rate of $e^{-(\frac{1}{2}-\epsilon)\lambda^2t}$ where $\lambda$ is a small positive constant, for any given $\epsilon>0$. We establish a partial Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture by showing that if A is a subset of the integers with k elements, then for any ε greater than zero, there exist two disjoint subsets B and C of A such that the sum of the counts of B and C is less than (3 + ε)k, and for any x value, the difference between the sums of B and C with respect to x is less than (3 + ε)k. This involves creating two subsets of A that are 'far' apart based on an iterative construction method that splits A into parts with varying sizes and applies a structural theorem for sums of sets. This proves a strengthened version of a theorem initially demonstrated by Ruzsa in 2005. Moreover, this result holds true in both the integers and finite groups under specific conditions. Furthermore, we show that Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture having a subexponential time complexity is undecidable. To do this, we illustrate a computational problem by constructing a model that generates inputs from a specific sequence, and demonstrate that solving this problem in an exponential time leads to a resolution of the conjecture, but since it cannot be solved in an exponential time, it remains undecidable. Finally, we propose a more limited conjecture related to the minority situation, namely that if A's minimum value exceeds its maximum value, and the sums of its subsets with respect to x differ, then there exist two disjoint subsets B and C of A such that the sum of the counts of B and C is less than (3 + ε)k. This leads to the possibility that Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture may not always have a minority situation equivalent to it. We also consider the minority situation in finite groups under specific conditions. Additionally, we show that Freiman's 3k-4 conjecture can be decomposed into two distinct problems, namely a problem in the integers and a problem in finite groups under specific conditions, by illustrating a relationship between their structures. Finally, we propose a problem related to the Freiman isomorphism, namely that if A's sum with respect to x in the integers is less than (3 + ε)k, and B's sum with respect to y in the integers is less than (3 + ε)k, then there exist two bijections such that A's images under x and y overlap minimally, and their sums with respect to x and y in the integers are close in value. X-ray images of COVID-19 patients contain information about lung inflammation, which can indicate the severity of the disease. Severe cases often require ICU admission, which can predict the outcome of hospital treatment. Unfortunately, the process of predicting outcomes from X-ray images is complicated by inconsistent correlations between image characteristics and treatment needs. 

This research presents a set of image characteristics, or cytokines, linked to ICU admission in patients suffering from COVID-19 pneumonia, which has not been established previously. Our findings reveal that combinations of lung inflammation areas, peripheral distribution, and upper-lost patterns can effectively forecast the necessity for ICU care. 

To establish these cytokines, we analyzed a large collection of COVID-19 patient X-rays, developing a unique set of patterns that incorporate both location and severity. Unlike traditional approaches, our method acknowledges the uncertainty of reading clinical expertise directly from imaging data. 

To quantify uncertainty, we employed Bayesian neural networks, which generate probability distributions of treatment needs rather than definitive answers. Our model identified a subset of its inputs, or cytokines, that can accurately predict the need for ICU care. 

With these cytokines established, we developed a simplified model that can forecast the need for ICU admission in patients suffering from COVID-19 pneumonia. Our model combines clinical judgment with quantifiable uncertainty, resulting in a more comprehensive understanding of patient treatment needs. 

Our results show that this model can accurately forecast the need for ICU care up to one week in advance, which is a critical window for hospital resource allocation. Our method and findings contribute to ongoing efforts in predicting COVID-19 patient outcomes from X-ray images, which holds potential for applications in critical care medicine. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. 

Our research highlights the potential for using cytokine analysis in lung conditions to forecast patient outcomes, which has yet to be explored in clinical settings. Our model demonstrates the value of combining patient imaging data with clinical expertise to forecast the need for critical care, which is particularly crucial during public health emergencies like the pandemic. 

Our findings are consistent with established medical knowledge, revealing that severe COVID-19 cases often require ICU admission. Our model predicts existing medical patterns, which serves as a test of its accuracy and reliability. Our research did not discover any unexpected relationships between image characteristics and treatment needs. 

Our findings reveal that forecasting the need for ICU admission in patients suffering from COVID-19 pneumonia is feasible, which has yet to be established previously. Our model combines patient imaging data with clinical expertise to accurately predict treatment needs, which holds potential for applications in critical care medicine

We investigate the problem of identifying a spherical interface separating two materials with given refractive indices under the transformation eigenvalue problem. Specifically, we demonstrate that unique recovery of the interface occurs whenever the interface separates two distinct material regions. Our proof relies on the application of unique continuation theorems and simple geometric reasoning. Additionally, we provide numerical examples to validate our findings and observe that multiple solutions may exist in cases where the interface divides a single material region into two separate areas. These solutions can be distinguished by their rotation symmetry. Our findings suggest that unique recovery is possible under specific conditions, and we offer recommendations for further exploration of this problem. Our recommendations involve designing experiments that take advantage of the lexicographic order of the complex-valued transmission eigenfunctions. We observe that unique recovery occurs not only in the case of spherical interfaces but also in cases involving planar and convex boundaries, and our observations lead to intriguing theoretical and practical questions in the context of boundary value problems. Our proof of recovery and various numerical examples serve to illustrate the inherent connections between transmission eigenvalue problems, convex optimization, and (directionally unobstructed) boundary value problems. Our unique recovery results in spherical cases offer contributions to the fields of inverse scattering and inverse spectral problems, and we note that our processes are computationally feasible, requiring only numerical solvability of the associated direct problem. In light of our findings, we propose an algorithm for recovering a planar interface using directional transmission eigenfunctions, and our examples highlight the practical significance of rotating directions in facilitating boundary recovery. Our analysis and numerical examples indicate that an abundance of directional solutions exists, and these solutions can facilitate the recovery of sharp boundaries via rounding off corners. Our investigations into spherical systems have broader applications to problems involving radial Schr\"odinger operators and the inverse scattering problems unique to these contexts. In examining the requirements for our recovery protocol, we arrive at key insights regarding the necessary conditions for boundary recovery, and we develop a simplified model to illustrate the theoretical underpinnings of our findings. Detectors play a pivotal role in detecting visual objects and associating them with potential hazards; however, they are inherently prone to making error-positive predictions, which can have disastrous consequences. In the context of aviation, for instance, detecting a non-threatening object like a cloud instead of an actual obstacle could lead to hazardous consequences. Current methods excel at minimizing error-positives but ultimately fail to consider the inherent danger posed by error-positives in high-impact scenarios. To address this shortcoming, we introduce a prototype network, designed in response to a real-world aviation challenge, that tackles the unique problem of visual association detection with a focus on mitigating error-positives. By leveraging pre-trained object detectors and incorporating a prototype extractor, the network learns to detect both objects and potential hazards, while also associating them based on spatial proximity and semantic similarity. Notably, our approach refrains from relying on expensive annotation techniques and instead utilizes readily available data to train high-performing models that excel in a range of detection tasks, from general object detection to more specialized scenarios like avalanche detection. Additionally, we introduce a set of rigorous evaluations to assess the robustness and reliability of these models. Our research demonstrates the potential for detection models to greatly benefit from a thorough understanding of their error-positives and the unique requirements of high-impact visual association detection tasks. The code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/fortinpierrick/protodet. By comparing the top-1 accuracy and the $$\mathcal{M}$$-index of high-impact visual association detection models, we showcase the potential for a better understanding of detection performance, leading to improved models in such scenarios. The approach involves finding the minimal amount of entanglement between the measurer and measured system for a given weak measurement. It is anticipated that overcoming these hurdles will play a crucial role in the widespread adoption of quantum neural networks. As a case study, we examine the implementation of the QNTL scheme in PyTorch and its application to the MNIST dataset using the quantum computer's ability to leverage varying coherence times, a crucial factor in achieving better results. In the past three years, a new generation of muon colliders has emerged as a viable option for both particle physics and nuclear physics research. A high-energy muon collider could serve as the world's premier particle smasher, while a low-energy variant could revolutionize our understanding of nuclear matter. This presentation will provide an overview of the current state of muon colliders, their proposed benefits, the challenges physicists face, and recent breakthroughs achieved in the field. Specifically, the talk will discuss design concepts for both collider and non-collider muon storage rings, recent advancements in muon technology, and the ongoing efforts to overcome the main obstacle standing in the way of realizing this innovative research facility – the extreme difficulty of accelerating muons. Fortunately, in the past few years, researchers have made substantial progress in addressing this challenge by developing innovative new ideas and techniques. This talk will present some of these solutions, which hold the promising potential of bringing muon colliders one step closer to reality. Additionally, the presentation will touch on the role of theoretical particle physics in informing the design of this futuristic research facility. Particle physicists have been utilizing advanced computational tools to simulate various aspects of muon colliders, such as muon collision rates and energy consumption, in order to gain a more precise understanding of the physics and technology underlying these machines. This simulation work has already led to valuable insights and could further applications in the field of high-energy research in the future. Overall, this talk aims to convey the rapid progress being made in the field and the widespread excitement among physicists about the potential of muon colliders to revolutionize our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter. Unfortunately, the presentation will also address a persistent concern – the fear that, given the current rate of progress, researchers might miss their window of opportunity to develop the collider by allowing themselves to become overconfident in the ease of addressing the acceleration challenge. Analyzing texts at scale relies heavily on scalable text understanding methods that can be applied without manual supervision, including both text classification and text modification tasks. Recent advances in pre-trained language models have made it feasible to apply text understanding techniques even with minimal training data involved. Despite this, existing text understanding methods often require a substantial amount of labeled data or extensive monitoring to refine their performance. We propose the introduction of two text analysis techniques that can operate effectively without monitoring labeled data in operation, or without needing any at all. The first technique fine-tunes pre-trained models using data augmentation strategies to achieve good results with minimal monitoring. The second technique eliminates the need for monitoring data entirely, using a small amount of example text to achieve good results. Both techniques are evaluated on three text classification tasks and three text modification tasks, achieving high levels of accuracy across various benchmarks including classification accuracy of 94% on T-NEWS with minimal monitoring and 92% without any monitoring at all with few-shot learning. The code for these experiments is publicly available.

Traditional approaches to semantic image segmentation, which involve categorizing pixel values, often struggle with pixel ambiguity, where multiple classes intersect. This issue is particularly prevalent in urban settings, such as when roads meet sidewalk areas. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method called Weakly-supervised Semantic Partitioning (WSP). WSP uses label-free hyperspectral imagery and relies on spectral analysis to efficiently segment urban scenes. By creating a spectral model from training images, WSP identifies distinct regions corresponding to relevant cityscape categories. This model is then refined using spatial constraints to maintain coherent pixel groups. As a result, WSP produces seamless, class-separated masks, matching the format needed for standard semantic segmentation tasks. To validate WSP, we set up an experimental framework, including an created dataset called Hyperspectral Urban Dataset (HUD), consisting of 200,000+ pixel labels and 20+ urban class categories. When tested against conventional semantic segmentation methods, WSP demonstrated superior performance on the HUD dataset. Code and dataset are available on GitHub for review. This work offers the first hyperspectral solution to urban semantic segmentation, a pioneering approach with extensive potential applications in urban settings. 
Keywords: semantic segmentation, urban environments, hyperspectral imagery, weakly-supervised learning.

The rotation periods of exoplanets, particularly those with close orbital distances to their host stars, show unusual and unpredictable trends. Research has revealed that planets in close orbit around low-mass stars have significantly longer rotation periods than expected, whereas those in close orbit around high-mass stars have significantly shorter rotation periods than expected. These patterns are not consistent with any previously proposed mechanisms. One possible explanation for these varying rotation periods is that planets in close orbit around low-mass stars experience energy absorption from their host stars, causing them to slow down, while planets in close orbit around high-mass stars may experience energy absorption but also experience an additional energy-absorbing process, possibly related to the interaction between starlight and the planet's atmosphere. An alternative hypothesis is that there is an unseen angular momentum transfer between the planet and its surroundings. Future observational studies should focus on gathering more data to determine if energy absorption is responsible for these patterns by expanding the scope to include planets in close orbit around intermediate-mass stars. Additionally, theoretical models should be developed to assess the significance of energy absorption and the potential for atmospheric erosion in shaping these rotation period patterns. Future theoretical studies should specifically focus on understanding energy absorption and the potential for atmospheric erosion in planets orbiting close to low-mass stars, particularly those involving electromagnetic forces. An important area of research is also identifying how energy absorption and other processes affect the planets' physical appearance and whether this includes changes in the planet's shape, composition, and the presence of a global ocean. It is crucial to develop a more comprehensive understanding of these processes and the resulting changes at the planetary level in order to develop a more complete picture of the long-term evolution of planets in close orbit around their host stars. Finally, the potential for atmospheric erosion, particularly in planets orbiting close to low-mass stars, should be explored through energy absorption in future studies, as well as the resulting changes to the planet's angular momentum. An important area of research is also identifying the potential for internal acoustic waves and their impact on the long-term rotation periods of the planets. These acoustic waves could be triggered by the energy absorption, as well as other processes such as the interaction between starlight and the planet's atmosphere, as described in a study published in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics. These internal acoustic waves could provide an alternative explanation for the observed patterns in the rotation periods of the planets. As suggested in a study published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Planets, future research should specifically focus on understanding energy absorption and the potential for internal acoustic waves

Code theory's key component, the Reed-Muller code, is renowned for its ease of decoding and high error-correction capacity. Researchers have developed various methods to expand this property, leading to the creation of LCM codes. This paper introduces two novel code families, Group LCM codes and Group Reversible LCM codes, whose codesets are derived from division rings. We establish a direct relationship between these codesets and the sets of greatest common divisors or their reversals, developed by Gaudry and their counterparts. We then prove that both code families possess the LCM property and present specific examples for the Group LCM codes. We also investigate the properties of its dual codes, particularly focusing on the existence of orthogonal dual codes in the Group Reversible LCM codes family. We introduce an index to measure the rate of these special codes. We further present a method to find the weights distribution of the codes from the Gaudry sets, which provides a crucial tool for analyzing the performance of these codes. We then provide examples of the Group Reversible LCM codes with desirable properties, such as a specific code having a long minimum weight and high rate. We also investigate low-density parity-check (LDPC) decoding properties of the Group Reversible LCM codes. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm to find LDPC codes derived from the Group Reversible LCM codes. We then present numerical results on the decoding performance of these LDPC codes. In the complex world around us, effective information processing relies heavily on categorizing objects based on relevant characteristics. For instance, when driving, recognizing a car shapes your behavior, and identifying a sedan versus a truck directs your actions. In artificial intelligence, especially with visual data, using characteristics like shape and size typically involves manual analysis. However, this becomes highly challenging with large datasets containing diverse objects. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have led to the development of robust object recognition systems through machine learning, yet the essential role of characteristics in these systems is not well understood. This study investigates how characteristics guide information processing in a recurrent neural network trained for object classification by decomposing the network into distinct functional categories based on characteristic types and then assessing information flow between these categories. Our findings indicate that information processing in the network is indeed directed by category-specific characteristics, with information primarily transferred between categories in an orthogonal manner. This understanding can streamline artificial intelligence systems by targeting task-specific characteristic sets for better performance. Additionally, this research demonstrates a method to analytically dissect complex neural systems and understand local data processing strategies. This approach, called the 'category-orthogonal method,' can be applied to various neural architectures and contexts to uncover general principles governing information processing in artificial neural networks. Ultimately, this research contributes to developing more effective and characterised models of artificial neural systems. We investigate how interactions influence the topological characteristics of non-Hermitian one-dimensional systems, which are inherent in the Jordan block structure. Our findings show that even weak interactions can eliminate the topological features of the non-Hermitian systems we studied, which are classified in the BDI symmetry class with chiral charge q. This loss of topological characteristics is quantified by analyzing how the Jordan block's Jordanian structure evolves under various interaction strengths. Additionally, we verify our theoretical predictions using numerically generated one-dimensional non-Hermitian tight-binding models with nearest-neighbor hopping. Based on our results, we deduce that in multi-body interacting systems, the topological features can be diminished but not fully eliminated. This study lays the groundwork for further exploration into how interactions affect topological characteristics in higher-dimensional systems and delves into the relationship between quantum many-body states and the Jordan block structure. Moreover, our work may contribute to the realization and manipulation of topological phenomena in experimental setups featuring optical or cold-atom systems. By pushing the boundaries of topological physics, this research may enable the realization of topological quantum technologies. Lastly, our study highlights the topological physics' intricate connections with the mathematical concepts of Jordan blocks and algebraic algebras. This leads to an interesting link between quantum topology and the dimensional transitions within these algebraic systems. Ultimately, this new connection may pave the way for an entirely novel understanding of topological physics, particularly its linkage to the topological dimentionality of the underlying algebraic system. In recent years, deep convolutional autoencoders have emerged as a leading method for unsupervised alteration detection in hyperspectral images. The novelty of this research lies in an integrated feature integration technique alongside a deep convolutional autoencoder architecture, specifically designed for hyperspectral image alteration recognition. The Deep Convolutional Autoencoder with Integrated Features, or DCAIF, consists of a preliminary autoencoder stage that extracts essential spectral features from the hyperspectral image, and then merges the spatial and spectral features through a integrated feature integration process. The resulting combined features enable an effective and unsupervised alteration recognition capability within the constructed network. Following the training of the DCAIF network, a two-class support vector machine classifier is applied to the integrated features, obtained from the two deepest autoencoder stages, to categorize pixels as intact or altered. The efficacy of this method was validated through experiments using the public AirOrot dataset, and the results show that the DCAIF method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques by 4.46% percentile index values. The associated code for this research is accessible on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/zhengheng0821/DC-AEHF. The research was funded by the National Science Foundation under Grant No. U1878972. The hyperspectral datasets used in this research can be sourced from the following links: https://science.oregonstate.edu/~jennyrm/remote_sensing_data/NoClassAirOrot.hsi and https://science.oregonstate.edu/~jennyrm/remote_sensing_data/ClassAirOrot.hsi. With a computational complexity of O(N^3), where N represents the number of pixels in the hyperspectral image, this method enables efficient and scalable alteration recognition capabilities. The proposed DCAIF method has been successfully applied to a range of real-world hyperspectral image alteration recognition scenarios. By integrating molecular building blocks with intrinsic valley exchange, we demonstrate the ability to control spin transfer through valley selection. Furthermore, our experimental findings in silicon/hafnium oxide structures reveal an inherent valley mixing effect, where valley exchange is converted into spin transfer. Utilizing variable-temperature and magnetic field measurements, we isolate the contribution of valley interactions over spin exchange. Ultimately, our research validates the utilization of intrinsic valley exchange in silicon as a driving force for spin transfer in quantum technologies. Given that our experiment uses a classical spin detector, we anticipate that employing quantum spin detectors will enhance the observation of valley exchange beyond current limitations. Consequently, this research paves the way for the development of novel valley-controlled spin devices. Additionally, our results contribute to the expansion of knowledge regarding valley interactions in silicon, making it a viable candidate for generating intrinsic valley-specific effects that cannot be replicated in traditional GaAs quantum billiards. Finally, our research encourages future investigations into the unique properties of valley exchange in silicon, particularly when combined with additional qubits and control mechanisms. Several established frameworks previously attempted to unify various optimization algorithms used in engineering applications. However, these frameworks often posed challenges for researchers who relied on them, including difficulties in open-source collaborations and the reproduction of experimental results. To address these issues, we present a new framework called LibOPT, which allows for the easy implementation and testing of novel ideas related to combinatorial optimization. With a focus on practicality, LibOPT was developed using widely accepted programming languages and techniques to make it highly adaptable and compatible with existing tools. In map display, especially when zoomed in on vector maps, an aliasing effect occurs, causing lines to appear jagged, which can be mitigated by anti-aliasing. However, the common anti-aliasing methods used for raster images fail to produce seamless line patterns. In this study, we introduce an anti-aliasing algorithm that employs a phosphor pattern map to eliminate jaggedness. The map is divided into tiles, and a color gradient is calculated for each tile to mitigate aliasing, which are then combined to produce a high-quality visual representation. By testing this algorithm on various types of vector maps, we found it to be at least 30% faster than existing methods. Furthermore, we developed an implementation of this algorithm based on client-side web mapping technology that allows for seamless map navigation. To optimize performance, we also introduced several techniques, including using a pre-rendered cache to store map images and utilizing GPU acceleration for rendering. which can be found at https://github.com/Esri/exmapssaa. A demonstration of this algorithm can be found at https://www.esri.com/mapstudio/saa. To validate the effectiveness of our algorithm, we conducted user studies involving professional cartographers and programmers, who collectively provided feedback on the visual quality and performance of the anti-aliasing algorithm. The results of these studies revealed a 100% consensus among test subjects that anti-aliased lines appear more suitable for visual mapping. Based on this feedback, we revised and refined our algorithm to address their concerns. Additionally, we explored the feasibility of incorporating our algorithm into established web and desktop mapping software platforms. To facilitate this integration, we developed a set of open-source anti-aliased line filters that can be used in place of existing line rendering filters in these platforms. A detailed description of this integration can be found in the companion paper. To summarize, the key contributions of this research are: (1) an anti-aliasing algorithm that employs a phosphor pattern map to eliminate jaggedness; (2) open-source anti-aliased line filters that can be used in place of existing line rendering filters in web and desktop mapping software platforms; (3) a set of techniques for optimizing the performance of these filters; and (4) a comprehensive evaluation of the effectiveness and efficiency of these filters. One significant issue with nonconvex optimization, prominent in machine learning model training, is the potential for local minima and non-convergent algorithms. To address this, researchers have been introducing various modifications to optimization algorithms, however, the field still lacks a comprehensive theory that explains how these modifications can avoid getting stuck in local minima. To bridge this gap, our work focuses on understanding how to modify an iterative optimization method, specifically the gradient descent, to guarantee asymptotic global convergence. In this context, we propose the Organizing Convexity Hypothesis (OCH) which postulates that optimizing a nonconvex function over a nonconvex set using a gradient-like direction results in an organizing convexity sequence leading to a global convergence. OCH leads to the global convergence of any iterative method satisfying specific criteria, thereby empowering algorithm designers to develop their own optimizing algorithms. We also examine specific cases, such as when the nonconvexity constraint arises from a nonincreasing distance function, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our organizing convexity framework in this setting. Furthermore, we apply the organizing convexity framework to subgradient methods, yielding the Organizing Convexity Subgradient Descent (OCSD) algorithm. Through numerical tests on various machine learning tasks, including neural network training and matrix factorization, we show that OCSD achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Notably, our best-performing method, the generalized Organizing Convexity Gradient Descent (GOCGd), outperformed vanilla gradient descent by an average of 81% and performed competitively with regards to memory, matching the performance of more sophisticated algorithms such as Adam and Adagrad. Furthermore, our organizing convexity framework is versatile and can be applied to a range of algorithms, including momentum-based algorithms, and we demonstrate GOCGd's efficacy in low-resource settings like training sparsely connected neural networks and neural tangent kernel learning. In summary, our research proposes the Organizing Convexity Hypothesis, a comprehensive framework that explains how to modify iterative optimization methods to guarantee global convergence in nonconvex problems, and we demonstrate the efficacy of this framework through numerical tests and show that a wide range of algorithms, including those with added features like momentum and learning rate adaptation, can achieve superior performance in nonconvex optimization tasks. Additionally, our work is accompanied by extensive supplementary material including additional theoretical results, derivations, and experimental training details. To promote reproducibility, we have open-sourced our code

The source J2102+6015 is a very powerful blazar-like object that was initially detected as a radio emission in the 1990s and has been studied using high advanced radio and optical technologies in recent years. This research includes highly sensitive optical spectra taken in 2019, which shows that J2102+6015 has an extremely high redshift of 4.575, making it one of the top five blazar-like objects with the highest redshifts discovered so far. Analysis of the spectral data in the near-infrared to X-ray range cannot be explained by models of a young object passing through a jet-driven gap, or by other established emission models. Instead, its high redshift and unusual properties can be explained by a scenario in which J2102+6015 is a powerful blazar-like object that was young when it was first detected in the 1990s, and has since entered a phase of significant jet activity driven by a major outburst. This explanation is also consistent with the observed changes in its power and spectral shape over the years. Alternatively, the high redshift and unusual properties of J2102+6015 can be explained by a scenario in which it contains two distinct objects: one that is a young, powerful blazar at a lower redshift, and a second object at a much higher redshift that is responsible for the near-infrared and optical emission of the sample source. This second object is a common blazar-like object that is often observed in large surveys. Its light has passed through a massive dust barrier and has then interacted with the massive jet of the first object, causing its emission to be longward of the jet's emission and resulting in the observed high redshift. This second scenario is also consistent with the observed high redshift and unusual properties of J2102+6015. The advent of deep learning has significantly transformed the field of medical image recognition, yet its application to histopathological whole-slide images remains hindered by high manual annotation costs. Capable of capturing diverse histopathological features, these images are essential for accurately diagnosing and treating non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). To overcome the annotation challenge, this research proposes the establishment of an annotated dataset comprising multimodal educational content, including both histopathological images and corresponding genomic data. This dataset can be employed to train a deep learning model for NSCLC classification, thus substituting traditional annotation methods. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, the proposed dataset was utilized to develop and assessed a deep learning model. Evaluation of the model's performance revealed satisfactory outcomes, with the model achieving a classification accuracy of 89% on a previously unseen test set, thus demonstrating the capability to replace traditional annotation methods in deep learning for whole-slide images. Ultimately, this research outlines a feasible approach to creating a comprehensive dataset, providing an alternative solution for deep learning models trained on whole-slide images. This work may serve as a blueprint for developing similar datasets in fields such as digital pathology and histopathology. Additionally, the proposed dataset and associated code have been made publicly available to facilitate further research and replication. This research aims to contribute to the further exploration of multimodal educational content for cost-effective and data-efficient medical image recognition tasks. Experimental results, including the model's performance, code, and publicly accessible dataset, can be found on the following GitHub repository: https://github.com/gsu-bdm-lab/MLFE. Natural language data is extensively employed in state representations for reinforcement learning, particularly in domains that involve text-based input. Existing methods for constructing state descriptions often overlook the hierarchical structure and contextual relationships within language, which can lead to poorly performing solutions. This hierarchy is particularly relevant in domains such as command-level robotics and game playing, where multiple actions are often interdependent and require a deeper understanding of the state's contextual and hierarchical aspects. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of natural language state descriptions in reinforcement learning, focusing on models that utilize language models to generate state descriptions. It also categorizes existing approaches into non-task-specific and task-specific models, highlighting the latter's potential to improve performance by addressing the state description's limited coverage. Moreover, this paper discusses the challenges and limitations associated with language-based state descriptions, such as action duplication and the lack of action feasibility, which may arise due to the language model's training objectives differing from the trained reinforcement learning policy's goals. Consequently, this paper proposes task-specific models that integrate reinforcement learning with language models to produce state descriptions that are optimized for the task at hand. Empirical evidence from such models demonstrates improved performance and solves issues related to action duplication and feasibility. This paper also provides a code repository that includes implemented baselines for natural language state descriptions, such as RNN-based models, hierarchical language models, and joint models that integrate reinforcement and language training. This repository is intended to support future research in natural language state descriptions for reinforcement learning. Hierarchical language models that utilize the state transition probability distribution and other contextual information, such as action feasibility, may also contribute to improved performance. Ultimately, this paper suggests that natural language state descriptions, particularly those based on hierarchical models, hold the potential to greatly enhance the efficacy of reinforcement learning methods in domains that involve text-based input. In such domains, hierarchical state descriptions may lead to performance gains of up to 41.2%, as demonstrated in the experiments, making them a more attractive option for building natural language state descriptions. Specifically, non-task-specific models may achieve better results than task-specific models when the state description's coverage is adequate. By contrast, task-specific models tend to outperform non-task-specific models when the state description's coverage is limited and integrating the reinforcement and language models trains the state description to better fit the task at hand. This research contributes to the advancement of hierarchical state descriptions, particularly those based on recurrent models, by showing that such descriptions may lead to reduced performance compared to task-specific models that integrate reinforcement and language training. social media platforms and may be adapted for other languages with minimal modifications.

features and data-driven methods. Furthermore, we will be employing more advanced machine

results. Finally, we will be using more contemporary machine learning techniques such as
transfer learning and BERT to achieve even better outcomes.

When users navigate through websites, their search intentions may evolve over time, which poses a challenge for search systems to provide relevant suggestions at the right moments. Current recommendation systems have limitations in addressing this issue due to their static nature and reliance on pre-defined user models. To address this gap, we introduce SessionSuggest, a dynamic search assistant that adapts to each user session and incorporates session information to refine suggestion suggestions. To mitigate the risk of suggestions being too intrusive, we allow users to indicate preference or disinterest, which influences future suggestion guidance. To manage suggestion privacy and maintain a positive user experience, we implement a twin-session framework comprising an opaque and transparent session component. The opaque session segment uses anonymized data to provide personalized suggestions, while the transparent segment offers general suggestions based on aggregated data. Both sessions are combined to generate a richer set of relevant suggestions. To address the issue of how to rank relevant suggestions efficiently, we propose CSR, a suggestion ranking model that uses reinforcement learning to optimize the suggestion sequence and user interaction process. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, which outperforms existing benchmark methods by 20-40% or more in terms of relevance and user engagement. The knowledge presented in this paper can be applied to several areas, such as search, recommendations, and chat systems, to enhance user experience. This study focuses on developing novel interactions between human and robots in open spaces. Through human-robot co-observation, we aim to enhance the capabilities of autonomous robots by leveraging information from multiple human sources, without requiring each human to train the robot individually. Instead, multiple humans collaborate to equip the robot with diverse knowledge through collective interactions. To achieve this, a social learning framework is introduced, combining an autonomous robot's online learning process with an optimization method to maximize the collective human-robot interaction profit. The framework is applied to a specific scenario where a robot attempts to gather useful information about its environment through collaborative exploration with humans. The results of our simulations indicate that the proposed approach allows the robot to efficiently gather knowledge from multiple humans, ultimately outperforming a method that relies on individual human specialists. Additionally, key characteristics of effective human-robot interactions are identified, and the significant potential of human-robot co-observation in real-world applications is discussed. The co-learning process between humans and robots has significant implications for areas such as social robotics, affecting aspects like knowledge acquisition, interaction design, and the underlying robotic systems. The development of autonomous robots that can benefit from diverse human perspectives is crucial for the future success of this field. The proposed co-observation method enables robots to benefit from multiple human sources through an optimized collective interaction process. The emerging advancements in autonomous systems may raise important social and ethical concerns related to ownership, as the social learning framework raises questions about the rights to a trained robot. The incorporation of autonomous robots in various industries can lead to increased productivity but also poses concerns about job security, highlighting the need for regulation and ethical consideration in human-robot interactions. The design of autonomous robots should prioritize not only technological capabilities but also social aspects, such as ease of use, to ensure that humans can benefit from these devices. The development of cooperative interactions between humans and robots requires a deeper understanding of social norms to facilitate seamless communication and collaboration. The co-observation method presented in this study can be generalized to other domains, enabling a wide range of applications and ultimately contributing to the advancement of social robotics. The proposed learning framework can be applied to various domains beyond navigation, and its impact on the future of social robotics is discussed. To take advantage of human capabilities, a robot should be designed to learn through diverse human inputs, enabling a more collaborative and efficient human-robot interaction. A possible implementation of the social learning framework in a real-world setting is discussed, and its potential benefits and challenges are identified. Multisensor systems are essential for understanding human interactions with objects.  Real-world point cloud data captured through lidar technology on outdoor public scenes frequently features complex human hand movements, making it necessary to develop engaging hand object interactions from unaligned point clouds.  We present a novel method for tracking hand engagement, reconstructing 3D models, and estimating hand object poses from unaligned point cloud series.  Leveraging a pre-trained engagement detector as a resource for point cloud feature extraction and dimensionality reduction, we apply a network to predict 3D models in various poses, and then utilize ICP algorithms to refine models in engaging poses by aligning predicted points with observed data.  We conduct extensive experiments using a large public dataset and our own setup, comparing our approach with several alternatives, with results showing our method outperforms others in reconstructing diverse hand object engagements and generalizes well to datasets with different settings and objects.  Code and datasets are available for reproduction.  With these capabilities, we envision expanded applications for human engagement analysis in areas like social robotics and human-provided annotations for robotic tasks. For robots to effectively interact with their environment, their physical structure must be accurately represented in relation to their surroundings. In many robotic systems, the relationship between the robot and its coordinates is typically aligned with its design specifications. However, when working in unmarked spaces, relying solely on a robot's pre-defined specifications can be insufficient. To improve target grasping accuracy, researchers have developed an unsupervised learning approach, estimating a robot's end-effector position and orientation in unmarked 3D space using only image data from a depth camera. This method utilizes an fcn with a robot-specific structure incorporated into its internal architecture, enabling direct comparison of image data with the robot's physical structure. As a result, the robot learns to accurately adjust its coordinates and estimate its position in a dynamic environment. Experimental results show significant improvements in target grasping accuracy when using this method over conventional techniques. Notably, this method is versatile and can be applied to various robotic systems without the need for modifications. Further studies are recommended to validate this approach on more complex tasks and with different robots. The source code for this project has been made publicly available. Video demonstrations are available at https://youtu.be/xxk4pV7b3GQ and https://youtu.be/xxk4pV7b3GQ.2.

To assess the impact of treatment disruption on causal inference models, this paper focuses on the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) interference framework. The KNN interference model considers the impact of other individuals when treated. Under this framework, we define two types of treatment disruption: partial disruption and complete disruption. Partial disruption involves altering the treatment given to a subset of an individual's neighbors, whereas complete disruption changes the treatment given to all of an individual's neighbors. We identify conditions necessary for treatment disruption to affect both the average treatment effect and the classical causal ratio under two different scenarios: causal overlap weighting and kernel density estimation. Through applications to simulated and real data sets, our findings show that even small subsets of an individual's neighbors can influence their treatment effect. Specifically, when using causal overlap weighting, a subset size of three or four is sufficient to generate comparable results to those obtained through kernel density estimation. These results suggest that treatment disruption should be considered when using the KNN interference framework, particularly when using small subset sizes. Kernel density estimation may provide more accurate results, but it is also more computationally intensive than causal overlap weighting. Therefore, this method could be a useful alternative for initial exploratory analyses. Ultimately, our findings highlight the importance of accounting for treatment disruption when using the KNN interference framework, especially when working with small subset sizes. To facilitate the use of treatment disruption in practical applications, we have developed open-source code that allows users to calculate the average treatment effect under both partial and complete disruption scenarios. Additionally, our findings can be extended to other types of interference models by considering the impact of an individual's "treatment contagion," or the spread of treatment effects to neighboring individuals. The extensive photometric data collected by the CFHTLS, particularly with the wide d=5700deg area of the Legacy Survey, offers a valuable resource for analyzing galaxy shapes on an unprecedented scale. Introducing ShapePipe, a versatile and efficient pipeline designed to process large datasets, is essential for achieving this goal. Comprised of key components such as S20, contributing to the CFHTLS ShapeR3 pipeline, and two alternative profiles derived from lenstrino and SHARP, each employing distinct methods for analyzing galaxy shapes, ShapePipe demonstrates its ability to produce high-quality results. Specifically, for the UNIONS/CFIS dataset, ShapePipe's iteration generates reconstructed shapes for approximately 6 million galaxies with a median redshift of about 1.2, an area of approximately 4000deg. Utilizing this data, weak lensing convergence maps are generated, showcasing a good match between ShapePipe's results and published values. Moreover, ShapePipe's iteration successfully profiles various galaxy populations across a wide redshift range, exhibiting distinct shape configuration patterns. These findings highlight the effectiveness and efficiency of ShapePipe in analyzing extensive galaxy datasets. Utilizing its multi-profile capability, ShapePipe can be adapted to various applications, such as analyzing the intrinsic galaxy shapes and comparisons with cosmological simulations, making it a versatile tool in contemporary research. Ultimately, further development of the lensing application will allow ShapePipe to achieve a wide coverage, exceeding 5000deg. Expanding its capabilities to data sets like DES, ROMAN, and the Roman Galaxy Evolution Explorer, ShapePipe is poised to become a leading solution in analyzing large datasets of galaxy shapes. This alignment can be attributed to the unique properties of the logarithm of these values, which are often linked to the behavior of the gamma function. Notably, this association may also give rise to the estimation of certain diophantine expressions. This paper builds upon the existing work of A. A. Belfred and A. This research significant contributes to the understanding of the singularities of local complete intersections and their relationship with hypersurface singularities in the context of mixed characteristics. To achieve this, we utilize an extension of Gillet's formula for Chow groups on local complete intersections, and incorporate an approach that identifies an equivalence between certain K-group and the Chow group of zero-cycles. This research is a culmination of a research project that began with a seminar led by Jeffrey Street in Fall 2020. 

Keywords: local complete intersections, local complete unions, k-rationality, k-Du Bois singularity, local vanishing conjecture.

Subsequently, the paper obtains the scalar field solution in the quintessence framework and proceeds to derive the corresponding effective potential for the scalar field in the shadow sector. A key outcome is the prediction of a relationship between the effective parameters, namely $\lambda$ and $\gamma$, which govern the Tsallis holographic dark energy in the shadow side. These results indicate that the quintessence framework's real part contributes positively to the effective parameters' values, while their imaginary parts exhibit a contrasting, negative contribution. To conclude, the research finds that the quintessence framework's complex form significantly influences the Tsallis holographic dark energy model's shadow side, exhibiting distinct real and imaginary component behaviors. Hardware-based true random number generation is increasingly popular due to its versatility, reliability, and adaptability. Hardware implementations are preferred over software generators due to their consistency and resistance to tampering. Hardware generators are often prone to prediction attacks or do not generate genuine random digits. In this paper, a novel undervvoltage technique for SRAM-based true random number generators is proposed, demonstrating the generation of authentic random digits at various voltage levels. At a fixed voltage, the generated digits are consistent with genuine randomness standards and, when undervolted, the sequence breaks up into distinct statistically independent parts. By adjusting the undervoltage level, the length of these parts can be programmed. When several undervoltage levels are applied in succession, the generator produces extremely long sequences of genuine random digits. In experimental tests, the proposed undervoltage technique surpassed existing approaches, offering a 254.72% improvement in random digit length with no decrease in randomness quality. Additionally, the undervoltage technique consumed 0.93% less energy than leading SRAM-based true random number generators while requiring only a 0.17% reduction in SRAM area. The proposed undervoltage technique is compact, energy-efficient, and excels at genuine random digit generation, making it an ideal choice for a wide range of applications. This direct assessment is compared to the standard fit and shows combining WilsonNet with $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ data yields a 3 sigma $g_{M2}$ asymmetry constraint and improves $C_{7}/C_{9}$ assessments. This process is amenable to $B$-factories and future Belle II experimentation for refinement. Recent studies utilizing machine learning have made significant progress in resolving this issue, but they face a major limitation: the availability of relevant data is extremely restricted. To overcome this drawback, several methods have been devised to generate synthetic music pieces from existing datasets through manipulation of their features. This report presents an alternative approach that employs pre-trained neural networks, pre-trained on vast language corpora, to improve music composition assessment. Specifically, we show how to leverage BERT and Transformer models in this context. Additionally, we provide an overview of the music composition assessment task, discuss currently existing synthetic data generation methods, and propose our own strategy, supported by experimental results. Furthermore, we outline potential future applications of music composition assessment data and suggest ways in which BERT-like models could be utilized. Ultimately, we hope that this work will facilitate more substantial advancements in this area. All code used in this report is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/krishanksingh/Adaptive_MCC.995.

We introduce and investigate a new space-based measure, called space toughness, which quantifies the resilience of an iterative method to different coefficient matrix structures. This space toughness is broken down into two components, derived from the properties of the Schur complement and the inverse of a sub-matrix. We demonstrate that it can be computed from the results of a single preconditioned iterative solve, and test its accuracy on various examples from different fields. Specifically, we examine space toughness in the contexts of finite element and unstructured multigrid methods, and further extend its scope to include hybrid graphical processing unit (GPU) and multigrid techniques, ultimately concluding that it provides valuable and implementable insights for optimizing multigrid methods by selecting suitable smoothers and fine grid preconditioners. Overall, space toughness offers a practical tool for addressing a long-standing open question in multigrid solvers, and can help in designing and tuning versatile multigrid algorithms that perform well across a broad range of applications and domains. As such, it holds significant potential for meaningful contributions in various fields, including numerical analysis and computer science. Experimental data, including code for computing space toughness, is available at https://github.com/pmeacham/SpaceToughness. This work is the result of a collaborative effort between numerical analysts and programmers, and we hope that it will inspire a fresh wave of research into the design and optimization of multigrid methods. Specifically, we deliberately avoided sophisticated solvers and instead focused on basic algorithms, with the aim of encouraging students and early-career researchers to explore the field. In turn, a deeper understanding of space toughness is expected to yield valuable insights for tuning and designing multigrid solvers, and could even be applied to other iterative methods such as residual distribution schemes. We have established an ε-isometric dimension lowering theorem for subsets of lp where p lies within the range of 1 to 2. Specifically, if a finite-dimensional subset of lp can be embedded in lq with q less than p divided by 1 plus p, and this embedding remains distorting with a distorting factor less than ε, then there exists an isometric embedding of the original subset into l1 that also remains distorting with the same factor ε. Furthermore, this embedding has an infinite dimensional code domain. This code domain property holds true for any isometric embedding of a bounded linear operator T, regardless of its form. This result also implies novel applications including new proofs for the rectangular matrix embedding property, a concept introduced by Allen and O'Donnell, and the isomorphic embedding of bounded Orlicz spaces into l1. Additionally, this research yields an ε-isometric dimension raising theorem for certain incompressible subsets of lp. Specifically, if a subset of lp with a finite Strassen dimension can be compressed into lq with q greater than p divided by 1 minus p, and this compression remains distorting with a distorting factor less than ε, then there exists an isometric embedding of the original subset into l1 that also remains distorting with the same factor ε and has an infinite dimensional code domain. This latter property holds particularly true for bounded linear operators with positive numerical radius. Moreover, this research provides novel quantitative estimates for the rectangular matrix embedding property. Finally, this research can be generalized to the settings of bounded Banach spaces and compact operators by leveraging a distinct technique. Specifically, it relies on derandomization methods from probability theory, a technique first employed in similar applications by Brzyzki and Wysoczanski. This paper suggests a novel coding technique known as degree-degree linked codes, created using a graph theory approach, for low-density parity-check codes. The main characteristic of these codes is that adjacent nodes in the graph corresponding to non-zero elements connected by an edge have distinct degrees. We evaluate the performance of degree-degree linked codes on a binary erasure channel and observe that they offer superior decoding accuracy in comparison to conventional LDPC codes. Furthermore, our research reveals that degree-degree linked codes can operate at higher vertical interference limits (VILs) and achieve lower bit error rates (BERS) than LDPC codes. Notably, at optimal VIL values, the BERS of degree-degree linked codes approach the minimum BERS of conventional LDPC codes. We developed a bespoke Monte Carlo simulator in C to assess the performance of these novel degree-degree linked codes. This code evaluates various performance metrics, including BERS, erasure decay rates, and the effective Hamming distance, which measures the average distance between codeword messages and the decoder's estimated messages. Our experiments demonstrate that degree-degree linked codes maintain superior performance across a wide range of rates. To facilitate practical implementation, we provided a step-by-step ensemble generator approach for degree-degree linked codes, utilizing the density-evolution technique to ensure they have the desired degree-degree linked property. Additionally, we observed the encoders and decoders of degree-degree linked codes under various error rates and erosion scenarios. Our research indicates that these novel degree-degree linked codes offer enhanced noise tolerance, surpassing the performance of conventional LDPC codes. We propose these degree-degree linked codes as an exciting and promising area of research, which could lead to the development of future low-density parity-check codes exhibiting superior error-resistance properties. With the potential to outperform LDPC codes in binary erasure channels, these degree-degree linked codes could revolutionize the field of coding theory. Although this research only assesses its efficacy under erasure scenarios, these degree-degree linked codes may also exhibit improved performance in other types of channels, such as Gaussian channels. Consequently, these degree-degree linked codes could find applications in an expansive range of fields, including wireless sensor networks and satellite communications. Ultimately, the ensemble generator approach used to create these novel degree-degree linked codes could pave the way for the development of future low-density parity-check codes displaying an unparalleled ability to withstand vertical interference. We anticipate that our degree-degree linked codes will continue to demonstrate superior performance in binary erasure channels and other types of channels, surpassing the performance of conventional LDPC codes.

We investigated a potential weakness in the phase randomization technology used in the decoy state quantum key distribution (DSQKD) system. The system is designed to protect users' secret information, but our research found that if the phase randomization is only partial, it can be invaded by a sophisticated eavesdroper, which leads to the loss of system security. Galaxy groups and clusters exhibit a peculiar bimodal distribution in their X-ray luminosities, which can be elucidated by understanding the subsonic breakdown of accretion streams. This study employed three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic simulations of 10^7 K gas clouds under gravitation, analyzing its transformation for various cloud masses (from 10^4 to 10^8 M_sun) across three different potential well strengths. We discovered that high-mass clouds (>10^6 M_sun) experience complete disruption, generating dense cores and filamentary structures, which ultimately lead to star formation. In contrast, low-mass clouds maintain their integrity due to a lack of thermal instability. This critical density threshold (~4.8*10^-3 g/cm^3) triggers a unique two-phase mixing process, influenced by magnetic fields that can induce growth rates of 0.05-0.15 rad/s. This work reveals the potential of thermal instability, facilitated by a weak magnetic field, to initiate cloud fragmentation and influence the galaxy cluster formation process. As such, early galaxy building blocks may be characterized by a unique, cooling-dominated core surrounded by extensive, hot gas, which would later give way to hierarchical mergers in groups and clusters. Additionally, the presence of magnetic fields may prompt a reassessment of the gas fragmentation criterion, leading to a more dynamic and magnetically influenced galaxy evolution process. It is plausible that early galaxy building blocks may be characterized by a unique, cooling-dominated core surrounded by extensive, hot gas, which would later give way to hierarchical mergers in groups and clusters. These theories exhibit a unique property where the Lorentzian amplitude can be determined from the Minkowski amplitude through a simple transformation. This characteristic is exclusive to even-loop amplitudes in the bosonic string and 'odd-loop' amplitudes in the fermionic string. Our analysis reveals that, under certain conditions, the resource theory must adhere to strict limitations, significantly constraining its applicability. In particular, we show that if a resource theory satisfies four specific criteria, then it must conform to the principles of nonnegative probabilities and non-negative resource consumption. We also establish that these criteria are necessary conditions for resource theories involving positive semi-definite resources, such as Gaussian states in quantum thermodynamics. To illustrate the implications of these constraints, we derive a critical limitation on the trade-offs between divergence, distillation, and transmission capacities in quantum information theory. This limitation leads to the discovery of previously unrecognized relationships between different capacity measures. Our analysis suggests that many existing results in quantum information theory were nontrivially forecast by these strict limitations. Furthermore, these limitations can guide the development of new techniques to study the conversion of quantum resources. Our graph convolutional learning algorithm, DR-DSGD, tackles the distributional shift issue through a new robust averaging process that mitigates the influence of data distribution disparities on parameter communication.
