This novel approach tackles the long-standing partial alignment problem by leveraging large deformation regularization, effectively merging input partial shapes into a complete shape through a registered point cloud. PRNet captures rich geometric and structural information, producing a complete shape with accurate registration points, which guides the prediction of corresponding points in unknown areas. By applying a simple and efficient U-net structure, PRNet achieves significant performance enhancements over existing methods, surpassing state-of-the-art techniques on challenging datasets, including the widely-used TUSK benchmark. Furthermore, PRNet demonstrates robust domain adaptation capabilities, being able to accurately align new shapes with minimal training on a limited dataset, while also generalizing to diverse datasets without the need for supervision. This versatility stems from its ability to produce a complete shape point cloud, which serves as a robust shape representation, reducing the problem of aligning partial shapes to a single point cloud matching task. With its exceptional performance and flexibility, PRNet opens up new avenues for partial shape alignment, offering simple and efficient implementation. The proposed method, referred to as the strong trajectory approach, is particularly relevant to time-resolved experimental measurements and incorporates model and parameter uncertainties. The approach is evaluated through its application to an inverse problem associated with nitric oxide's interaction with myoglobin in proteins. The results demonstrate the approach's capability in providing comprehensive and accurate information about complex dynamical systems. 

Myoglobin, a protein containing a heme group with nitric oxide (NO) binding properties, is used as the system of interest. NO binding to myoglobin is chosen as the system to test the strong trajectory approach, with focus on characterizing the binding and dissociation rates, as well as timescales related to protein dynamics (electronic and nuclear motions). The study aims to validate the approach's capacity in providing sturdy inversion of time-resolved data, with a focus on evaluating its sensitivity to various parameters such as initial conditions, data noise, data sparsity, and system complexity. NO binding to myoglobin is chosen due to its intricate dynamics, spanning across multiple timescales, with cross-talk between electronic and nuclear motion, and influenced by binding and dissociation rates, further necessitating the need for a robust analytical approach.

The study demonstrates the approach's tolerance for various parameters such as initial conditions, data noise, data sparsity, and system complexity. The approach is also found to be more sensitive to timescales and rates in systems with significant nuclear motion contribution. The study further validates the approach's capability in providing a sturdy understanding of electronic and nuclear motion dynamics in systems with intricate dynamics.

The classic Cyclic Division Generative Adversarial Network (CDGAN) model demonstrates promising performance in this context, although it assumes a prior knowledge about the number of domains, which is often impractical in real-world scenarios. Building upon the CDGAN framework, this study proposes an enhanced model that can automatically determine the number of domains involved. The proposed instance partitioning framework, consisting of a global generator and multiple local discriminators, learns to partition domains into distinct groups based on the diversity of samples, both individually and collectively. By integrating a global adversarial discriminator and a division loss term, this model encourages disentanglement of domain information, resulting in well-segregated groups in each domain. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, this study evaluates the effectiveness of the proposed model across various domain adaptation scenarios. The results show that the proposed model surpasses CDGAN and other recent state-of-the-art approaches in partitioning tasks, as well as domain adaptation challenges. Furthermore, the generated partitions are consistently applied to multiple domain adaptation scenarios, demonstrating the model's ability to automatically determine domain numbers and partition domains effectively. Predicting actions in knowledge graph embedding (KGE) models can be seen as a next prediction task. Current models excel at forecasting the next action, but their ability to predict actions further ahead is lacking. To tackle this issue, models have adapted KGE's feature mapping to various architectures. In this study, we introduce the RBF kernelized feature mapping to the Long Short-Term (LST) architecture, resulting in the RBF-Kernelized Feature Mapping Long Short-Term (RFMLST) model. By using the RBF kernel's transfer property, RFMLST can learn informative features that capture both short-term and long-term dependencies. Moreover, the RBF-Kernelized Feature Mapping Long Short-Term (RFMLST) model has been proven to outperform previous models in various action prediction tasks. To validate the effectiveness of the RBF-Kernelized Feature Mapping Long Short-Term (RFMLST) model, we conducted comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets, and the model's source code is available on GitHub for reproducibility. Additionally, the predicted actions can be utilized in challenging link prediction tasks. To further push the limit of action prediction, we proposed the Next-Article Coreference Task, where the model needs to forecast articles that share coreferences with existing ones in a knowledge graph. The proposed RFMLST model achieved superior performance on this task. A detailed analysis and visualization of the model are presented, and we also explored the ability of RFMLST to generalize to other KGE tasks by using the RBF kernel's transfer property. To further verify the effectiveness of the model, we performed a pairwise comparison with other state-of-the-art action prediction models. The results of these experiments demonstrated the RFMLST model's ability to predict more accurate results up to 143.76% better than other models, and the model's ability to handle frozen embeddings and the RBF kernel's impact on its performance were also investigated. To further push the limit of KGE models, we explored the application of the RBF kernel to the interaction-based (IB) architecture. However, the resulting model performed poorly, and further analysis suggested that the poor performance might be due to the IB architecture's lack of a short-term dependency component. Based on these findings, we proposed the general RBF kernelized feature mapping mechanism for various KGE models and demonstrated its effectiveness. To further validate the proposed mechanism, we conducted a comprehensive comparison between short-term and long-term dependency components using the R Bernstein dataset. The idea is to identify independent sections of code via a partitioning approach and ensure they can be executed independently without relying on external dependencies.  A program can be divided into a fixed number of sections, and each execution unit can be designated to run a particular section independently.  To implement this concept, a program needs to be converted into a flattened form, where all variables are explicitly present, and then reorganized into distinct sections based on variable access patterns.  Each execution unit should be loaded with a separate partition of the program's instructions.  Execution can then proceed in parallel, but any data dependencies between sections must be addressed through data forwarding or waiting on completion.  Control flow instructions can be handled by assigning multiple execution units to the same section, and a corresponding number of execution units can be assigned to the following section, ensuring smooth execution.  This approach can be applied to a wide range of parallel execution architectures, including VLIW, EPIC, and out-of-order superscalar processors. This paper outlines the reasoning behind the design of a dependable automotive system using a failure-functional approach, with particular reference to ensuring safety through fail-operational design. The primary goal of this system is to manage and navigate an vehicle in the event of multiple simultaneous failures of its perception and processing components. Building on existing research in dependable automation, we design a fail-operational system using a failure inaction strategy, with regular state updates ensuring that the vehicle remains in a safe state with minimal deviations from the original state. To validate this design against potential failures, we employ a timely state update protocol, with associated proof of the system's effectiveness. Ultimately, this paper contributes to the dependability literature by providing a formal validation, albeit in an abstract model, of an advanced automotive system operating at a high level of dependability. The associated design and proof have been formally documented using the Fiform formal proof tool. 

In this research, we leverage the following key concepts and methodologies: 
i. A failure inaction strategy for handling failures, 
ii. A state model with regular state updates, 
iii. An automotive system model, 
iv. A timing model, 
v. An error detection model, 
vi. A state update protocol, 
vii. A dependability analysis, 
viii. A formal validation, 
ix. A fail-operational design. 

The design and proof of this research can be accessed through the following Fiform link: https://fiform.inria.fr/en/-/status/20210225T135444.

The $k$-Center problem is a classic facility location problem where we seek to place $k$ facilities to minimize the maximum distance from a demand point to its nearest facility, considering a weighted graph and up to $L$ highway nodes. Unlike doubling measures that cap the highway node distance ratio, the highway measure considers the cumulative ratio of highway nodes to a demand point. This study focuses on the $k$-Center problem with the highway measure and develops efficient algorithms for both the parameterized and approximation versions. Specifically, we derived a parameterized algorithm with an exponential time complexity, limited by a parameter $k$ and the highway measure, when $L \leq 2$. Furthermore, we derived an approximation algorithm with a solution ratio complexity, influenced by $k$ and the highway measure. Notably, our results for the parameterized and approximation algorithms with the highway measure surpass previous results based on doubling measures. Additionally, we include comprehensive examples and experimental validation, including comparisons with existing solutions, to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed algorithms in various scenarios. The experimental results show that our parameterized algorithm outperforms the best-known approximation algorithm when $L=2$ and surpasses another approximation algorithm when $L>2$. The source code of our experiments is available on GitHub at the specified link. The study concludes by highlighting the unique properties of the highway measure and suggesting potential directions for further research in this area. The highway measure may offer additional advantages over doubling measures and could be more suitable in specific application scenarios, such as emergency services, where the cumulative ratio of specialized facilities to a demand point might be more relevant than the maximum distance ratio to nearest facilities. The study thus contributes to the ongoing exploration of facility location problems with varying highway measure properties. Specifically, we demonstrate that ultra-light bosonic dark matter can be effectively described as scattered monochromatic plane waves, and their interaction with the detector will result in a change in direction, leading to a non-colinear e-ray. This scattering process causes a change in the phase of the plane wave, which is then measured as a modification in the far-field pattern of the e-ray. This paper explores the coherence phenomenon in basis pursuit, a continuous version of the problem. We show that for any basis pursuit instance with a non-degenerate objective function value, there either is a single minimizer or two distinct minimizers. We also prove that if the parameter lambda increases beyond a certain threshold, unique minimizers emerge. To achieve these results, we prove a larger theorem relating to the continuity of minimizers in convex optimization, which may have broader applications. Additionally, we examine the complexity of generating continuous minimizers through an infinite-dimensional basis pursuit algorithm. As a result, we devise a simple and efficient algorithm and establish its correctness. Moreover, we investigate the relationship between minimizers of continuous basis pursuit and discrete instances with a restricted codomain. This leads to a method for generating discrete solutions from continuous minimizers with a limited number of discrete basis vector components. We also provide computational examples and advice on implementing this strategy. Finally, we examine the relationship between continuous basis pursuit and the null space residual in the discrete case with a restricted codomain. This leads to a simple algorithm and theoretical justification for using the null space residual in the discrete setting. We also provide computational examples and implementation guidance. Lastly, we contrast our results with existing discrete basis pursuit findings, particularly regarding uniqueness, sparsest solutions, and the use of the null space residual. We demonstrate that distinct continuous concepts can lead to different theoretical results and algorithms for basis pursuit. Moreover, we suggest that many of these ideas can be extended to other problems in compressed sensing and sparse representation. Ultimately, this paper aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of the continuous foundation of basis pursuit and provide useful algorithms and theoretical results in the process.

In model-parallel distributed training, data parallel and model parallel techniques are often combined to overcome memory limitations. However, distributed computation strategies for learning large neural networks often result in prolonged convergence times. This paper introduces an novel approach called regional evaluator training, which addresses both the memory and efficiency challenges. By restructuring the neural network into layers and assigning them to different machines, and having each machine evaluate a segment of the network, a significant reduction in communication data is achieved. This reduction comes from lower dimensionality of the exchanged data. Additionally, as the number of machines increases, the amount of information exchanged per training iteration increases at a sublinear rate, resulting in near linear communication overhead. This training strategy was proven and demonstrated on a 16-node, 32-core machine, where a 62-layer Profound Neural Network was trained using the MNIST dataset with 99.77% efficiency. This result surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art distributed computation methods by at least 2 orders of magnitude. Furthermore, regional evaluator training was shown to outperform other model-parallel approaches such as pipeline and tree-based parallelism by an average of 1.3 orders of magnitude. This training strategy can be applied to various model-parallel algorithms and is compatible with existing data parallel techniques, making it a versatile tool for learning large neural networks. The code used in this research is publicly available at a specified link. It includes an implementation of regional evaluator training on CNN and Profound Neural Network using the TensorFlow framework. The code can be modified to apply this training strategy to other neural network structures and distributed computation strategies. Parameters such as the number of machines, machine cores, and evaluator segments can be changed to reproduce the results shown in this research. Additionally, a set of useful tools is included in the code for evaluating the performance of regional evaluator training under a variety of conditions. These tools allow for the adjustment of training variables, such as learning rates and batch sizes, as well as network variables, such as layer sizes and types. It is also possible to swap out the Profound Neural Network with a standard neural network consisting of similar layers in a smaller size. This review article discusses a method to estimate thermal states and their associated thermodynamic properties, specifically the entropy, using a technique called Nested Sampling. The NS algorithm provides a reliable and unbiased method for calculating Bayesian evidence and other integrals that are often challenging to solve. One such integral represents the thermal energy of a system and, by employing an accurate temperature-dependent density of states, offers a novel approach to entropy calculation. This review article focuses on the integration of NS with the Monte Carlo e-fold method, known for its efficient evaluation, and highlights the NS method's capabilities in estimating thermal systems. A key aspect of this integration is the concept of entropy density, which is redefined and shown to be equivalent to the standard definition when the density of states is constant, thus providing a comprehensive framework for thermal calculations. This integrated method is then applied to three specific problems: (i) a random energy model with uniform density, (ii) a spin chain with competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, and (iii) Lennard-Jones dimer system. Numerical estimates of entropy for these systems are also available in the literature, allowing for a detailed comparison with the NTM results. A crucial finding from these applications is that many commonly used approximate entropy models are actually too simplistic and fail to accurately represent the true entropy of a system, as demonstrated by the NTM method's findings. This review article concludes by outlining areas for further development and research. It also emphasizes the NTM method's broad applicability and showcases its potential to calculate thermal properties not only of model systems but also of real-world systems, thus requiring immediate attention from theorists. Due to its unbiased nature, the NTM method can serve as an essential validation and measurement tool. The code used in this review article's results is publicly accessible at a designated GitHub link. Furthermore, the NTM approach's employment in various fields, including astrophysics, biology, and finance, is briefly mentioned to illustrate its extensive range of applications. Initially, we consider a conservation law with discontinuous, bounded and Lipschitz continuous data within a bounded domain. As time approaches zero, measure-valued solutions emerge due to an infinite number of expanding waves with vanishing speeds. These weak solutions are represented as feeble solutions, a type of distribution solution, providing the optimal regularity for the conserved quantity. This background measure represents the long-term time-dependent behavior of feeble solutions for any nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law across multiple dimensions. This distinctive property stems from solving a system of partial differential equations, where solutions exhibit a combination of regularity and singularity. Recent breakthroughs in physics, such as Einstein's and QM, were driven by scientists like Einstein who applied broader, theoretical frameworks to guide physics development. Despite physics having a solid foundation now, the field still lacks a clear, overarching theoretical structure. Einstein's own search for universal physical principles is a great example of how great minds have sought this in the past. A new study utilizes information theory to propose a more comprehensive structure for physics and even identifies inherent inconsistencies within current physical theories when evaluated through this broader framework. When evaluated using information theory's axioms, physical laws and theories appear to violate a key global principle known as the Global Lever Principle, with many inconsistencies stemming from a related concept known as the Global Lever Effect. When evaluated using Shannon entropy, QM and GR align perfectly, but EM and SR do not. When evaluated using Kolmogorov entropy, all classical physical laws align perfectly, but QM and GR do not. When considering various entropy options, a clear hierarchy emerges, with Shannon entropy being the most suitable for guiding physical theory development. Finally, when considering all entropy options, a clear hierarchy emerges, with all classical physical laws, SR, EM, and QM consequences following logically and predictively from a few global physical principles. These results show that re-examining and re-evaluating well-established theories through a broader framework can still reveal new and insightful understandings of the physical world. To confirm its effectiveness, this method is tested on various examples including Higgs production coupled with two gluons and light-by-light scattering, showing promising results at the QCD accuracy standard. Recent observations by ALMA have revealed a spiral feature in the Galaxy's far side, specifically a spiral arm located about 3 kiloparsecs away from the Galactic center. This new arm, which we will refer to as the 3-kpc arm, is distinct from two other spiral arms found closer to the Galactic center. Analysis of the 16 GHz water maser spectrum from the spiral arm indicates an expansive velocity pattern of approximately 35 km per second, and the average spiral density profile is characterised by a relatively gentle slope. This new feature's proximity to the Galactic centre and its orientation suggest it could be a spiral arm similar to those closer to the core, but undergoing a clockwise precession. Observations indicate the 3-kpc arm's mass is substantial, estimated to be in the order of one million times that of the solar mass. This new discovery indicates there are more spiral arms at various distances from the Galactic core, and the known spiral arm structure's mass is significantly surpassed by this newly discovered feature. Further study of the 3-kpc arm's properties and the Galaxy's overall spiral arm structure is essential. We examine a real-world application of the housemate problem in a 3D setting. Our model involves four individuals, known as homeowners and applicants, each of whom has unique preferences. Homeowners strive to form a optimal arrangement with an investor, aiming to maximize their individual benefits, or in some cases, the global maximum would be preferred. Our main achievement is the development of a polynomial-time algorithm to determine stable outcomes that account for additively distinct preferences in this 3D context. Additionally, our experiments using various preference distributions indicate that nearly every situation can be resolved through a stable arrangement. Our results indicate that the stable outcome with the highest overall benefit is the most prevalent solution when applying randomly generated preferences. Furthermore, the characteristics of the preferences can be utilized to derive a lower bound on the number of stable arrangements. In cases where the homeowners' preferences conflict, we demonstrate the existence of a stable arrangement that prioritizes their individual interests over the investor's. Our approach includes presenting the housing unit's configuration in a way that maximizes the benefit for each homeowner, or in some cases, the global maximum would be preferred. When dealing with a large number of homeowners and investors, we identify the minimum subset of individuals whose preferences should be taken into account to determine a stable arrangement. Our generalization of the housemate problem concept to applications that have similarities with these ideas represents a novel application of our model. Gromov's category of metric spaces includes a notion of growth, specifically GH-category, which emerges from considering the Hausdorff distance between certain compact metric spaces. We introduce a concept called cloud to serve as a geometric representation of a metric space's (alpha, beta)-Gromov-Hausdorff stable structure, where alpha and beta represent categories of metric spaces. The cloud is defined by a set of limiting geodesic balls' diameters, along with the radii of these balls. This allows us to examine the GH-category's relationship with scaling phenomena and the stability of metric spaces. We demonstrate that the GH-category's behavior can be understood through analyzing a space's cloud at an arbitrarily small scale. This leads to the idea of approximating a space by a simple model, specifically a uniform space, which is a type of exact Gromov-Hausdorff stable space. We define an equivalence relation, called cloud equivalence, on the set of uniform spaces, which represents a type of extreme metric stability. We then show that this relation corresponds to a finite ordinal and that it can be viewed as a metric. We define a type of space metrically closest to uniform spaces and demonstrate that its GH-category behaves predictably. Furthermore, we show that a space's GH-category does not change when it is embedded in a certain type of topological space. We then isolate a particular scale at which a space's cloud is consistent across all possible embeddings. We define a concept called center to be the set of GH-categories of spaces obtained by contracting a given space within various scales. We demonstrate that the center of a space is either empty or consists of a single ordinal and that it can be thought of as a robust, scale-independent representation of the space. We propose the center as a useful tool for understanding a space's inherent properties and show that it remains unchanged when a space is embedded in a certain type of topological space. We then illustrate the theory through examples, including the cases of a uniform space and a space with a particular scale-dependent structure. We conclude by highlighting potential applications and further research directions. We also provide an alternative definition and representation of a space's cloud, along with a detailed theorem regarding its properties and a scale-independent metric on the set of uniform spaces, along with a brief outline of its proof. Due to a limitation on the abstract length, these ideas are described in the paper in more detail. We also provide an annotated bibliography for further reference. Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and reduced power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers. In this study, a CLICTD detector, a monolithic device with small collection electrodes, was built using the International Linear Collider's detector requirements and was tested with different sensor thicknesses and substrate materials. The research revealed that increasing the thickness of the epitaxial layer or changing the substrate type to InGaAs does not significantly impact the collection efficiency, but the InGaAs substrate offers a promising alternative without epitaxial layer enhancement. Ultimately, a 200 $\mu$m thick detector made from standard silicon material demonstrated the best results, with an effective sensor thickness of 300 $\mu$m using a particle-shifting technique. Collection efficiency reached as high as 96% for this thick detector. Additionally, the study's findings and test results have been published in an open-access paper. 

Due to the capital expenses associated with the CMOS sensor production, selecting the optimal sensor thickness and substrate type is crucial to ensuring feasibility. Based on the research, using a 200 $\mu$m thick detector made from standard silicon material is the most cost-effective and efficient option available. 

The full research paper can be found at the arXiv website, document number 2101.08511.

Currently, most particle simulation methods employ a single time-step approach, where the collision time of interacting particles is assumed to be comparable to or greater than their time step. This often requires a compromise between sufficient collision resolution and economically feasible computational burdens. To address this limitation, a novel multi-time-step technique is introduced, enabling the simulation of collisions spanning multiple time steps with support for both elastic and dissipative interactions. By breaking down the collision process into distinct time steps, the proposed method effectively mitigates unphysical particle postures and evaluates the collision duration more accurately. Furthermore, a comprehensive validation suite evaluates the performance of the multi-time-step method across diverse systems, demonstrating its enhanced collision resolution capabilities compared to traditional single time-step approaches. When paired with a realistic collision duration of 10 microseconds for simulating submarine biofouling, the multi-time-step method yields highly detailed and realistic collision evolutions, surpassing the performance of single time-step methods. By leveraging advanced computing hardware such as FPGAs and GPUs, the multi-time-step method can be accelerated while maintaining a realistic collision duration, thereby facilitating large-scale particle-resolved simulations with a practical computational cost. Moreover, the method's framework can be adapted to model various other-type of events. Lastly, the study shows that, with the advent of modern accelerators, it is feasible to perform large-scale particle-resolved simulations of realistic aquatic environments with millions of particles. Our paper presents the results of measuring X-ray polarization in the supernova remnant Cassiopeia A using the IXPE mission. Between June and July 2022, the remnant was targeted in four observations totaling 234 ks. By analyzing X-rays emitted from the remnant's center and outer regions, we measured a horizontal polarization of 11% ± 3% and 20% ± 4%, respectively, with a significant polarization detected in all observations. The polarization measurements are consistent with the presence of a large-scale magnetic field of 2-10 milligauss and a smaller-scale magnetic field of 1-4 milligauss in the outer regions. The polarization's vertical and horizontal components indicate that the X-ray emission is primarily of electron-positron bubbles, with an age of 100-1000 years. By analyzing the polarization's angle distribution, we found that the large-scale magnetic field's orientation matches the remnant's tangent field. The measurements show that the X-ray emission is older than the 580-year gamma-ray ejection. Using the X-ray emission's brightness and polarization, we estimated the number of positrons ejected in Cassiopeia A to be (1-4)10^41 s^-1. Our study demonstrates how X-ray polarization measurement can quantify particle ejection in supernova remnant. The data and analysis code are accessible through DOI 10.5170/MASTO-000.002.

In a letter to Paul Erdos in 1992, Frank Gaughan and Matti Linna proposed a combinatorial conjecture related to unique sums of integers. Erdos expressed skepticism about the conjecture having an elementary proof. We provide modified versions of the Erdos conjecture by altering the conditions for uniqueness sums of $k$ integers. Our analysis considers the scenario where there are fewer than $k$ distinct integers available to form the sums, and we offer new lower bounds for this scenario. We have verified that our lower bounds are near optimal through counterexamples. We plan to explore further generalizations of the Erdos conjecture in future work. 

Specifically, we investigate the unique sums of $k$ integers in a given field, and our main contributions are as follows. For a given positive integer $k$, there exists a finite set $S$ with less than $k$ elements such that the sumset $S + S + \dots + S$ ($k$ times) contains at least one element that is nonnegative, unless $k$ is less than or equal to four. When $k$ is greater than four, there exists a finite set $S$ with less than $k$ elements such that the sumset $S + S + \dots + S$ ($k$ times) contains only nonnegative integers if and only if $k$ is an even number. We have proven that the smallest possible size of the set $S$ for which the above condition holds can be quantified as $s_{\mathrm{min}}(k)$, where $s_{\mathrm{min}}(k)$ increases at a rate of $O(k^{1/\lceil \log_{2} k \rceil + 1})$. We have established a computational method to determine the exact value of $s_{\mathrm{min}}(k)$ for many $k$ values, and our analysis shows that this value is within a constant factor of $k$ when $k$ is greater than or equal to six. We have discovered that our findings for unique sums in a finite field can be applied to both integers and rational numbers under specific conditions. We have explored connections between our work and existing research on sumsets by investigating the unique sums of $k$ integers in a given arithmetic progression. Our analysis has yielded novel lower bounds for this scenario. In future work, we plan to delve into further generalizations and applications of the Erdos conjecture.

Consequently, the simulated fluid behavior exhibits an extremely complex and self-similar pattern. By applying our new simulation, we clarify the long-standing debate regarding the energy consumption in the turbulence range and the nature of the fluid fluctuations. Furthermore, our study provides an innovative explanation for the apparent stability of the liquid surface in the middle of a breaking droplet's collapse, triggered by an unusually viscous and turbulent state in that specific scenario. In many areas of science and technology, delayed systems hold significant importance. The cause can be structural lag, genetic transmission, or information propagation through neural connections or the stock market. Researchers have discovered an unconventional technique to stimulate chaotic behavior in these systems by modulating the time delay. By creating an adaptive delay function with periodic, high-frequency fluctuations, even small in amplitude (less than 10^-6), this approach can lead to significant amplification. Notably, increasing the carrier frequency and scale of these fluctuations can enhance chaos generation while minimizing energy input. Although the highest amplification occurs with high frequencies, there's an optimal balance between frequency and amplitude that produces the largest output. Researchers have used numerical simulations to study this phenomenon in two areas: the Eckmann system, a model for fish swimming, and a financial model based on contagion theory. The results show that, under real-world constraints with noise, the response can be an orderly change. Surprisingly, these findings reveal that the interaction between the delay fluctuation and the dynamics supports the idea of active control over chaotic behavior in delayed systems through time modulation. This breakthrough could facilitate the development of innovative, delay-active controllers for chaotic systems. Additionally, as a practical application, the technique has successfully generated chaos in a solar power system with real-world parameters, providing a practical example of active control over dynamics. This research may unlock new possibilities for active control over delay dynamics in various scientific and technological contexts. Further investigation will be necessary to explore these applications in more detail. Valuable directions for future research have also been identified. Specifically, the authors acknowledge the absence of an analytical solution for this problem and suggest that finding a reliable model for the system behavior would be an important area of exploration. Moreover, they have released the associated code on GitHub to facilitate replication and modification of the presented results. As this research has the potential to significantly impact various fields, the authors have published the findings on bioArXiv and have registered the study as a report on allabolag.se, complying with the guidelines set forth by the journals PLOS ONE and bioArXIV. In the end, the authors express their gratitude to Dr. Alan C. C. Yao for his guidance and feedback on the research.

We establish two novel semantics for the probabilistic lambda-calculus. Firstly, we devise a probability measure on the domain of closures, demonstrating that every probabilistic lambda-term has a well-defined probability value. Alternatively, we define a probability distribution on the domain of closed terms, showing that every probabilistic lambda-term has a well-defined probability value, which can be calculated by integrating the probabilities of its closed extensions. Both measures conform to the principles of linearity and strictness inherent to the probabilistic lambda-calculus. The framework of this paper can be generalized to accommodate other types of structured evidence in probabilistic logic. Moreover, we propose a corresponding denotational semantics for the probabilistic lambda-calculus, and we discuss how the developed semantics can be used for purposes such as termination prediction and complexity analysis. Unlike other known approaches to probabilistic lambda-calculus, the present framework explicitly models a non-deterministic choice operator, which is shown to be equivalent to a probabilistic version of the paradoxical omega-term. As such, the developed semantics provide a fundamental understanding of the probabilistic lambda-calculus. We also discuss how the probabilistic lambda-calculus can be used for expressing and predicting the termination of recursive algorithms with probabilistic annotations. Finally, we outline directions for future research in this area. In particular, we propose the development of a type system for the probabilistic lambda-calculus based on expectation constraints. Such a type system is expected to aid in the identification of type-safe algorithms and provide a fundamental understanding of the expressive power of the probabilistic lambda-calculus. We provide a preliminary outline of this type system, followed by potential research directions. This work outlines several methods to enhance the accuracy of final cross-correlation results between spectroscopic datasets, focusing on the techniques employed by the Spectroscopic Survey for Galactic Astronomy. We introduce an initial filtering method aimed at eliminating noisy data, as well as a moving median filter to remove isolated anomalies. Building upon this, we develop an algorithm approximating a moving median filter with a weighted, moving average function. This 'MVMA' filter leverages four user-specified parameters: the data point neighborhood to consider, the number of data points to average, a weighting decay factor, and an exponential weighting factor. This allows the MVMA filter to effectively eliminate noisy data similar to a moving median filter. We demonstrate that the MVMA filter outperforms a moving median filter when dealing with data containing outliers close to the peak value. Furthermore, we introduce an interpolation method to fill data gaps, utilizing Chebyshev polynomials to minimize discrepancies between interpolated and original data. We find that this interpolation method produces data less prone to oscillations compared to cubic spline interpolation. This work culminates in a comprehensive flowchart illustrating the data processing sequence, as well as accompanying Python code available on GitHub and Gemino, with Gemino serving as the data management system. Even though the code was initially written with SAGA in mind, the methods and algorithms are versatile and can be applied to a range of astronomical spectroscopy applications. We anticipate that future enhancements will include an efficient data compression method using neural networks to optimize data quality, ultimately replacing the current Python code with a fully optimized version. In various fields, medication similarity assessment holds significant importance for multiple purposes. Initially used in creating generic and innovative medications by identifying similar products, it's also employed in developing artificial intelligence systems capable of prescribing medications. As a result, there's been a surge in the development of innovative methods for medication similarity assessment in recent years. Due to the characteristics of this data set, including a large number of categories and irregularly distributed data points, as well as the benefits provided by graph models in processing complex data, graph-based methods have become popular for this application. Nonetheless, several concerns persist with these current methods. Firstly, they fail to address the relationships between non-connected pairs of medications. Additionally, there's a lack of cohesiveness in existing models to ensure they're prepared for real-world medication similarity assessment tasks. Lastly, there's limited flexibility in these models to accommodate diverse requirements of different applications. To tackle these challenges, we propose an approach that leverages relational deep learning to evaluate medication similarities, characterized by a network structure comprising multiple interconnected nodes, where each node represents a medication and is connected to others based on their similarities. By addressing the mentioned concerns, we implement a novel strategy that incorporates edge enhancements, node updates, and a cohesive loss function to optimize our model. To evaluate our model's performance, we conducted comprehensive experiments using six publicly accessible data sets, and our results indicate that our proposed approach surpasses traditional and comparison models in both overall accuracy and the evaluation of cohesive medication similarities. To facilitate the reproduction of our work, we provide our model's source code and experimental settings for others to reproduce. Our work offers a valuable contribution to the field of relational deep learning by addressing the challenges in medication similarity assessment and providing flexible solutions for a range of tasks. As a result, our model can be utilized for various applications beyond our experiments, such as identifying potential drug dangers and developing personalized medication regimens. Ultimately, our research seeks to optimize the relationship between medications in the graph model to enhance its overall cohesiveness and prepare it for real-world medication similarity assessment tasks. To verify our model's effectiveness in a real-world setting, we conducted a detailed case study to analyze its performance in a medication similarity assessment application. Our results indicate that our model surpasses comparison models in both overall accuracy and the evaluation of cohesive medication similarities. To facilitate the reproduction of our work, we provide our model's source code and experimental settings for others to reproduce. Our work offers a novel contribution to the field of relational deep learning by addressing the challenges in medication similarity assessment and providing flexible solutions

Several countries are experiencing an increase in road harm incidents which lead to loss of life among young people. Current approaches using deep learning, such as Transferable and Adaptive Transferable, can adapt a model trained on a local dataset to a different nation's dataset, but face challenges in adapting to a third nation's dataset. To address this issue, we introduce a new paradigm, called 2dTCA, which allows a model to adapt to models from two other nations before being adapted by a third nation's dataset. Our model does this by leveraging pre-trained convolutional neural networks in a unified structure that identifies road harm. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we collected and analyzed harm images from Australia, Canada, and the US, and conducted five experiments that exchanged models or datasets. Our results show that 2dTFA consistently achieves higher Adam L1 loss, MAE, and F1-score micro values compared to existing approaches, particularly when adapting to a third nation's dataset after being adapted by two other nations. Furthermore, 2dTFA achieved significantly higher F1-score micro values when comparing models that only exchanged data or adapted models. We also present an evaluation by experts of the selected models, along with presenting our dataset, structure, and results in detail. Ultimately, 2dTFA reduces the gap between local and transfered models by utilizing information from two other nations, making it easier to develop a universal harm identification model in a different country. We hope that this approach will contribute to saving more lives in a different country. The code for this structure, along with the dataset used in this study, can be found at the link at the end of this abstract. In contrast to existing approaches, 2dTFA reduces the gap between local and transferred models by leveraging two sources of information from other nations. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we collected and analyzed a large number of images from Australia, Canada, and the US, and conducted five experiments that exchanged models or datasets. Our results show that 2dTFA consistently achieves higher accuracy when adapting to a third nation's dataset after being adapted by two other nations. We also present an evaluation by experts of the selected models, along with presenting our structure, results, and dataset in detail. Ultimately, 2dTFA allows for a smoother transition between local and transferred models, making it easier to develop a universal harm identification model in a different country. The code for this structure, along with the dataset used in this study, can be found at the link at the end of this abstract.

We introduce an novel task called cross-domain mimicry, where from raw data in one domain, we mimic interventions in another domain without direct changes. This is demonstrated through a real-world application - cross-branch medical treatment recommendation. Given a patient's sensitive medical information in one branch of medicine, we observe how a therapist conducts an audit and achieves a desired outcome. Utilizing this information, we train a model that can generate effective treatments in a different branch of medicine. This trained model can then provide recommendations to unseen patient data in another branch, even without having seen the therapist's actions on this data. Our approach requires minimal supervision and successfully completes this complex task in an empirical setting. The code for this is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/plebani/cdm. The early stages of star formation in primordial clouds determine whether subsequent generations of stars will be born from planetesimal-driven or core-accretion protostar mergers, or from the more conventional stellar mergers.  Initially, massive (Population III) stars form through the same process, and the presence of magnetic fields can significantly impact the initial stages by limiting gas collapse and forming a disk.  Recent discoveries of exponential growth in primordial magnetic field strength could alter these predictions, and we investigate the effect of this field on a 20 M_sun Population III star using two-dimensional MHD simulations that incorporate the effects of self-gravity and radiative cooling.  The strength of this field reaches 30-40 mG, powerful enough to prevent the formation of a disk and instead propel mass away from the star's equator, reducing the initial mass loss by a factor of five.  The field lines collapse with the surrounding gas, preventing the formation of a distinct disk.  This change affects the typical properties of a Population III star's surrounding structure, and we find that the mass and energy carried by gas ejected from the star equator differ significantly from recent estimates.  The exponential growth in magnetic field strength could alter predictions for subsequent planetary and stellar formation processes by significantly altering the characteristics of a Population III star's surrounding structure.

Our analysis shows that the confidence level is affected by the number of shared items in transactions, while the implication factor is influenced by the total number of shared items among distinct transaction groups. Unlike previous studies, our team comprised researchers from diverse backgrounds, including social workers, psychologists, and lawyers, to ensure a comprehensive exploration of the topic. Our analysis revealed that participation in therapy led to significant improvements in psychological well-being among incarcerated individuals. Notably, we observed variations in outcome according to the type of therapy, with certain forms of treatment yielding better results. Our review also explored the underlying factors contributing to these differences and suggested potential strategies to enhance the effectiveness of psychotherapy for this population. Ultimately, our findings indicate that the criminal justice system can play a constructive role in promoting the mental health of individuals within its system through the implementation of evidence-based therapeutic programs. Based on our conclusions, we propose key recommendations for further research and practice. Specifically, we suggest investigating the mechanisms driving differences in effectiveness among various treatment types and exploring the potential long-term impacts of these programs on mental health. Additionally, we propose that judges and policymakers consider the benefits of requiring incarcerated individuals to engage in therapy as a condition of their sentence, similar to fines or community service. Notably, the DP-HMM model achieved an accuracy score of 0.92 on the IEEE dataset, surpassing the state-of-the-art accuracy score of 0.80. Achieving complete data protection while ensuring data utility is an ongoing challenge in differential privacy research. The presentation focuses on an issue in one-sided differential privacy where an attacker can access protected data, given that nearby records contain sensitive information. The paper proposes a model to evaluate and fix privacy breaches using characterization-dependent privacy. The idea behind this approach is to increase the privacy when there's a high probability of sensitive information among selected records. The results indicate that using characterizations in releasing dependent data results in more stringent privacy restrictions and consequently, reduced data utility. However, with proper characterization selection, this framework can limit breaches and improve utility when records contain sensitive information. The benefits of this framework are observed in release examples involving dependent data such as event recordings and school data. Overall, the framework provides a way to address privacy breaches and is a crucial step in addressing the limited data utility issue in differential privacy research. Observations of stellar motions in the Milky Way's bulge have used megapixel images to select target stars, but existing studies have overlooked the inherent uncertainties associated with choosing these stars. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of "stellar threads," which were previously calculated from data from the Gaia DR2 and APOGEE-1 surveys without considering the potential variations in selection. We employed a model-based approach to re-examine the bulge's vertical structure and 2D velocity distribution at specific latitudes. We discovered that choosing fewer dots, representing different stages in the selection process, leads to reduced oscillations in the results, and that excluding some data points eliminates dependence on selection effects, yielding more stable outcomes. These 'optimal' sets show the bulge's velocity distribution peaks at 155 km/s with a full width at half maximum of 70 km/s, and reveal a 5% higher concentration of metal-rich stars at -8 degrees compared to -6 degrees. These results accurately match the observed vertical density distribution and point to a presence of metal-rich stars in the bulge's inner regions. We conclude that employing a model-based approach to analyze stellar data eliminates the need to dissect individual dots, instead using the complete dataset to achieve more reliable and stable outcomes. Moreover, we suggest reviewing the findings on the bulge's vertical structure and velocity profiles from earlier studies in light of these improved results. These outcomes also highlight the importance of utilizing more sophisticated techniques to fully utilize the vast datasets generated by future astronomical observations. We propose these methods will be crucial for efficiently analyzing and understanding the data from future astronomical observations. Key findings are summarized in the summary. We introduce two novel high-dimensional expansion theorems derived from Stein's method and covering techniques respectively. Our first proof utilizes a complex development of high-dimensional expansions, yielding a versatile approach to establishing such results in various contexts. Conversely, our second proof, based on a simpler form of covering, provides a more direct and efficient solution that often requires less technical assumptions. Our covering method can also serve as a general framework for other researchers to apply it as an alternative to Stein's method. To demonstrate the efficacy of our newly formulated high-dimensional expansion, we apply it to show the asymptotic independence of two random variables, a sum of independent random variables being indistinguishable from the mean, and a non-degenerate random variable. Additionally, we employ our high-dimensional expansion to provide a straightforward and efficient proof of a generalized version of D\"{o}bling's celebrated theorem. Furthermore, we apply our high-dimensional expansion to show that asymptotic independence holds for arbitrary sums of independent random variables that satisfy specific moment conditions. Our proof of this result is more straightforward and less technical than existing proofs requiring only the establishment of certain properties of the sum. Our high-dimensional expansion also enables the derivation of precise rate limits for the convergence of the distribution of a sum of independent random variables to a product of their expectations. We achieve this by leveraging our high-dimensional expansion to approximate the distribution of a sum of independent random variables using only the first two non-trivial moments of the sum. We also introduce novel high-dimensional expansions for random graphs and networks. We derive these expansions by applying our high-dimensional expansion to the set of all possible graphs or networks, thereby yielding expansions for specific graph or network characteristics such as the number of spanning trees, the maximum cut size, the chromatic number, the subgraph frequency distribution, and the distribution of small set coverages. We then employ these expansions to prove asymptotic results for random graphs and networks that involve sums of graph or network characteristics. We demonstrate the efficacy of our high-dimensional expansion by applying it to obtain precise estimates for the number of graphs that exhibit a specific property. We achieve this by approximating the distribution of the number of such graphs using only the first two non-trivial moments of this number. We also utilize our high-dimensional expansion to prove a generalized version of a celebrated result first established by Erdős and Rényi. Furthermore, we introduce a novel high-dimensional expansion for the bicolored random graph model. We derive this expansion by applying a novel form of high-dimensional expansion that takes into account the dependence between adjacent vertices.

We establish a link between the $\mathscr{L}$-invariants of a local Galois extension ($K|k$, $K$ a local field over a base field $k$) and the $p$-adic eigenspaces of Artin modules, effectively generalizing the existing work of Darmon-Rideau and Darmon-Vallis. Additionally, our work in Section 2 provides a novel interpretation of the $p$-adic $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of a local $\mathbb{Q}_p(\mu_{p-1})$ extension via Artin modules, which stems from the observations made by Darmon-Vallis. Section 3 focuses on computing the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant of the Galois group $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\mu_{p-1})/\mathbb{Q})$ using modular forms and a specific type of modular abstraction, as well as its connection to Artin modules, which is key to our argument. This computation, combined with the modularity theorem for certain $\mathbb{Q}(µ_{p-1})$-extensions, offers an alternative approach to Darmon-Vallis' existing results. Lastly, in Section 4, we derive explicit Artin module eigenspace descriptions for specific $\mathbb{Q}(\mu_{p-1})$-extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$, which originate from level-$p$ congruence subgroups of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{Z}_p)$. This section also connects the described subgroups to Darmon-Vallis' type 2C1 modules, which have proven useful in previous studies on $p$-adic abelian integrals. This work is heavily influenced by Darmon-Vallis' ongoing research. All computations presented in Sections 3 and 4 have been verified using the software package Magma. The effectiveness of machine learning (ML) depends on large datasets like train, validation, and test sets. Obtaining these datasets is a labor-intensive and resource-consuming process. Several issues can arise during data acquisition, such as data corruption, inconsistencies, and domain shift. These problems can be identified as data faults, affecting the performance of an ML model by distorting its predictions. To resolve these faults, a new approach is proposed, data troubleshooting, analogous to program debugging. Most current debugging techniques focus on models, overlooking the crucial role of data. An innovative data troubleshooting method based on the Shapley value is introduced, allowing the calculation of a data set's importance for prediction accuracy. This framework identifies problematic data sets, estimates their impact on accuracy, and pinpoints data faults, all within an end-to-end ML workflow. To demonstrate its efficacy, experiments were conducted using various datasets, and the framework shows promising results in a real-world scenario. Ultimately, this framework provides a significant contribution to the field of ML, enabling the data analyst to work collaboratively with the model developer by identifying data-related issues. The code for this research is available on GitHub at: https://github.com/datahuggingface/dashboards/tree/main/data_troubleshooting_with_SHAP. This research will be presented at the 2022 IEEE Conference on Big Data Conference, held in Washington D.C., USA. A shorter version of this research will be presented at the 2022 NeurIPS Workshop on Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence for Life Sciences, taking place in Orlando, Florida, USA. This research focuses on how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in the triangular antiferromagnet Mn$_3$Sn. A recent study demonstrated that a phase transition from a long-range incommensurate order to a long-range hexagonal structure under pressure could transform the anomalous Hall effect. Building on this discovery, our research applies the method of magnetic structure evaluation based on neutron diffraction to investigate the phase transition triggered by pressure. Similar to Mn$_3$Sn, increasing pressure transforms Eu$_3P$_2 and Eu$_3Ga$_2 from an incommensurate phase to a long-range hexagonal structure, resulting in a corresponding change in the anomalous Hall effect. Conversely, pressure's effect on the Hall effect can be reversed by altering the chemical composition, achieving the desired phenomenon without exceeding the critical pressure required for the phase transition. Ultimately, this composition adjustment achieves a long-range hexagonal structure at ambient pressure, resulting in a substantial Hall effect. A comprehensive analysis of trimerization's role reveals that regulating this process through pressure and composition can control the anomalous Hall effect. In digital content creation, hypergraphs offer a powerful framework for modeling relationships between data sets beyond simple pair-wise interactions. While graph algorithms have been successfully applied to hypergraph problems in the past, their findings are often limited to theoretical insights with little practical value. To address this discrepancy, we develop a novel hypergraph representation, incorporating guidance from existing graph-based restoration methods to facilitate effective reconstruction of damaged hypergraphs. Building on this framework, we introduce guided hypergraph restoration (GHR) as a practical approach to hypergraph repair, leveraging the guidance to ensure plausible results. Through both qualitative and quantitative analysis, we demonstrate the performance of GHR under various scenarios, highlighting its potential to improve current state-of-the-art hypergraph restoration methods. Furthermore, we release GHR as an open-source tool to facilitate future research in hypergraph restoration. This source code can be accessed through https://github.com/chenxi911/guidedHR. Experimental results indicate that GHR achieves superior reconstruction quality compared to existing methods, with a significant improvement of at least 10%. Notably, GHR outperforms state-of-the-art methods by up to 30% in multichannel image compression recovery. GHR also produces more authentic reconstruction by up to 20% compared to existing methods. GHR exhibits robust generalizability across various hypergraph repair scenarios, with reconstruction quality degradation of less than 10% even with double the original edge complexity. This exceptional performance is attributed to GHR's ability to provide guidance to existing graph-based restoration methods while ensuring the integrity of the hypergraph structure. As a result, GHR can be used to improve the reconstruction quality of numerous state-of-the-art hypergraph restoration methods, effectively bridging the theoretical and practical insights in hypergraph repair. Additionally, GHR can be employed in real-world applications such as hypergraph-based image restoration, hypergraph-based compressed sensing, and hypergraph-based semantic segmentation to ensure plausible reconstruction results. With its potential applications in various domains, GHR can contribute to advancing the field of hypergraph restoration. Text-based games present a difficult problem for AI, as existing solutions typically cap at around 50 moves per second. To resolve this, text game emulation has emerged as a promising approach. By representing game states as vectors and actions as discrete changes, environments can be easily duplicated and used to train advanced agents. However, current implementations have several limitations: they are slow, requiring several seconds to simulate a single move, or they sacrifice essential game features for faster processing. In this research, we introduce TextWorldExpress, a high-speed text game emulator capable of processing up to one million moves per second. To achieve this, we leveraged the advancements of modern hardware, including GPU and TPU acceleration, as well as several optimization strategies, such as the efficient use of cache and parallel data processing. In addition to exceeding previous performance benchmarks by three orders of magnitude, TextWorldExpress also outperforms existing text game benchmarks in terms of accuracy, as our evaluations demonstrate. Furthermore, TextWorldExpress's high-speed emulation enables the exploration of previously unexplored agent training durations, including lengthy training periods of days, weeks, or even months. While current agents do not fully utilize the potential of text game emulators, as their performance plateaus after training for around ten days, extensive future research could likely capitalize on text game emulators' unparalleled processing capabilities. As a result, text game emulators could become a key solution for resolving AI's challenging "text problem." The developed emulator is open-source and available for public use at https://github.com/banaue/textworldexpress. Related pre-compiled Docker containers are also available for convenience. In the future, we intend to expand TextWorldExpress to support additional game features, as well as adapt it for related problems, such as text-based data extraction tasks. To facilitate this, we will also establish a public challenge to attract additional researchers and create a text game benchmark suite that significantly surpasses current benchmarks in difficulty. The text game extraction task will be modeled after a complex real-world environment, where relevant information needs to be identified within vast text-based descriptions. In the spirit of transparency and public collaboration, the challenge details will be made publicly available at a later date. For now, we welcome any interested researchers to join this effort and contribute their expertise to this project. The text game extraction task presents an exciting opportunity for cross-domain research, as it combines the challenges of resolving uncertainty within ambiguous descriptions with the necessity of extracting relevant information from lengthy text passages. To succeed in this task, agents must possess exceptional abilities in text comprehension

To study non-resonant Higgs boson production in the 13 TeV LHC environment using the matrix element technique, we examine the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ process. By implementing this approach on simulated events, which are either two TeV Higgs boson decays or Drell-Yan productions tagged with three jets as triggers, we found significant separation between the two TeV Higgs boson decays and QCD backgrounds in the $m_{\textrm{bb}}$-$m_{\textrm{WW}}$ mass plane. However, the separation did not improve when using the $p_{\textrm{T}}$ of the leading tag jet as an additional discriminant. In a region with $500 < m_{\textrm{bb}} < 700$ GeV and $70 < m_{\textrm{WW}} < 100$ GeV, the matrix element technique achieved a signal purity of about $10^{-3}$, resulting in an observed yield of 0.16 events and an expected yield of 0.15 ± 0.06 statistical uncertainties. Furthermore, we found that the loss of signal efficiency and QCD background reduction were comparable to previous studies using multivariate analysis methods on the same process. Utilizing the matrix element technique allowed an order of magnitude reduction in QCD background on the Higgs boson pair measurement, providing roughly a 5% improvement in sensitivity. To completely eliminate the QCD background, the matrix element technique would need to be complemented by additional experimental inputs or kinematic constraints not available in this experiment. In addition to Higgs boson pair analysis, we investigated the utility of the matrix element technique on single Higgs boson production in association with a vector boson, finding that it did not improve the analysis outcome. However, this approach had a negative impact on the measured cross section when the matrix element region was computed using the candidate decays of the Higgs boson and the vector boson rather than just the Higgs boson. A turntable is an effective tool in visual photography and scanning, but its application is limited when the object in question isn't designed for rotation. In contrast, this research demonstrates that almost any object can be an effective turntable if moved around in an irregular shape, thereby facilitating 3D shape reconstruction through observation. A simple, low-latency method is proposed to training a neural network, which effectively utilizes irregular paths to accurately determine an object's 3D position, thereby supporting downstream tasks including material editing, object manipulation, and shape reconstruction. The primary advantage of this method lies in its capacity for autonomous data collection, thereby eliminating the need for an initial 3D model scan. The observed results reveal that the turntable approach can consistently outperform state-of-the-art object reconstruction methods, even when trained on unorganized point cloud data. Furthermore, this technique exhibits robustness in the face of limited supervision, which makes it particularly suitable for real-world applications. The code for this project is openly accessible on GitHub. In addition to the proposed method, an open-source dataset containing over 50 million images of everyday objects in their natural settings is also being made available as a public resource. This dataset, denoted as the "Unintended Turntable Dataset" (UTD), can serve multiple purposes, such as training object detection models and supporting downstream tasks mentioned above. Ultimately, the primary intention behind this research is to promote more effective autonomous data collection techniques that don't rely on expensive equipment or complex algorithms. The demonstrated results reveal that 3D shape reconstruction can be achieved through observed irregular movements, which has far-reaching implications across multiple domains. The proposed method also highlights the significance of autonomous data collection in deep learning, which can potentially be extended to other areas beyond object reconstruction. In particular, this technique can be adapted to various applications including but not limited to autonomous driving and navigation in irregular terrain. In conclusion, the main contribution of this research lies in the deployment of a turntable as a means of achieving 3D shape reconstruction using observed irregular movements, which has led to the establishment of a large-scale open dataset containing over 50 million images. In addition to supporting 3D shape reconstruction, the same approach can also be used in material editing, object manipulation, and other related tasks. The code for this project, as well as the UTD dataset itself, are being made available as public resources. In particular, the UTD dataset can be utilized for training models that require 3D shape information, which encompasses a range of object-related tasks

The power graph of a group is defined as the set of elements resulting from raising other elements to various positive powers. The proof of our degree estimate involves several complex concepts, including the Discrete Logarithm Problem, the Polya Enumeration Formula, and the transfer homomorphism. These tools yield approximate degree counts, but often yield exact degrees in the groups we examine. Conversely, some of our degree estimates remain precise, while others require further refinement. We employ both combinatorial and group-theoretic approaches to confirm our degree estimates. Ultimately, our power graph investigations seem to be novel in the literature, and so our methods and conclusions are likely analogous for other groups with similar characteristics. We hope our work will spur further research into power graphs and related problems. We pose an associated question: does every finite group have a power graph with bounded degree? We establish that finite groups with a power graph of degree two must have rank at most three. A key concept in decision theory, ambiguity quantifies the uncertainty associated with making decisions in the absence of complete information. This issue explores the measurement of ambiguity within the context of machine learning. We discuss existing methods for calculating ambiguity and outline key criteria for comparison, before evaluating and comparing different approaches through representative examples. Our analysis highlights the importance of ambiguity in mapping complex relationships between sensory input and behavior in biological systems, such as vision. Ultimately, we suggest future directions for research in this field. Specifically, we propose developing more sophisticated ambiguity metrics that take into account how output variables change in response to varying input conditions. We also suggest employing theoretical frameworks such as game theory to investigate the effect of ambiguity on decision-making performance. Furthermore, we encourage researchers to explore the role of ambiguity in shaping the structure of sensory information and how this, in turn, influences behavioral decisions. By pursuing these lines of inquiry, we believe that the study of ambiguity in machine learning can gain valuable insights from theoretical frameworks in cognitive science and decision theory. At the same time, incorporating elements from modern machine learning, decision theory, and game theory can make the study of ambiguity more relevant and useful in real-world applications. In particular, we propose that incorporating methods for handling ambiguity in decision-making processes can improve algorithmic performance in tasks such as active learning, reinforcement learning, and regression problems. In this research, we examine the complexity of solving the optimal policy for large-scale Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) by converting the problem into a sequence of linear equations with convex constraints. By approximating the constraints, we adapt the Generalized Minimum Residual (GMRES) method to this context. Considering that the relative error in approximating the constraints can be represented by two bounds, alpha and beta, we define an "a-b interval of convergence" for iterative methods. These bounds are reflected in the a-b GMRES algorithm, which iteratively tightens the interval until it converges to the optimal solution. We calculate the computational complexity of each iteration and propose an "early termination" approach to reduce unnecessary computations. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the a-b GMRES algorithm often requires fewer iterations than current state-of-the-art methods, particularly for large-scale MDPs. It is also revealed that the method is capable of delivering either interior or boundary solutions, which are verified to be optimal or near-optimal in the tested scenarios. Building upon these findings, we suggest a line search strategy to enhance the performance of the a-b GMRES method in finding the optimal policy. We validate the proposed algorithm through both theoretical analysis and numerical examples. Notably, the algorithm has passed the scrutiny of a rigorous bibliometric evaluation, which assesses the reliability of numerical results. The research is therefore confident in the findings, and the proposed algorithm is presented as an open-source solution on public repositories for public utilization. Using public data, we verify that the algorithm surpasses the performance of established methods in various applications, and we propose several directions for further investigation. Additionally, we provide a publicly accessible code at https://github.com/Jia-Weigong/abGMRES. This repository includes the implementation of the a-b GMRES algorithm, which can be used to solve both convex and concave MDPs in accordance with the specifications of extensive MDPs. Moreover, we provide a series of numerical examples that demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in a diverse range of scenarios. These examples encompass various applications, including the optimization of a real-world air conditioning model and a numerical examination of the solution space. In the examined cases, the a-b GMRES method consistently delivered results within a few iterations, and it often terminated after the first iteration when an early termination was implemented. For instance, when solving a problem with 180 decision states, the method required merely five iterations to find the optimal solution. To improve model robustness to label noise, several approaches have been proposed, but they all assume a global perspective on corruption. This has led to a gap in understanding how to effectively utilize regional information from data. In this research, we investigate under what conditions regional queries can enhance reliable entropy estimation. Our study reveals that baseline methods using free latent variables or pseudo-likelihood achieve the best results when data is evenly distributed across classes. However, these approaches significantly decline in performance on imbalanced datasets and in the presence of adversarial label corruption. Conversely, a real-time estimation of reliability-based entropy, developed in a previous study, performs well on diverse datasets but poorly on datasets with significant class skewness. On the other hand, a novel hybrid approach combining global and regional features offers superior robust learning performance when data is skewed towards certain classes. Therefore, our findings indicate that regional queries offer beneficial insights for robust learning, particularly in scenarios involving skewed datasets and class skewness. We validate these conclusions through comprehensive experiments on synthetic datasets, as well as by applying our research to real-world image classification challenges with label corruption. The proposed research is a fundamental contribution to the field of robust machine learning, aiming to bridge the existing knowledge gap in this area.
